abstract: We have mathematically shown that cortical maps in the primary sensory cortices can be reproduced by using three hypotheses which have physiological basis and meaning. Here, our main focus is on ocular.dominance column formation in the primary visual cortex. Monte Carlo simulations on the segregation of ipsilateral and contralateral afferent terminals are carried out. Based on these, we show that almost all the physiological experimental results concerning the ocular dominance patterns of cats and monkeys reared under normal or various abnormal visual conditions can be explained from a viewpoint of the phase transition phenomena. (2) Synapses also sprout or retract according to the concurrence of presynaptic spike activity and postsynaptic local membrane depolarization. paragraphs: The paper develops a mathematical account of how organized sensory maps can emerge through changes in neural connections. Its main example is the formation of ocular dominance columns, where inputs associated with the two eyes become spatially organized in primary visual cortex. The authors treat this organization as a process arising from interacting physiological mechanisms.

Three hypotheses drive the model: synapses compete for trophic factors, their growth or retraction depends on coincident presynaptic activity and postsynaptic depolarization, and lateral connections exist before modification begins. Coupled equations describe electrical activity and connection density. Because electrical activity changes much faster than synapses grow or retract, the analysis uses an approximation that separates those time scales.

Monte Carlo simulations examine the segregation of inputs from the two sides. The authors report that a phase-transition interpretation explains almost all the physiological findings they consider for cats and monkeys raised under normal or abnormal visual conditions. The result connects local rules for synaptic change with large-scale cortical patterns and their dependence on visual experience.
summary.tldr: A physiologically motivated model explains ocular dominance pattern formation through synaptic competition, activity-dependent change, and phase-transition behavior.

title: Theory of Self-Organization of Cortical Maps
Speech Recognition: Statistical and Neural Information Processing Approaches

abstract: We would like to incorporate speaker-dependent consistencies, such as gender, in an otherwise speaker-independent speech recognition system. In this paper we discuss a Gender Dependent Neural Network (GDNN) which can be tuned for each gender, while sharing most of the speaker independent parameters. We use a classification network to help generate gender-dependent phonetic probabilities for a statistical (HMM) recogni(cid:173) tion system. The gender classification net predicts the gender with high accuracy, 98.3% on a Resource Management test set. However, the in(cid:173) tegration of the GDNN into our hybrid HMM-neural network recognizer provided an improvement in the recognition score that is not statistically significant on a Resource Management test set.

paragraphs: This paper investigates whether a speech recognizer can use speaker-related consistency while retaining a largely speaker-independent model. It focuses on gender as the conditioning variable. The proposed Gender Dependent Neural Network can be tuned for each gender while sharing most of its parameters across speakers, combining specialization with a common recognition model.

A classification network helps generate gender-dependent probabilities for speech sounds. These probabilities feed a statistical recognizer based on a hidden Markov model, making the method part of a hybrid neural-network and HMM system. The intended benefit is to incorporate a persistent speaker characteristic into the probabilities used for recognizing continuous speech.

The gender classifier achieves 98.3% accuracy on a Resource Management test set. However, integrating the gender-dependent network produces a recognition-score improvement that is not statistically significant on that test set. The findings separate two outcomes: the system can predict the conditioning category accurately, but that success does not establish a reliable improvement in the final speech-recognition task.
summary.tldr: Gender-conditioned speech modeling achieves accurate gender classification but no statistically significant improvement in overall recognition.

title: Modeling Consistency in a Speaker Independent Continuous Speech Recognition System

abstract: While exploring to find better solutions, an agent performing on(cid:173) line reinforcement learning (RL) can perform worse than is accept(cid:173) able. In some cases, exploration might have unsafe, or even catas(cid:173) trophic, results, often modeled in terms of reaching 'failure' states of the agent's environment. This paper presents a method that uses domain knowledge to reduce the number of failures during explo(cid:173) ration. This method formulates the set of actions from which the RL agent composes a control policy to ensure that exploration is conducted in a policy space that excludes most of the unacceptable policies. The resulting action set has a more abstract relationship to the task being solved than is common in many applications of RL. Although the cost of this added safety is that learning may result in a suboptimal solution, we argue that this is an appropri(cid:173) ate tradeoff in many problems. We illustrate this method in the domain of motion planning. "'This work was done while the first author was finishing his Ph.D in computer science at the University of Massachusetts, Amherst.

paragraphs: The paper addresses a difficulty in online reinforcement learning: an agent can behave unacceptably while exploring. In motion planning, reaching a failure state may carry consequences that make unrestricted experimentation unsuitable. The authors propose using domain knowledge to reduce failures during the learning process.

Their method changes the actions available to the agent. These actions have a more abstract relationship to the task than is typical, and their construction limits the control policies the learner can assemble. By shaping this policy space, the method excludes most unacceptable policies before exploration proceeds. Safety is therefore partly built into the choices from which behavior is composed.

The paper explicitly recognizes the cost of this restriction: the learner may arrive at a suboptimal solution because some policies are unavailable. It argues that fewer failures can justify this loss of optimality and illustrates the method in motion planning. The contribution is a concrete tradeoff between exploration freedom and acceptable behavior, using task knowledge to shape learning.
summary.tldr: Domain-informed action sets reduce failures during reinforcement-learning exploration, at the possible cost of a suboptimal final policy.

title: Robust Reinforcement Learning in Motion Planning

paragraphs: The paper asks how a network with many hidden units can still generalize well. For two-layer networks with sigmoidal hidden units, it derives a generalization-error bound involving expected network complexity, input dimension, and the number of training examples. Complexity is expressed through a random hidden-unit count bounded by the network's available units.

The distribution of that count is determined by a prior over network weights. The authors connect this prior to a Gibbs distribution associated with a regularizer. This relationship makes it possible to describe explicitly how the regularization term affects the network's balance between bias and variance.

The bound can be obtained analytically for a broad class of commonly used priors and can also help estimate expected complexity in practice. Its central implication is that the total number of available hidden units does not by itself settle the generalization question. The way regularization shapes expected complexity provides a quantitative explanation for why a large network can nevertheless predict well beyond its training data.
summary.tldr: A generalization bound links regularization to expected network complexity, helping explain why large networks can generalize well.

title: Generalization Error and the Expected Network Complexity

abstract: A central theme of computational vision research has been the re(cid:173) alization that reliable estimation of local scene properties requires propagating measurements across the image. Many authors have therefore suggested solving vision problems using architectures of locally connected units updating their activity in parallel. Unfor(cid:173) tunately, the convergence of traditional relaxation methods on such architectures has proven to be excruciatingly slow and in general they do not guarantee that the stable point will be a global mini(cid:173) mum. In this paper we show that an architecture in which Bayesian Be(cid:173) liefs about image properties are propagated between neighboring units yields convergence times which are several orders of magni(cid:173) tude faster than traditional methods and avoids local minima. In particular our architecture is non-iterative in the sense of Marr [5]: at every time step, the local estimates at a given location are op(cid:173) timal given the information which has already been propagated to that location. We illustrate the algorithm's performance on real images and compare it to several existing methods.

paragraphs: Estimating a scene property at one image location often requires measurements from elsewhere in the image. Locally connected processing units offer a way to spread this information in parallel. Traditional relaxation methods, however, can converge very slowly and may settle at solutions that are not globally best.

The proposed architecture passes Bayesian beliefs about image properties between neighboring units. Its defining property is that each location's estimate is optimal given the information that has reached it so far. The authors describe this as non-iterative: incoming information expands the basis for an estimate, rather than requiring the same local computation to gradually relax toward a solution.

The paper reports convergence several orders of magnitude faster than traditional methods and avoidance of local minima within the presented architecture. Performance is illustrated on real images and compared with existing approaches. The contribution ties the way information travels across an image to the quality of intermediate estimates, making propagation itself the organizing principle of inference.
summary.tldr: Propagating Bayesian beliefs between neighboring image locations yields locally optimal intermediate estimates and much faster reported convergence.

title: Interpreting Images by Propagating Bayesian Beliefs

abstract: We present a method for learning complex appearance mappings. such as occur with images of articulated objects. Traditional interpolation networks fail on this case since appearance is not necessarily a smooth function nor a linear manifold for articulated objects. We define an ap(cid:173) pearance mapping from examples by constructing a set of independently smooth interpolation networks; these networks can cover overlapping re(cid:173) gions of parameter space. A set growing procedure is used to find ex(cid:173) ample clusters which are well-approximated within their convex hull; interpolation then proceeds only within these sets of examples. With this method physically valid images are produced even in regions of param(cid:173) eter space where nearby examples have different appearances. We show results generating both simulated and real arm images.

paragraphs: Generating images of articulated objects from examples is difficult because nearby configurations need not have smoothly changing appearances. A single interpolation model can therefore combine examples in inappropriate ways. This paper addresses the problem by learning several independently smooth appearance mappings, each responsible for a suitable set of examples.

A set-growing procedure identifies clusters that can be approximated well within their convex hull, the region spanned by combinations of those examples. Interpolation is restricted to these accepted sets. The networks may cover overlapping parts of the parameter space, so the method does not require one exclusive partition or one smooth mapping for every possible configuration.

The authors demonstrate the approach with both simulated and real arm images. They report physically valid outputs even where nearby examples look different. The central contribution is a way to decide which examples can safely be interpolated together. This preserves the usefulness of smooth interpolation while accommodating the more complicated appearance changes produced by articulated figures.
summary.tldr: Overlapping local interpolation models generate valid articulated-object images where a single smooth appearance model would fail.

title: Example-Based Image Synthesis of Articulated Figures

abstract: We present a model of binding of relationship information in a spatial domain (e.g., square above triangle) that uses low-order coarse-coded conjunctive representations instead of more popular temporal synchrony mechanisms. Supporters of temporal synchrony argue that conjunctive representations lack both efficiency (i.e., combinatorial numbers of units are required) and systematicity (i.e., the resulting representations are overly specific and thus do not support generalization to novel exemplars). To counter these claims, we show that our model: a) uses far fewer hidden units than the number of conjunctions represented, by using coarse-coded, distributed representations where each unit has a broad tuning curve through high-dimensional conjunction space, and b) is capable of considerable generalization to novel inputs.

paragraphs: The paper studies how a model can represent relationships between objects, such as a square being above a triangle. Its approach uses low-order conjunctive representations, which encode combinations of information. The authors address two criticisms of such representations: that they require too many units and that they become too specific to generalize to unfamiliar inputs.

The model uses coarse coding and distributed representations. Each hidden unit responds broadly across a space of possible conjunctions, so the representation of a relationship is spread across units rather than requiring a dedicated unit for every combination. This is the mechanism offered for representing many conjunctions with relatively few hidden units.

The authors show that their model uses far fewer hidden units than the number of conjunctions it represents and achieves considerable generalization to novel inputs. These findings counter the claimed efficiency and generalization problems for this model. They demonstrate a viable way to bind relational information without relying on the temporal synchrony mechanisms discussed as an alternative.
summary.tldr: Distributed, broadly tuned conjunctive representations encode spatial relationships with relatively few units and generalize considerably to novel inputs.

title: Generalizable Relational Binding from Coarse-coded Distributed Representations

abstract: We consider the general problem of utilizing both labeled and un(cid:173) labeled data to improve classification accuracy. Under t he assump(cid:173) tion that the data lie on a submanifold in a high dimensional space, we develop an algorithmic framework to classify a partially labeled data set in a principled manner . The central idea of our approach is that classification functions are naturally defined only on t he sub(cid:173) manifold in question rather than the total ambient space. Using the Laplace Beltrami operator one produces a basis for a Hilbert space of square integrable functions on the submanifold. To recover such a basis , only unlab eled examples are required. Once a basis is ob(cid:173) tained , training can be performed using the labeled data set. Our algorithm models the manifold using the adjacency graph for the data and approximates the Laplace Beltrami operator by the graph Laplacian. Practical applications to image and text classification are considered.

paragraphs: The paper develops a classification framework that uses both labeled and unlabeled examples. Its central assumption is that the data lie on a submanifold within a high-dimensional space. Under that assumption, the classifier is naturally defined on the lower-dimensional structure occupied by the data, making that structure the domain of the learning problem.

The Laplace–Beltrami operator supplies a basis for square-integrable functions on the manifold. Unlabeled examples are sufficient to recover such a basis, after which labeled examples train the classifier. This gives the two kinds of data distinct roles: unlabeled observations reveal the geometry used to represent functions, while labels determine the classification behavior within that representation.

For computation, the method represents the manifold using an adjacency graph of the data and approximates the continuous operator with a graph Laplacian. The paper considers applications to image and text classification. Its contribution is a principled connection between the manifold assumption and a practical learning procedure, showing how unlabeled observations can contribute a function space in which supervised training takes place.
summary.tldr: Assuming data lie on a manifold, the method uses unlabeled examples to construct a graph-based function basis and labeled examples to train a classifier.

title: Using Manifold Stucture for Partially Labeled Classification

abstract: In this paper we propose an efficient algorithm for reducing a large mixture of Gaussians into a smaller mixture while still preserv- ing the component structure of the original model; this is achieved by clustering (grouping) the components. The method minimizes a new, easily computed distance measure between two Gaussian mixtures that can be motivated from a suitable stochastic model and the iterations of the algorithm use only the model parameters, avoiding the need for explicit resampling of datapoints. We demon- strate the method by performing hierarchical clustering of scenery images and handwritten digits.

The method minimizes a new, easily computed distance measure between two Gaussian mixtures that can be motivated from a suitable stochastic model and the iterations of the algorithm use only the model parameters, avoiding the need for explicit resampling of datapoints. paragraphs: A large Gaussian mixture represents a distribution through many component distributions. This paper asks how to replace that model with a smaller mixture while preserving its component structure. The proposed approach groups the original components, making model reduction itself a clustering problem.

The algorithm minimizes a new distance measure between Gaussian mixtures. That measure is easy to compute and has a motivation based on a suitable stochastic model. Crucially, each iteration operates directly on the mixture's parameters. The procedure therefore avoids explicitly drawing a new set of data points from the model to carry out the reduction.

The authors demonstrate the method through hierarchical clustering of scenery images and handwritten digits. These applications show how grouping components can produce progressively coarser organization while working with an existing probabilistic representation. The central contribution is an efficient route from a detailed mixture to a smaller one, using a computationally accessible objective and parameter-based updates to retain the original model's component organization.
summary.tldr: The paper reduces Gaussian mixtures by clustering their components using an easily computed distance and updates that require no explicit data resampling.

title: Hierarchical Clustering of a Mixture Model

abstract: Capturing dependencies in images in an unsupervised manner is important for many image processing applications. We propose a new method for capturing nonlinear dependencies in images of natural scenes. This method is an extension of the linear Independent Component Analysis (ICA) method by building a hierarchical model based on ICA and mixture of Laplacian distribution. The model parameters are learned via an EM algorithm and it can accurately capture variance correlation and other high order structures in a simple manner. We visualize the learned variance structure and demonstrate applications to image segmentation and denoising.

We propose a new method for capturing nonlinear dependencies in images of natural scenes. This method is an extension of the linear Independent Component Analysis (ICA) method by building a hierarchical model based on ICA and mixture of Laplacian distribution. The model parameters are learned via an EM algorithm and it can accurately capture variance correlation and other high order structures in a simple manner. We visualize the learned variance structure and demonstrate applications to image segmentation and denoising.

paragraphs: The paper develops an unsupervised model for nonlinear dependencies in natural-scene images. Its starting point is linear independent component analysis, which the authors extend through a hierarchy incorporating a mixture of Laplacian distributions. The objective is to represent image structure beyond what the original linear model captures.

The model's parameters are learned using expectation-maximization. The authors report that this construction accurately captures variance correlations and other higher-order structure in a simple way. Variance correlations concern relationships in how component variability changes, giving the model a way to describe dependencies beyond the components' individual behavior.

The paper visualizes the learned variance structure and demonstrates the model in image segmentation and denoising. These applications connect the statistical representation to concrete image-processing tasks. The contribution is both a model of nonlinear image dependencies and a demonstration that its learned structure can be used in those tasks, with the reported accuracy claim referring to its capture of image statistics.
summary.tldr: A hierarchical ICA model with Laplacian mixtures captures nonlinear image dependencies and is demonstrated in segmentation and denoising.

title: Modeling Nonlinear Dependencies in Natural Images using Mixture of Laplacian Distribution

abstract: We argue that when objects are characterized by many attributes, clustering them on the basis of a relatively small random subset of these attributes can capture information on the unobserved attributes as well. Moreover, we show that under mild technical conditions, clustering the objects on the basis of such a random subset performs almost as well as clustering with the full attribute set. We prove a finite sample generalization theorems for this novel learning scheme that extends analogous results from the supervised learning setting. The scheme is demonstrated for collaborative filtering of users with movies rating as attributes.

We prove a finite sample generalization theorems for this novel learning scheme that extends analogous results from the supervised learning setting. The scheme is demonstrated for collaborative filtering of users with movies rating as attributes.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether clustering objects using only some of their attributes can reveal meaningful structure in attributes that were never observed. The setting involves objects described by many attributes, with clustering performed on a relatively small random subset. The desired generalization is therefore across attributes, rather than simply to additional objects.

The authors show that, under mild technical conditions, clustering from this random subset performs almost as well as clustering from the full attribute collection. They establish finite-sample generalization theorems for this learning scheme, extending analogous ideas from supervised learning. The random selection of attributes and the stated technical conditions are part of the setting supporting that conclusion.

A collaborative-filtering demonstration treats users as objects and movie ratings as attributes. In this setting, the result concerns whether groupings based on some ratings can capture information about other ratings. The paper gives theoretical support for learning useful group structure from partial attribute information, alongside an application illustrating what generalization to unobserved features means.
summary.tldr: Under mild technical conditions, clustering on a small random subset of attributes performs almost as well as using all attributes.

title: Generalization in Clustering with Unobserved Features

abstract: Generalized linear models are the most commonly used tools to describe the stim- ulus selectivity of sensory neurons. Here we present a Bayesian treatment of such models. Using the expectation propagation algorithm, we are able to approximate the full posterior distribution over all weights. In addition, we use a Laplacian prior to favor sparse solutions. Therefore, stimulus features that do not critically inﬂuence neural activity will be assigned zero weights and thus be effectively excluded by the model. This feature selection mechanism facilitates both the in- terpretation of the neuron model as well as its predictive abilities. The posterior distribution can be used to obtain conﬁdence intervals which makes it possible to assess the statistical signiﬁcance of the solution. In neural data analysis, the available amount of experimental measurements is often limited whereas the pa- rameter space is large. In such a situation, both regularization by a sparsity prior and uncertainty estimates for the model parameters are essential. We apply our method to multi-electrode recordings of retinal ganglion cells and use our uncer- tainty estimate to test the statistical signiﬁcance of functional couplings between neurons. Furthermore we used the sparsity of the Laplace prior to select those ﬁlters from a spike-triggered covariance analysis that are most informative about the neural response.

paragraphs: Models of neural responses often have many possible stimulus features but relatively few experimental observations. This paper gives generalized linear models of spiking neurons a Bayesian treatment that addresses both feature selection and uncertainty. Instead of reporting only fitted weights, the method approximates the posterior distribution over all weights using expectation propagation.

A Laplacian prior favors sparse solutions, helping exclude features that do not critically influence neural activity. This makes the resulting model easier to interpret and supports prediction. The posterior also supplies uncertainty intervals, allowing the authors to assess the statistical significance of estimated effects rather than treating every fitted relationship as equally well supported.

The authors apply the method to recordings from multiple retinal ganglion cells and use parameter uncertainty to evaluate functional couplings between neurons. They also use sparsity to select informative filters from a spike-triggered covariance analysis. Together, these applications show how selecting a smaller set of features and quantifying uncertainty can support neural analysis when observations are limited relative to model size.
summary.tldr: Bayesian spiking-neuron models combine sparse feature selection with uncertainty estimates to interpret stimulus responses and functional couplings.

title: Bayesian Inference for Spiking Neuron Models with a Sparsity Prior

abstract: This paper describes a new model for human visual classification that enables the recovery of image features that explain human subjects' performance on different visual classification tasks. Unlike previous methods, this algorithm does not model their performance with a single linear classifier operating on raw image pixels. Instead, it models classification as the combination of multiple feature detectors. This approach extracts more information about human visual classification than has been previously possible with other methods and provides a foundation for further exploration.

paragraphs: GRIFT studies visual classification by asking which image features can explain human performance. Its goal is to recover those features from human data across different classification tasks. This makes the model a tool for investigating the information people use when making visual judgments, as reflected in their observed task performance.

The central modeling choice is to combine multiple feature detectors. Earlier methods represented performance through a single linear classifier acting directly on image pixels. Allowing several detectors gives the model a way to describe classification as the combined contribution of distinct features, rather than compressing the explanation into one linear pixel-based decision.

The authors report that this approach extracts more information about human visual classification than previous methods. The significance lies in the richer explanation it can recover from behavioral data: multiple detected features can contribute to the account of performance. The paper presents this model as a foundation for further exploration of visual classification, with feature recovery as its central contribution.
summary.tldr: GRIFT models human visual decisions through multiple feature detectors to recover richer explanations of classification performance from behavioral data.

title: GRIFT: A graphical model for inferring visual classification features from human data

abstract: In this paper, we address the question of what kind of knowledge is generally transferable from unlabeled text. We suggest and analyze the semantic correlation of words as a generally transferable structure of the language and propose a new method to learn this structure using an appropriately chosen latent variable model. This semantic correlation contains structural information of the language space and can be used to control the joint shrinkage of model parameters for any specific task in the same space through regularization. In an empirical study, we construct 190 different text classification tasks from a real-world benchmark, and the unlabeled documents are a mixture from all these tasks. We test the ability of various algorithms to use the mixed unlabeled text to enhance all classification tasks. Empirical results show that the proposed approach is a reliable and scalable method for semi-supervised learning, regardless of the source of unlabeled data, the specific task to be enhanced, and the prediction model used.

Empirical results show that the proposed approach is a reliable and scalable method for semi-supervised learning, regardless of the source of unlabeled data, the specific task to be enhanced, and the prediction model used.

paragraphs: Unlabeled text can come from many different tasks, raising the question of what knowledge remains useful across them. This paper proposes semantic correlations between words as transferable structure. The goal is to extract relationships in the language space that can help a particular prediction task even when the unlabeled collection mixes several sources.

The authors learn these correlations with a latent-variable model. They then use the learned structure in regularization, controlling how model parameters are shrunk together for a target task. In this approach, unlabeled documents contribute relationships that guide supervised learning rather than needing to correspond exclusively to the target classification problem.

The empirical study constructs 190 text-classification tasks from a real-world benchmark and mixes their unlabeled documents. It compares how algorithms use this shared pool to improve the individual tasks. Results support the proposed method as reliable and scalable across the tested data sources, tasks, and prediction models. This breadth of empirical support is the basis for its claim of generally transferable language structure.
summary.tldr: Semantic word correlations learned from mixed unlabeled text guide regularization across many classification tasks.

title: Learning the Semantic Correlation: An Alternative Way to Gain from Unlabeled Text

abstract: We address the problem of learning classifiers when observations have multiple views, some of which may not be observed for all examples. We assume the existence of view generating functions which may complete the missing views in an approximate way. This situation corresponds for example to learning text classifiers from multilingual collections where documents are not available in all languages. In that case, Machine Translation (MT) systems may be used to translate each document in the missing languages. We derive a generalization error bound for classifiers learned on examples with multiple artificially created views. Our result uncovers a trade-off between the size of the training set, the number of views, and the quality of the view generating functions. As a consequence, we identify situations where it is more interesting to use multiple views for learning instead of classical single view learning. An extension of this framework is a natural way to leverage unlabeled multi-view data in semi-supervised learning. Experimental results on a subset of the Reuters RCV1/RCV2 collections support our findings by showing that additional views obtained from MT may significantly improve the classification performance in the cases identified by our trade-off.

paragraphs: The paper studies classification when examples have several possible views, but some views are missing. It assumes that view-generating functions can approximately supply the missing information. Multilingual document classification provides the motivating example: a document may exist in only some languages, while machine translation can generate versions in others.

The authors derive a generalization-error bound for classifiers trained with these artificially created views. The bound reveals a trade-off involving the amount of training data, the number of views, and the quality of the functions that generate them. Consequently, additional views are beneficial in particular circumstances identified by the analysis, rather than being automatically useful whenever they can be created.

Experiments on a subset of Reuters RCV1/RCV2 support this trade-off: translated views may significantly improve classification in the identified cases. The framework also extends naturally to semi-supervised learning with unlabeled multiview data. The result gives a theoretical basis for judging when approximate additional representations can strengthen a classifier.
summary.tldr: A generalization bound identifies when approximately generated views, such as machine translations, can improve classification.

title: Learning from Multiple Partially Observed Views - an Application to Multilingual Text Categorization

abstract: We present the Copula Bayesian Network model for representing multivariate continuous distributions. Our approach builds on a novel copula-based parameterization of a conditional density that, joined with a graph that encodes independencies, offers great flexibility in modeling high-dimensional densities, while maintaining control over the form of the univariate marginals. We demonstrate the advantage of our framework for generalization over standard Bayesian networks as well as tree structured copula models for varied real-life domains that are of substantially higher dimension than those typically considered in the copula literature.
originalAbstract: We present the Copula Bayesian Network model for representing multivariate continuous distributions. Our approach builds on a novel copula-based parameterization of a conditional density that, joined with a graph that encodes independencies, offers great flexibility in modeling high-dimensional densities, while maintaining control over the form of the univariate marginals. We demonstrate the advantage of our framework for generalization over standard Bayesian networks as well as tree structured copula models for varied real-life domains that are of substantially higher dimension than those typically considered in the copula literature.

paragraphs: The paper presents Copula Bayesian Networks, a model for probability distributions involving many continuous variables. The challenge is to describe how variables depend on one another while retaining control over the distribution of each variable individually. Those individual distributions are the univariate marginals, and the proposed framework keeps their form manageable while allowing flexible joint behavior.

The model combines a new copula-based representation of conditional densities with a graph that records independence relationships. These components play complementary roles: the graph expresses which dependencies the model needs to represent, while the conditional density representation supplies flexibility in describing them. Together, they provide a way to model high-dimensional continuous data without giving up control over individual-variable distributions.

The authors report better generalization than standard Bayesian networks and tree-structured copula models across varied real-world domains. The evaluated domains have substantially more dimensions than those typically considered in the copula literature described by the paper. The findings support the framework as a way to bring flexible dependence modeling to larger multivariate problems.
summary.tldr: Copula Bayesian Networks combine graphical independence structure with flexible continuous densities and show improved generalization in high-dimensional real-world domains.

title: Copula Bayesian Networks

abstract: All the existing multi-task local learning methods are defined on homogeneous neighborhood which consists of all data points from only one task. In this paper, different from existing methods, we propose local learning methods for multi-task classification and regression problems based on heterogeneous neighborhood which is defined on data points from all tasks. Specifically, we extend the k-nearest-neighbor classifier by formulating the decision function for each data point as a weighted voting among the neighbors from all tasks where the weights are task-specific. By defining a regularizer to enforce the task-specific weight matrix to approach a symmetric one, a regularized objective function is proposed and an efficient coordinate descent method is developed to solve it. For regression problems, we extend the kernel regression to multi-task setting in a similar way to the classification case. Experiments on some toy data and real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed methods.
originalAbstract: All the existing multi-task local learning methods are defined on homogeneous neighborhood which consists of all data points from only one task. In this paper, different from existing methods, we propose local learning methods for multi-task classification and regression problems based on heterogeneous neighborhood which is defined on data points from all tasks. Specifically, we extend the k-nearest-neighbor classifier by formulating the decision function for each data point as a weighted voting among the neighbors from all tasks where the weights are task-specific. By defining a regularizer to enforce the task-specific weight matrix to approach a symmetric one, a regularized objective function is proposed and an efficient coordinate descent method is developed to solve it. For regression problems, we extend the kernel regression to multi-task setting in a similar way to the classification case. Experiments on some toy data and real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed methods.

paragraphs: Local learning predicts an outcome from nearby data points. The paper asks how this idea should work when several tasks are learned together. It departs from neighborhoods containing examples from only one task and instead forms neighborhoods using data points from all tasks, creating a direct route for sharing information locally.

For classification, the authors extend the k-nearest-neighbor rule so that neighbors from different tasks contribute through task-specific voting weights. They introduce a regularizer that encourages the task-weight matrix to be close to symmetric, and develop an efficient coordinate descent algorithm for the resulting objective. The weighting mechanism lets contributions depend on task relationships rather than treating all neighboring points identically.

For regression, the paper extends kernel regression using the same general strategy of neighborhoods spanning tasks. Experiments on toy data and real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed methods. The contribution is a way to combine the local character of neighborhood prediction with explicit, learned weighting of information from multiple tasks.
summary.tldr: The proposed classification and regression methods share information through neighborhoods spanning multiple tasks, using task-specific weights.

title: Heterogeneous-Neighborhood-based Multi-Task Local Learning Algorithms

abstract: We investigate the problem of learning the structure of a Markov network from data. It is shown that the structure of such networks can be described in terms of constraints which enables the use of existing solver technology with optimization capabilities to compute optimal networks starting from initial scores computed from the data. To achieve efficient encodings, we develop a novel characterization of Markov network structure using a balancing condition on the separators between cliques forming the network. The resulting translations into propositional satisfiability and its extensions such as maximum satisfiability, satisfiability modulo theories, and answer set programming, enable us to prove the optimality of networks which have been previously found by stochastic search.

It is shown that the structure of such networks can be described in terms of constraints which enables the use of existing solver technology with optimization capabilities to compute optimal networks starting from initial scores computed from the data. To achieve efficient encodings, we develop a novel characterization of Markov network structure using a balancing condition on the separators between cliques forming the network. The resulting translations into propositional satisfiability and its extensions such as maximum satisfiability, satisfiability modulo theories, and answer set programming, enable us to prove the optimality of networks which have been previously found by stochastic search.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to learn the structure of chordal Markov networks from data. The authors express network structure through logical constraints, allowing existing optimization-capable solvers to search for an optimal network. The process starts from scores computed from the data and combines those scores with constraints defining admissible structures.

The key technical contribution is a characterization based on a balancing condition involving separators between the network's cliques. This characterization supports efficient encodings of the structural requirements. The paper translates the learning problem into propositional satisfiability and related formalisms, including maximum satisfiability, satisfiability modulo theories, and answer set programming.

These translations do more than provide another way to search for networks: they enable proofs of optimality for networks previously found through stochastic search. Finding a high-scoring candidate and establishing that no better admissible candidate exists are distinct achievements. The work shows how a carefully designed structural encoding can connect statistical network learning to solver technology that supplies the latter kind of assurance.
summary.tldr: A constraint-based encoding lets optimization solvers learn chordal Markov networks and certify the optimality of previously discovered structures.

title: Learning Chordal Markov Networks by Constraint Satisfaction

abstract: Transfer learning algorithms are used when one has sufficient training data for one supervised learning task (the source/training domain) but only very limited training data for a second task (the target/test domain) that is similar but not identical to the first. Previous work on transfer learning has focused on relatively restricted settings, where specific parts of the model are considered to be carried over between tasks. Recent work on covariate shift focuses on matching the marginal distributions on observations $X$ across domains. Similarly, work on target/conditional shift focuses on matching marginal distributions on labels $Y$ and adjusting conditional distributions $P(X|Y)$, such that $P(X)$ can be matched across domains. However, covariate shift assumes that the support of test $P(X)$ is contained in the support of training $P(X)$, i.e., the training set is richer than the test set. Target/conditional shift makes a similar assumption for $P(Y)$. Moreover, not much work on transfer learning has considered the case when a few labels in the test domain are available. Also little work has been done when all marginal and conditional distributions are allowed to change while the changes are smooth. In this paper, we consider a general case where both the support and the model change across domains. We transform both $X$ and $Y$ by a location-scale shift to achieve transfer between tasks. Since we allow more flexible transformations, the proposed method yields better results on both synthetic data and real-world data.

paragraphs: Transfer learning uses a well-supplied source task to help a related target task with little labeled data. The paper examines cases where the domains differ more broadly than standard transfer assumptions allow. In particular, the target may contain values outside the source distribution's support, and the relationships between observations and labels may also change.

The authors discuss restrictions in covariate-shift and target-shift approaches, including assumptions that the source covers the target's relevant support. They consider a more flexible setting with limited target labels and smooth changes across distributions. Their method transforms both observations X and labels Y through location-scale shifts, allowing changes in where values lie and how they are scaled.

Transforming both sides of the supervised problem gives the method flexibility to handle changes in support as well as changes in the model. The authors report better results on synthetic and real-world data with these transformations. The findings support this particular approach to broader domain differences, while its stated mechanism remains the use of location-scale transformations.
summary.tldr: Location-scale transformations of both observations and labels enable transfer learning when domain support and model relationships change.

title: Flexible Transfer Learning under Support and Model Shift

abstract: This paper addresses the problem of $mz$-transportability, that is, transferring causal knowledge collected in several heterogeneous domains to a target domain in which only passive observations and limited experimental data can be collected. The paper first establishes a necessary and sufficient condition for deciding the feasibility of $mz$-transportability, i.e., whether causal effects in the target domain are estimable from the information available. It further proves that a previously established algorithm for computing transport formula is in fact complete, that is, failure of the algorithm implies non-existence of a transport formula. Finally, the paper shows that the do-calculus is complete for the $mz$-transportability class.
originalAbstract: This paper addresses the problem of $mz$-transportability, that is, transferring causal knowledge collected in several heterogeneous domains to a target domain in which only passive observations and limited experimental data can be collected. The paper first establishes a necessary and sufficient condition for deciding the feasibility of $mz$-transportability, i.e., whether causal effects in the target domain are estimable from the information available. It further proves that a previously established algorithm for computing transport formula is in fact complete, that is, failure of the algorithm implies non-existence of a transport formula. paragraphs: The paper studies when causal knowledge from several different environments can be transferred to a target environment. The target permits passive observations and only limited experimental data. The question is whether this combined information suffices to estimate a target causal effect despite differences among the contributing domains.

For this problem class, called mz-transportability, the authors establish a necessary and sufficient feasibility condition. Such a condition characterizes both when transfer is possible and when the available information cannot support it. They also prove that an existing algorithm for constructing transport formulas is complete: if it fails, no transport formula exists within the stated setting.

Finally, the paper establishes completeness of do-calculus for this transportability class. Together, these results connect a feasibility characterization, an algorithm for computing formulas, and the underlying causal reasoning rules. Their significance is that algorithmic failure has a definitive interpretation here, rather than merely indicating that one computational approach did not find an available formula.
summary.tldr: Completeness results characterize exactly when causal effects can be transferred across heterogeneous environments with limited experimental information.

title: Transportability from Multiple Environments with Limited Experiments: Completeness Results

abstract: Cross-language learning allows us to use training data from one language to build models for a different language. Many approaches to bilingual learning require that we have word-level alignment of sentences from parallel corpora. In this work we explore the use of autoencoder-based methods for cross-language learning of vectorial word representations that are aligned between two languages, while not relying on word-level alignments. We show that by simply learning to reconstruct the bag-of-words representations of aligned sentences, within and between languages, we can in fact learn high-quality representations and do without word alignments. We empirically investigate the success of our approach on the problem of cross-language text classification, where a classifier trained on a given language (e.g., English) must learn to generalize to a different language (e.g., German). In experiments on 3 language pairs, we show that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance, outperforming a method exploiting word alignments and a strong machine translation baseline.

In experiments on 3 language pairs, we show that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance, outperforming a method exploiting word alignments and a strong machine translation baseline.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to learn word representations that support transferring a classifier from one language to another. Many bilingual methods require knowing which individual words correspond across translated sentences. The authors instead use sentences aligned across languages, avoiding the additional requirement of matching their words individually.

Their autoencoder approach learns by reconstructing bag-of-words representations of sentences, both within a language and across the two languages. These representations describe which words occur without preserving their order. Reconstruction across languages supplies a learning signal that connects their word vectors, while reconstruction within each language also contributes to training. The result is a set of vector representations aligned between languages.

The authors evaluate the representations through cross-language text classification: training a classifier in one language and testing its ability to generalize to another. Across three language pairs, the method achieves reported state-of-the-art performance, surpassing a word-alignment method and a strong machine-translation baseline. These findings support sentence-level reconstruction as useful supervision for bilingual representation learning.
summary.tldr: Reconstructing aligned sentences with autoencoders learns effective bilingual word vectors without requiring word-level alignments.

title: An Autoencoder Approach to Learning Bilingual Word Representations

abstract: We consider the problem of online planning in a Markov decision process with discounted rewards for any given initial state. We consider the PAC sample complexity problem of computing, with probability $1-\delta$, an $\epsilon$-optimal action using the smallest possible number of calls to the generative model (which provides reward and next-state samples). We design an algorithm, called StOP (for Stochastic-Optimistic Planning), based on the optimism in the face of uncertainty" principle. StOP can be used in the general setting, requires only a generative model, and enjoys a complexity bound that only depends on the local structure of the MDP."

paragraphs: This paper studies online planning from a given initial state in a Markov decision process with discounted rewards. The planner has access to a generative model that supplies sampled rewards and next states. The objective is to choose an action whose value is within a specified tolerance of optimal, with a specified probability of success.

The authors focus on sample complexity: how many calls to that model are needed to meet the accuracy and confidence requirements. They introduce Stochastic-Optimistic Planning, or StOP, using optimism in the face of uncertainty. This principle guides planning through optimistic assessments of possibilities that have not yet been sufficiently resolved.

StOP applies in the general setting considered and requires only the generative model. Its complexity bound depends solely on the local structure of the decision process. This connects the sampling requirement to the structure relevant to planning locally from the starting state. The contribution is an algorithm and a theoretical bound addressing reliable action selection while seeking to limit the number of simulated transitions and rewards.
summary.tldr: StOP uses optimistic planning with a generative model to select near-optimal actions, with a sample-complexity bound determined by local MDP structure.

title: Optimistic Planning in Markov Decision Processes Using a Generative Model

abstract: Subspace clustering is an unsupervised learning problem that aims at grouping data points into multiple clusters'' so that data points in a single cluster lie approximately on a low-dimensional linear subspace. It is originally motivated by 3D motion segmentation in computer vision, but has recently been generically applied to a wide range of statistical machine learning problems, which often involves sensitive datasets about human subjects. This raises a dire concern for data privacy. In this work, we build on the framework of differential privacy'' and present two provably private subspace clustering algorithms. We demonstrate via both theory and experiments that one of the presented methods enjoys formal privacy and utility guarantees; the other one asymptotically preserves differential privacy while having good performance in practice. Along the course of the proof, we also obtain two new provable guarantees for the agnostic subspace clustering and the graph connectivity problem which might be of independent interests.

paragraphs: Subspace clustering groups observations so that each group lies approximately within a low-dimensional linear subspace. Although motivated by motion segmentation in computer vision, the method also appears in statistical learning tasks involving sensitive human data. This paper addresses how to perform that grouping while providing privacy protection through the framework of differential privacy.

The authors present two algorithms with different stated guarantees. One has formal guarantees for both privacy and utility, supported through theory and experiments. The other preserves differential privacy asymptotically and performs well in practice. The distinction matters because an asymptotic privacy statement describes limiting behavior, while the first method offers the stated formal combination of privacy and usefulness.

The analysis also yields new guarantees for agnostic subspace clustering and graph connectivity. These results arise during the privacy proofs but may be useful independently. Overall, the work connects privacy protection to a clustering task that seeks geometric structure, while examining whether the resulting groupings retain useful information and distinguishing the kinds of guarantees available for each method.
summary.tldr: Two subspace clustering algorithms combine useful clustering with privacy guarantees, including one whose differential privacy guarantee is asymptotic.

title: Differentially private subspace clustering

abstract: We present an algorithm for recovering planted solutions in two well-known models, the stochastic block model and planted constraint satisfaction problems (CSP), via a common generalization in terms of random bipartite graphs. Our algorithm matches up to a constant factor the best-known bounds for the number of edges (or constraints) needed for perfect recovery and its running time is linear in the number of edges used. The time complexity is significantly better than both spectral and SDP-based approaches.The main contribution of the algorithm is in the case of unequal sizes in the bipartition that arises in our reduction from the planted CSP. Here our algorithm succeeds at a significantly lower density than the spectral approaches, surpassing a barrier based on the spectral norm of a random matrix.Other significant features of the algorithm and analysis include (i) the critical use of power iteration with subsampling, which might be of independent interest; its analysis requires keeping track of multiple norms of an evolving solution (ii) the algorithm can be implemented statistically, i.e., with very limited access to the input distribution (iii) the algorithm is extremely simple to implement and runs in linear time, and thus is practical even for very large instances.

paragraphs: This paper presents one algorithmic framework for recovering planted solutions in stochastic block models and planted constraint satisfaction problems. It relates both settings to random bipartite graphs, allowing a shared recovery method and analysis. The algorithm uses power iteration with subsampling and runs in time linear in the number of edges it processes.

Its edge or constraint requirement for perfect recovery matches the best-known bounds within a constant factor. The authors report substantially better time complexity than spectral and semidefinite-programming approaches. Their main advance concerns bipartite graphs with unequal partition sizes, which arise in the reduction from planted constraint problems: the algorithm succeeds at substantially lower density than spectral methods.

That recovery result passes a barrier associated with the spectral norm of a random matrix. Analyzing the subsampled iterations requires tracking multiple norms of the evolving solution. The algorithm can also be implemented with very limited access to the input distribution. Its simple implementation and linear runtime make the proposed framework suitable for very large instances within the studied models.
summary.tldr: Subsampled power iteration recovers planted structures in linear time and improves the recovery density over spectral approaches for unequal bipartitions.

title: Subsampled Power Iteration: a Unified Algorithm for Block Models and Planted CSP's

abstract: In this paper we introduce a generative model capable of producing high quality samples of natural images. Our approach uses a cascade of convolutional networks (convnets) within a Laplacian pyramid framework to generate images in a coarse-to-fine fashion. At each level of the pyramid a separate generative convnet model is trained using the Generative Adversarial Nets (GAN) approach. Samples drawn from our model are of significantly higher quality than existing models. In a quantitive assessment by human evaluators our CIFAR10 samples were mistaken for real images around 40% of the time, compared to 10% for GAN samples. We also show samples from more diverse datasets such as STL10 and LSUN.

Our approach uses a cascade of convolutional networks (convnets) within a Laplacian pyramid framework to generate images in a coarse-to-fine fashion. paragraphs: This paper develops a model for generating natural images by organizing generation across multiple scales. It uses a Laplacian pyramid and a cascade of convolutional networks to build images from coarse structure toward finer detail. The approach gives image generation a sequence of scale-specific stages.

Each pyramid level has its own generative convolutional network trained with the generative adversarial network approach. The overall model therefore combines adversarial learning with a coarse-to-fine organization. The architectural idea matters because the generation process explicitly separates scales while combining their contributions into a finished image.

The authors report substantially improved sample quality relative to existing models. In a human evaluation, generated CIFAR10 images were mistaken for real images around 40% of the time, compared with 10% for GAN samples. They also present samples from STL10 and LSUN, which contain more diverse images. The human assessment provides a concrete perceptual comparison, while those additional samples illustrate the model's application beyond the dataset used for that reported measurement.
summary.tldr: A Laplacian pyramid of adversarial convolutional networks generates images from coarse to fine, improving reported perceptual sample quality.

title: Deep Generative Image Models using a ￼Laplacian Pyramid of Adversarial Networks

abstract: Collecting labeled data is costly and thus a critical bottleneck in real-world classification tasks. To mitigate this problem, we propose a novel setting, namely learning from complementary labels for multi-class classification. A complementary label specifies a class that a pattern does not belong to. Collecting complementary labels would be less laborious than collecting ordinary labels, since users do not have to carefully choose the correct class from a long list of candidate classes. However, complementary labels are less informative than ordinary labels and thus a suitable approach is needed to better learn from them. In this paper, we show that an unbiased estimator to the classification risk can be obtained only from complementarily labeled data, if a loss function satisfies a particular symmetric condition. We derive estimation error bounds for the proposed method and prove that the optimal parametric convergence rate is achieved. We further show that learning from complementary labels can be easily combined with learning from ordinary labels (i.e., ordinary supervised learning), providing a highly practical implementation of the proposed method. Finally, we experimentally demonstrate the usefulness of the proposed methods.

Such labels could be easier to collect because annotators need not select the correct answer from a long list. Each annotation supplies less information than an ordinary label, so learning requires a method that accounts for this different form of supervision.

The authors show that complementary labels alone can produce an unbiased estimator of classification risk if the loss function satisfies a particular symmetry condition. That condition is part of the result: the claim does not cover arbitrary losses. They also derive estimation error bounds and prove that the method achieves the optimal parametric convergence rate.

The framework can combine complementary labels with ordinary labeled data, allowing both annotation types to contribute to learning. Experiments demonstrate the proposed methods’ usefulness. The central finding is that ruling out classes can support principled classification learning, including theoretical error guarantees under the stated loss condition, rather than serving only as an informal hint.
summary.tldr: Complementary labels can support unbiased classification-risk estimation and optimal parametric convergence when the loss satisfies a specified symmetry condition.

title: Learning from Complementary Labels

abstract: The idea of uprooting and rerooting graphical models was introduced specifically for binary pairwise models by Weller (2016) as a way to transform a model to any of a whole equivalence class of related models, such that inference on any one model yields inference results for all others. This is very helpful since inference, or relevant bounds, may be much easier to obtain or more accurate for some model in the class. Here we introduce methods to extend the approach to models with higher-order potentials and develop theoretical insights. In particular, we show that the triplet-consistent polytope TRI is unique in being `universally rooted'. We demonstrate empirically that rerooting can significantly improve accuracy of methods of inference for higher-order models at negligible computational cost.

paragraphs: This paper extends a transformation technique for graphical models from binary pairwise models to models with higher-order potentials. Uprooting and rerooting produce related models in an equivalence class, where inference results for one can yield results for the others. This creates an opportunity to work with a representation on which inference or relevant bounds are easier or more accurate.

The authors introduce methods that support these transformations for higher-order interactions and develop theoretical insights into their behavior. One result identifies the triplet-consistent polytope, TRI, as uniquely possessing the property termed universally rooted. This is a specific structural characterization within the theory accompanying the extended transformation methods.

Experiments show that rerooting can significantly improve the accuracy of inference methods for higher-order models at negligible computational cost. The practical significance is that changing the model’s representation can improve an inference procedure while retaining access to results for the related models. The reported improvement is empirical and expressed as a capability, rather than a guarantee for every model and inference method.
summary.tldr: Rerooting extends to higher-order graphical models and can substantially improve inference accuracy at negligible computational cost.

title: Uprooting and Rerooting Higher-Order Graphical Models

abstract: Learning individual-level causal effects from observational data, such as inferring the most effective medication for a specific patient, is a problem of growing importance for policy makers. The most important aspect of inferring causal effects from observational data is the handling of confounders, factors that affect both an intervention and its outcome. A carefully designed observational study attempts to measure all important confounders. However, even if one does not have direct access to all confounders, there may exist noisy and uncertain measurement of proxies for confounders. We build on recent advances in latent variable modeling to simultaneously estimate the unknown latent space summarizing the confounders and the causal effect. Our method is based on Variational Autoencoders (VAE) which follow the causal structure of inference with proxies. We show our method is significantly more robust than existing methods, and matches the state-of-the-art on previous benchmarks focused on individual treatment effects.

paragraphs: Estimating how an intervention affects an individual from observational data requires accounting for confounders: factors that influence both the intervention and its outcome. A study may lack direct measurements of these factors while still containing noisy measurements that act as proxies. The paper addresses causal-effect estimation in this situation.

The authors use a variational autoencoder organized around the causal structure of inference with proxies. The model jointly estimates a hidden representation summarizing confounders and the causal effect of interest. Connecting those two estimation problems allows the proxy measurements to inform the representation used for causal inference, despite their uncertainty.

The reported results show substantially greater robustness than existing methods and performance matching the state of the art on earlier individual-treatment-effect benchmarks. The contribution is a way to use imperfect information about confounders within a deep latent-variable model. Its stated setting depends on having proxy information; the result does not establish that hidden confounding can always be resolved from observational data alone.
summary.tldr: A causal variational autoencoder jointly models hidden confounders from noisy proxies and estimates individual treatment effects.

title: Causal Effect Inference with Deep Latent-Variable Models

abstract: We propose a simple and general variant of the standard reparameterized gradient estimator for the variational evidence lower bound. Specifically, we remove a part of the total derivative with respect to the variational parameters that corresponds to the score function. Removing this term produces an unbiased gradient estimator whose variance approaches zero as the approximate posterior approaches the exact posterior. We analyze the behavior of this gradient estimator theoretically and empirically, and generalize it to more complex variational distributions such as mixtures and importance-weighted posteriors.

We analyze the behavior of this gradient estimator theoretically and empirically, and generalize it to more complex variational distributions such as mixtures and importance-weighted posteriors.

paragraphs: Variational inference learns an approximate posterior by optimizing a lower bound on the model evidence. The gradient used for this optimization is often estimated from samples, so its noise can affect the learning process. This paper proposes a simple modification to the standard reparameterized gradient estimator for that objective.

The modification removes the part of the total derivative associated with the score function. Despite dropping that term, the resulting gradient estimator remains unbiased. Its variance approaches zero as the approximate posterior approaches the exact posterior. This conditional property is the central result: increasingly accurate posterior approximation is accompanied by vanishing gradient noise in the stated limit.

The authors examine the estimator both theoretically and empirically, and extend the construction to more complex variational distributions, including mixtures and importance-weighted posteriors. The contribution is a change to gradient estimation that preserves the target gradient in expectation while improving its behavior near an exact posterior. The extensions broaden the range of variational representations to which the idea can apply.
summary.tldr: Removing a score-function term yields an unbiased variational gradient estimator whose variance vanishes as the approximate posterior becomes exact.

title: Sticking the Landing: Simple, Lower-Variance Gradient Estimators for Variational Inference

abstract: We consider stochastic gradient descent (SGD) for least-squares regression with potentially several passes over the data. While several passes have been widely reported to perform practically better in terms of predictive performance on unseen data, the existing theoretical analysis of SGD suggests that a single pass is statistically optimal. While this is true for low-dimensional easy problems, we show that for hard problems, multiple passes lead to statistically optimal predictions while single pass does not; we also show that in these hard models, the optimal number of passes over the data increases with sample size. In order to define the notion of hardness and show that our predictive performances are optimal, we consider potentially infinite-dimensional models and notions typically associated to kernel methods, namely, the decay of eigenvalues of the covariance matrix of the features and the complexity of the optimal predictor as measured through the covariance matrix. We illustrate our results on synthetic experiments with non-linear kernel methods and on a classical benchmark with a linear model.

paragraphs: This paper examines how often stochastic gradient descent should revisit training data in least-squares regression. Earlier theory suggested that one pass was statistically optimal, despite practical evidence favoring repeated passes. The authors show that the single-pass conclusion holds for easy, low-dimensional problems but does not cover the harder models they analyze.

They define difficulty using potentially infinite-dimensional models and concepts associated with kernel methods. Two ingredients matter: how quickly the feature covariance eigenvalues decrease and how complex the optimal predictor is when measured through that covariance. This gives a mathematical meaning to hardness and a basis for judging whether predictive performance is optimal.

For the hard problems studied, multiple passes achieve statistically optimal predictions while one pass does not. The optimal number of passes also grows with sample size in these models. Synthetic experiments using nonlinear kernels and a benchmark using a linear model illustrate the results. The contribution explains when revisiting data is necessary to attain the analyzed optimal prediction performance.
summary.tldr: For the hard least-squares models studied, multiple SGD passes achieve optimal predictive performance that a single pass cannot.

title: Statistical Optimality of Stochastic Gradient Descent on Hard Learning Problems through Multiple Passes

abstract: We propose to solve a label ranking problem as a structured output regression task. In this view, we adopt a least square surrogate loss approach that solves a supervised learning problem in two steps: a regression step in a well-chosen feature space and a pre-image (or decoding) step. We use specific feature maps/embeddings for ranking data, which convert any ranking/permutation into a vector representation. These embeddings are all well-tailored for our approach, either by resulting in consistent estimators, or by solving trivially the pre-image problem which is often the bottleneck in structured prediction. Their extension to the case of incomplete or partial rankings is also discussed. Finally, we provide empirical results on synthetic and real-world datasets showing the relevance of our method.

paragraphs: Label ranking asks a model to predict an ordering of labels, so its output has more structure than a single category or number. This paper treats that task as structured output regression. It represents rankings as vectors, learns to predict those vectors using a least-squares surrogate loss, and then converts the predictions back into rankings.

The choice of vector representation is central. A regression output does not automatically correspond to a valid ordering, so recovering a ranking can become the expensive part of the method. The paper studies embeddings that help in different ways: some yield consistent estimators, while others make this decoding step straightforward. These are alternative benefits of the representations, rather than a claim that every embedding provides both.

The authors also discuss extending these representations to incomplete or partial rankings, where an entire ordering is unavailable. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets support the approach's usefulness. The contribution is a framework connecting ordinary regression machinery to ranking prediction, with explicit attention to both statistical behavior and the practical difficulty of decoding.
summary.tldr: The paper predicts label rankings through vector regression, using ranking embeddings that support consistency or simplify decoding.

title: A Structured Prediction Approach for Label Ranking

abstract: We identify and study two common failure modes for early training in deep ReLU nets. For each, we give a rigorous proof of when it occurs and how to avoid it, for fully connected, convolutional, and residual architectures. We show that the first failure mode, exploding or vanishing mean activation length, can be avoided by initializing weights from a symmetric distribution with variance 2/fan-in and, for ResNets, by correctly scaling the residual modules. We prove that the second failure mode, exponentially large variance of activation length, never occurs in residual nets once the first failure mode is avoided. In contrast, for fully connected nets, we prove that this failure mode can happen and is avoided by keeping constant the sum of the reciprocals of layer widths. We demonstrate empirically the effectiveness of our theoretical results in predicting when networks are able to start training. In particular, we note that many popular initializations fail our criteria, whereas correct initialization and architecture allows much deeper networks to be trained.
