paragraphs: This paper examines why deep ReLU networks can fail at the beginning of training. It separates two problems involving activation length: an average magnitude that explodes or vanishes, and a variance that becomes exponentially large. Distinguishing these failures matters because controlling the average alone does not automatically control variability in every architecture.

The authors prove that the first failure can be avoided using symmetric weight initialization with variance 2/fan-in, together with appropriate scaling of residual modules in residual networks. Once this first problem is avoided, they prove that the second failure does not occur in residual networks. Fully connected networks behave differently: their variance problem can occur, and avoiding it requires keeping the sum of reciprocal layer widths constant.

The study provides rigorous conditions across fully connected, convolutional, and residual architectures, then tests how well the theory predicts whether training can begin successfully. The experiments support those predictions. Many popular initialization choices fail the proposed criteria, while suitable initialization and architecture permit much deeper networks to train, making network shape and starting weights jointly important.
summary.tldr: The paper identifies two early-training failures in deep ReLU networks and proves how initialization and architecture can prevent them.

title: How to Start Training: The Effect of Initialization and Architecture

abstract: We consider evidence integration from potentially dependent observation processes under varying spatio-temporal sampling resolutions and noise levels. We offer a multi-resolution multi-task (MRGP) framework that allows for both inter-task and intra-task multi-resolution and multi-fidelity. We develop shallow Gaussian Process (GP) mixtures that approximate the difficult to estimate joint likelihood with a composite one and deep GP constructions that naturally handle biases. In doing so, we generalize existing approaches and offer information-theoretic corrections and efficient variational approximations. We demonstrate the competitiveness of MRGPs on synthetic settings and on the challenging problem of hyper-local estimation of air pollution levels across London from multiple sensing modalities operating at disparate spatio-temporal resolutions.

paragraphs: Combining observations becomes difficult when sources measure at different spatial or temporal resolutions, have different noise levels, and may depend on one another. This paper introduces a multi-resolution, multitask Gaussian-process framework for integrating such evidence. It accommodates differences in resolution and fidelity both within an individual task and across tasks.

The authors develop two kinds of construction. Shallow Gaussian-process mixtures replace a difficult joint likelihood with a composite likelihood, making the integration problem more manageable. Deep Gaussian-process constructions handle biases naturally. The framework also includes information-theoretic corrections and efficient variational approximations, providing tools for carrying out inference in these models.

The paper demonstrates competitive performance in synthetic settings and in estimating air pollution at highly local scales across London. That application combines multiple sensing modalities operating at different spatial and temporal resolutions. The contribution is a modeling framework suited to this uneven evidence: it represents differences in how observations are collected while allowing their information to contribute to related estimation tasks.
summary.tldr: A Gaussian-process framework integrates potentially dependent observations collected at different resolutions, fidelities, and noise levels.

title: Multi-resolution Multi-task Gaussian Processes

abstract: Are two sets of observations drawn from the same distribution? This problem is a two-sample test. Kernel methods lead to many appealing properties. Indeed state-of-the-art approaches use the $L^2$ distance between kernel-based distribution representatives to derive their test statistics. Here, we show that $L^p$ distances (with $p\geq 1$) between these distribution representatives give metrics on the space of distributions that are well-behaved to detect differences between distributions as they metrize the weak convergence. Moreover, for analytic kernels, we show that the $L^1$ geometry gives improved testing power for scalable computational procedures. Specifically, we derive a finite dimensional approximation of the metric given as the $\ell_1$ norm of a vector which captures differences of expectations of analytic functions evaluated at spatial locations or frequencies (i.e, features). The features can be chosen to maximize the differences of the distributions and give interpretable indications of how they differs. Using an $\ell_1$ norm gives better detection because differences between representatives are dense as we use analytic kernels (non-zero almost everywhere). The tests are consistent, while much faster than state-of-the-art quadratic-time kernel-based tests. Experiments on artificial and real-world problems demonstrate improved power/time tradeoff than the state of the art, based on $\ell_2$ norms, and in some cases, better outright power than even the most expensive quadratic-time tests. This performance gain is retained even in high dimensions.

In some cases, power also exceeds that of expensive quadratic-time tests, with gains retained in high dimensions. The results connect a choice of geometry to both statistical sensitivity and computational practicality.
summary.tldr: For analytic kernels, L1-based distribution comparisons improve the power and computational efficiency of scalable two-sample tests.

title: Comparing distributions: $\ell_1$ geometry improves kernel two-sample testing

abstract: Many recent works have shown that adversarial examples that fool classifiers can be found by minimally perturbing a normal input. Recent theoretical results, starting with Gilmer et al. (2018b), show that if the inputs are drawn from a concentrated metric probability space, then adversarial examples with small perturbation are inevitable. A concentrated space has the property that any subset with Ω(1) (e.g.,1/100) measure, according to the imposed distribution, has small distance to almost all (e.g., 99/100) of the points in the space. It is not clear, however, whether these theoretical results apply to actual distributions such as images. This paper presents a method for empirically measuring and bounding the concentration of a concrete dataset which is proven to converge to the actual concentration. We use it to empirically estimate the intrinsic robustness to and L 2 and L infinity perturbations of several image classification benchmarks. Code for our experiments is available at https://github.com/xiaozhanguva/Measure-Concentration.

paragraphs: Small changes to an input can cause a classifier to make a mistake. Existing theory connects this vulnerability to concentration: a property of a probability space in which any set containing a substantial share of probability lies close to almost every point. Under the relevant concentration condition, small adversarial perturbations are inevitable.

The practical question is whether actual image distributions have the concentration needed for those theoretical conclusions. This paper introduces a method for measuring and bounding concentration empirically on a concrete dataset. The authors prove that the method converges to the actual concentration, linking a measurable estimate to the underlying mathematical property.

They apply the method to several image classification benchmarks to estimate intrinsic robustness against L2 and L-infinity perturbations. These estimates investigate limits associated with the data distribution itself. The contribution makes a previously abstract explanation of adversarial vulnerability empirically examinable, while preserving the central condition: the theoretical inevitability result depends on inputs coming from a concentrated space.
summary.tldr: A convergent empirical method measures data concentration to investigate distribution-dependent limits on image-classification robustness.

title: Empirically Measuring Concentration: Fundamental Limits on Intrinsic Robustness

abstract: Understanding the predictions of a machine learning model can be as crucial as the model's accuracy in many application domains. However, the black-box nature of most highly-accurate (complex) models is a major hindrance to their interpretability. To address this issue, we introduce the symbolic metamodeling framework — a general methodology for interpreting predictions by converting "black-box" models into "white-box" functions that are understandable to human subjects. A symbolic metamodel is a model of a model, i.e., a surrogate model of a trained (machine learning) model expressed through a succinct symbolic expression that comprises familiar mathematical functions and can be subjected to symbolic manipulation. We parameterize symbolic metamodels using Meijer G-functions — a class of complex-valued contour integrals that depend on scalar parameters, and whose solutions reduce to familiar elementary, algebraic, analytic and closed-form functions for different parameter settings. This parameterization enables efficient optimization of metamodels via gradient descent, and allows discovering the functional forms learned by a machine learning model with minimal a priori assumptions. We show that symbolic metamodeling provides an all-encompassing framework for model interpretation — all common forms of global and local explanations of a model can be analytically derived from its symbolic metamodel.

paragraphs: A highly accurate model can still be difficult to understand. This paper proposes explaining a trained model through a symbolic metamodel: a surrogate expressed as a compact mathematical formula. Because the formula uses recognizable functions and supports symbolic manipulation, it provides a form that people can inspect and analyze when trying to understand predictions.

The technical challenge is finding a useful formula without specifying its functional form too narrowly in advance. The authors parameterize their surrogates using Meijer G-functions, a broad mathematical family whose different parameter settings reduce to many familiar functions. This representation permits gradient-based optimization while allowing the search to cover varied functional forms with relatively few prior assumptions.

The paper presents this symbolic representation as a common foundation for interpretation. It states that common global explanations, concerning overall model behavior, and local explanations, concerning particular predictions, can be derived analytically from the metamodel. The resulting explanations describe the trained model through its surrogate, making the symbolic expression the central object from which multiple kinds of interpretation follow.
summary.tldr: Symbolic metamodels explain trained models through optimized mathematical expressions from which global and local explanations can be derived.

title: Demystifying Black-box Models with Symbolic Metamodels

abstract: Self-play methods based on regret minimization have become the state of the art for computing Nash equilibria in large two-players zero-sum extensive-form games. These methods fundamentally rely on the hierarchical structure of the players' sequential strategy spaces to construct a regret minimizer that recursively minimizes regret at each decision point in the game tree. In this paper, we introduce the first efficient regret minimization algorithm for computing extensive-form correlated equilibria in large two-player general-sum games with no chance moves. Designing such an algorithm is significantly more challenging than designing one for the Nash equilibrium counterpart, as the constraints that define the space of correlation plans lack the hierarchical structure and might even form cycles. We show that some of the constraints are redundant and can be excluded from consideration, and present an efficient algorithm that generates the space of extensive-form correlation plans incrementally from the remaining constraints. This structural decomposition is achieved via a special convexity-preserving operation that we coin scaled extension. We show that a regret minimizer can be designed for a scaled extension of any two convex sets, and that from the decomposition we then obtain a global regret minimizer. Our algorithm produces feasible iterates. Experiments show that it significantly outperforms prior approaches and for larger problems it is the only viable option.

This structural decomposition is achieved via a special convexity-preserving operation that we coin scaled extension. We show that a regret minimizer can be designed for a scaled extension of any two convex sets, and that from the decomposition we then obtain a global regret minimizer. Our algorithm produces feasible iterates. Experiments show that it significantly outperforms prior approaches and for larger problems it is the only viable option.

paragraphs: Regret minimization supports powerful self-play methods for sequential games, but extending it to correlated equilibria introduces a structural obstacle. The constraints describing correlation plans do not have the convenient hierarchy of individual players' strategy spaces, and they can contain cycles. This paper addresses large two-player general-sum games without chance moves.

The authors identify redundant constraints and remove them from consideration. They then construct the remaining space of correlation plans incrementally using an operation called scaled extension, which preserves convexity. They show how to build a regret minimizer for a scaled extension of two convex sets and combine these components into a regret minimizer for the full space.

This decomposition yields an efficient algorithm for computing extensive-form correlated equilibria while keeping its intermediate iterates feasible. That property means the iterates satisfy the correlation-plan constraints throughout the computation. In the reported experiments, the method substantially outperforms earlier approaches and is the only viable option among those approaches on the larger problems tested.
summary.tldr: A convex decomposition enables efficient regret minimization for correlated equilibria in two-player general-sum sequential games without chance moves.

title: Efficient Regret Minimization Algorithm for Extensive-Form Correlated Equilibrium

abstract: We present a new technique for the learning of continuous energy functions that we refer to as Wibergian Learning. One common approach to inverse problems is to cast them as an energy minimisation problem, where the minimum cost solution found is used as an estimator of hidden parameters. Our new approach formally characterises the dependency between weights that control the shape of the energy function, and the location of minima, by describing minima as fixed points of optimisation methods. This allows for the use of gradient-based end-to- end training to integrate deep-learning and the classical inverse problem methods. We show how our approach can be applied to obtain state-of-the-art results in the diverse applications of tracker fusion and multiview 3D reconstruction.

paragraphs: Many inverse problems estimate hidden quantities by finding the minimum of an energy function. The function assigns a cost to candidate solutions, so changing its weights can change which solution is preferred. This paper asks how to learn those weights when the quantity of interest is the location of the resulting minimum.

The proposed technique, Wibergian Learning, formally links energy-function parameters to minima by representing minima as fixed points of optimization methods. A fixed point is a state that an optimization update leaves unchanged. This formulation gives a way to describe how an estimated solution depends on the weights that shape the energy.

That dependency enables gradient-based training across the combined system, connecting deep learning with classical methods for inverse problems. Rather than learning an energy independently of how its minimum is used, the approach supports end-to-end optimization. The authors demonstrate applications to tracker fusion and multiview three-dimensional reconstruction, reporting state-of-the-art results in both. These examples show the relevance of learning through the optimization solution across distinct estimation tasks.
summary.tldr: Wibergian Learning links energy minima to trainable weights through optimization fixed points, enabling end-to-end learning for inverse problems.

title: Fixing Implicit Derivatives: Trust-Region Based Learning of Continuous Energy Functions

abstract: Neural network based end-to-end text to speech (TTS) has significantly improved the quality of synthesized speech. Prominent methods (e.g., Tacotron 2) usually first generate mel-spectrogram from text, and then synthesize speech from the mel-spectrogram using vocoder such as WaveNet. Compared with traditional concatenative and statistical parametric approaches, neural network based end-to-end models suffer from slow inference speed, and the synthesized speech is usually not robust (i.e., some words are skipped or repeated) and lack of controllability (voice speed or prosody control). In this work, we propose a novel feed-forward network based on Transformer to generate mel-spectrogram in parallel for TTS. Specifically, we extract attention alignments from an encoder-decoder based teacher model for phoneme duration prediction, which is used by a length regulator to expand the source phoneme sequence to match the length of the target mel-spectrogram sequence for parallel mel-spectrogram generation. Experiments on the LJSpeech dataset show that our parallel model matches autoregressive models in terms of speech quality, nearly eliminates the problem of word skipping and repeating in particularly hard cases, and can adjust voice speed smoothly. Most importantly, compared with autoregressive Transformer TTS, our model speeds up mel-spectrogram generation by 270x and the end-to-end speech synthesis by 38x. Therefore, we call our model FastSpeech.

FastSpeech accelerates this stage with a feed-forward Transformer that generates the spectrogram in parallel.

Parallel generation requires matching the length of the phoneme sequence to the longer sequence of spectrogram frames. The model learns phoneme durations using alignments extracted from an encoder-decoder teacher. A length regulator then expands the phoneme sequence according to those durations. This gives the model an explicit way to organize timing and adjust speaking speed.

On LJSpeech, the authors report speech quality matching autoregressive models, near elimination of skipped and repeated words in particularly difficult cases, and smooth speed adjustment. Relative to autoregressive Transformer TTS, spectrogram generation is 270 times faster and complete speech synthesis is 38 times faster. The different speedups distinguish acceleration of one processing stage from acceleration of the entire synthesis pipeline.
summary.tldr: FastSpeech uses predicted phoneme durations and parallel spectrogram generation to accelerate speech synthesis while improving reliability and speed control.

title: FastSpeech: Fast, Robust and Controllable Text to Speech

abstract: Discrete integration is a fundamental problem in computer science that concerns the computation of discrete sums over exponentially large sets. Despite intense interest from researchers for over three decades, the design of scalable techniques for computing estimates with rigorous guarantees for discrete integration remains the holy grail. The key contribution of this work addresses this scalability challenge via an efficient reduction of discrete integration to model counting. The proposed reduction is achieved via a significant increase in the dimensionality that, contrary to conventional wisdom, leads to solving an instance of the relatively simpler problem of model counting. Building on the promising approach proposed by Chakraborty et al, our work overcomes the key weakness of their approach: a restriction to dyadic weights. We augment our proposed reduction, called DeWeight, with a state of the art efficient approximate model counter and perform detailed empirical analysis over benchmarks arising from neural network verification domains, an emerging application area of critical importance. DeWeight, to the best of our knowledge, is the first technique to compute estimates with provable guarantees for this class of benchmarks.

paragraphs: Discrete integration requires summing values over sets that may contain exponentially many elements. Computing scalable estimates with rigorous guarantees is therefore difficult. This paper addresses the problem by converting discrete integration into model counting, replacing the original summation task with a counting problem that can be handled by an approximate model counter.

The reduction, called DeWeight, substantially increases the dimensionality of the representation. Here that increase is useful because it enables a transition to the relatively simpler counting problem. The work builds on an earlier reduction while removing its restriction to dyadic weights. Its contribution is thus a broader reduction, not a claim that increasing dimension generally simplifies computation.

The authors combine DeWeight with a state-of-the-art approximate model counter and evaluate it on benchmarks from neural network verification. They report that, to their knowledge, it is the first technique to obtain estimates with provable guarantees for this benchmark class. The results illustrate how changing the form of a computational problem can improve tractability even when the transformed representation has more dimensions.
summary.tldr: DeWeight increases dimensionality to reduce discrete integration to model counting, enabling guaranteed estimates on evaluated neural verification benchmarks.

title: Taming Discrete Integration via the Boon of Dimensionality

abstract: Under label shift, the label distribution $p(y)$ might change but the class-conditional distributions $p(x|y)$ do not. There are two dominant approaches for estimating the label marginal. BBSE, a moment-matching approach based on confusion matrices, is provably consistent and provides interpretable error bounds. However, a maximum likelihood estimation approach, which we call MLLS, dominates empirically. In this paper, we present a unified view of the two methods and the first theoretical characterization of MLLS. Our contributions include (i) consistency conditions for MLLS, which include calibration of the classifier and a confusion matrix invertibility condition that BBSE also requires; (ii) a unified framework, casting BBSE as roughly equivalent to MLLS for a particular choice of calibration method; and (iii) a decomposition of MLLS's finite-sample error into terms reflecting miscalibration and estimation error. Our analysis attributes BBSE's statistical inefficiency to a loss of information due to coarse calibration. Experiments on synthetic data, MNIST, and CIFAR10 support our findings.

paragraphs: Label shift describes a change in how common different classes are while the distribution of inputs within each class stays fixed. The paper studies how to estimate those changing class proportions. It connects two prominent approaches: BBSE, which matches information from confusion matrices, and MLLS, which uses maximum likelihood and had shown stronger empirical performance.

The authors provide a theoretical characterization of MLLS, including conditions under which its estimates become correct as data increases. Those conditions include classifier calibration and an invertible confusion matrix, with the latter also required by BBSE. Their common framework makes BBSE roughly equivalent to MLLS under a particular calibration choice, showing that the methods are more closely related than their different formulations suggest.

The analysis separates MLLS's finite-data error into contributions from miscalibration and estimation. It attributes BBSE's statistical inefficiency to information discarded by coarse calibration. Experiments on synthetic data, MNIST, and CIFAR10 support this account, connecting the observed performance gap to how classifier information is retained and calibrated.
summary.tldr: A shared framework explains label-shift estimators through calibration and information loss, providing consistency conditions and an error analysis for maximum likelihood estimation.

title: A Unified View of Label Shift Estimation

abstract: Off-policy evaluation provides an essential tool for evaluating the effects of different policies or treatments using only observed data. When applied to high-stakes scenarios such as medical diagnosis or financial decision-making, it is essential to provide provably correct upper and lower bounds of the expected reward, not just a classical single point estimate, to the end-users, as executing a poor policy can be very costly. In this work, we propose a provably correct method for obtaining interval bounds for off-policy evaluation in a general continuous setting. The idea is to search for the maximum and minimum values of the expected reward among all the Lipschitz Q-functions that are consistent with the observations, which amounts to solving a constrained optimization problem on a Lipschitz function space. We go on to introduce a Lipschitz value iteration method to monotonically tighten the interval, which is simple yet efficient and provably convergent. We demonstrate the practical efficiency of our method on a range of benchmarks.

paragraphs: Off-policy evaluation estimates a policy’s expected reward from previously observed data. A single estimate may be insufficient when acting on an overly optimistic assessment would be costly. This paper instead develops upper and lower bounds in a general continuous setting, aiming to characterize a range of rewards consistent with the observations.

The method considers Lipschitz Q-functions, whose values cannot change arbitrarily rapidly as their inputs change. Among all such functions consistent with the observations, it searches for the largest and smallest expected rewards. This turns interval estimation into constrained optimization over a function space. The Lipschitz restriction is central to the construction and to the meaning of the resulting bounds.

The authors introduce Lipschitz value iteration to tighten the interval monotonically and prove that the procedure converges. They describe the method as simple and efficient, and demonstrate practical efficiency across benchmarks. Its contribution is a provably correct bounding procedure within the stated framework, giving policy evaluation an interval-valued result that can be progressively refined.
summary.tldr: Lipschitz value iteration produces provably correct off-policy reward bounds and progressively tightens them within its function-class framework.

title: Off-Policy Interval Estimation with Lipschitz Value Iteration

abstract: Recent advances in image clustering typically focus on learning better deep representations. In contrast, we present an orthogonal approach that does not rely on abstract features but instead learns to predict transformations and performs clustering directly in image space. This learning process naturally fits in the gradient-based training of K-means and Gaussian mixture model, without requiring any additional loss or hyper-parameters. It leads us to two new deep transformation-invariant clustering frameworks, which jointly learn prototypes and transformations. More specifically, we use deep learning modules that enable us to resolve invariance to spatial, color and morphological transformations. Our approach is conceptually simple and comes with several advantages, including the possibility to easily adapt the desired invariance to the task and a strong interpretability of both cluster centers and assignments to clusters. We demonstrate that our novel approach yields competitive and highly promising results on standard image clustering benchmarks. Finally, we showcase its robustness and the advantages of its improved interpretability by visualizing clustering results over real photograph collections.

paragraphs: Images can differ in position, color, or shape while still belonging to the same meaningful group. This paper addresses those variations directly during clustering. Instead of relying on an abstract feature representation, it learns transformations and groups images in image space, keeping the connection between the clusters and the visible images explicit.

The authors introduce two frameworks based on gradient-trained K-means and Gaussian mixture models. Each jointly learns cluster prototypes and transformations, using deep learning modules to handle spatial, color, and morphological changes. The transformation learning fits into the existing training objectives without additional losses or hyperparameters. The desired invariances can also be adapted to the task.

Because cluster centers remain image-based prototypes, the approach makes both the centers and assignments easier to interpret. Experiments show competitive results on standard image clustering benchmarks. Visualizations on real photograph collections further demonstrate robustness and the interpretability advantages. The contribution is a way to incorporate chosen image variations into clustering while preserving a visually understandable account of the resulting groups.
summary.tldr: The method jointly learns image prototypes and transformations to produce interpretable clusters that account for spatial, color, and morphological variation.

title: Deep Transformation-Invariant Clustering

abstract: In this paper, we propose a deep reinforcement learning (DRL) based framework to efficiently perform runtime channel pruning on convolutional neural networks (CNNs). Our DRL-based framework aims to learn a pruning strategy to determine how many and which channels to be pruned in each convolutional layer, depending on each individual input instance at runtime. Unlike existing runtime pruning methods which require to store all channels parameters for inference, our framework can reduce parameters storage consumption by introducing a static pruning component. Comparison experimental results with existing runtime and static pruning methods on state-of-the-art CNNs demonstrate that our proposed framework is able to provide a tradeoff between dynamic flexibility and storage efficiency in runtime channel pruning.
originalAbstract: In this paper, we propose a deep reinforcement learning (DRL) based framework to efficiently perform runtime channel pruning on convolutional neural networks (CNNs). Our DRL-based framework aims to learn a pruning strategy to determine how many and which channels to be pruned in each convolutional layer, depending on each individual input instance at runtime. Unlike existing runtime pruning methods which require to store all channels parameters for inference, our framework can reduce parameters storage consumption by introducing a static pruning component. Comparison experimental results with existing runtime and static pruning methods on state-of-the-art CNNs demonstrate that our proposed framework is able to provide a tradeoff between dynamic flexibility and storage efficiency in runtime channel pruning.

paragraphs: Channel pruning reduces the channels used by a convolutional neural network. Runtime pruning can adapt those choices to each input, but the paper identifies a storage problem: existing runtime methods still require all channel parameters to be stored for inference. Dynamic computation therefore does not automatically provide a corresponding reduction in parameter storage.

The proposed framework uses deep reinforcement learning to learn a pruning strategy. For each input, the strategy decides both how many channels to prune and which channels to remove in each convolutional layer. A static pruning component reduces the parameters that must be stored, while runtime decisions retain input-dependent flexibility.

Experiments compare the framework with existing runtime and static pruning methods on state-of-the-art convolutional networks. The results demonstrate a tradeoff between dynamic flexibility and storage efficiency. The contribution is the combination of these two pruning roles: permanent pruning addresses storage consumption, while learned runtime choices adapt the remaining computation to individual inputs.
summary.tldr: A reinforcement-learning pruning framework combines input-dependent channel selection with static pruning to balance flexibility and parameter storage.

title: Storage Efficient and Dynamic Flexible Runtime Channel Pruning via Deep Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Modern recording techniques can generate large-scale measurements of multiple neural populations over extended time periods. However, it remains a challenge to model non-stationary interactions between high-dimensional populations of neurons. To tackle this challenge, we develop recurrent switching linear dynamical systems models for multiple populations. Here, each high-dimensional neural population is represented by a unique set of latent variables, which evolve dynamically in time. Populations interact with each other through this low-dimensional space. We allow the nature of these interactions to change over time by using a discrete set of dynamical states. Additionally, we parameterize these discrete state transition rules to capture which neural populations are responsible for switching between interaction states. To fit the model, we use variational expectation-maximization with a structured mean-field approximation. After validating the model on simulations, we apply it to two different neural datasets: spiking activity from motor areas in a non-human primate, and calcium imaging from neurons in the nematode \textit{C. elegans}. In both datasets, the model reveals behaviorally-relevant discrete states with unique inter-population interactions and different populations that predict transitioning between these states.

paragraphs: Large neural recordings capture many neurons across several populations, but interactions between those populations can change over time. This paper models that variation by assigning each population its own low-dimensional latent variables. Those hidden variables evolve dynamically and provide the space through which the populations interact.

A discrete set of dynamical states allows the interaction pattern to switch rather than remain fixed throughout a recording. The transition rules are parameterized to capture which populations are associated with switches between interaction states. The model is fitted using variational expectation-maximization with a structured mean-field approximation, combining inference about latent activity with learning the switching dynamics.

After simulation validation, the authors apply the model to primate motor-area spiking and C. elegans calcium imaging. Both applications reveal behaviorally relevant states with distinct inter-population interactions, along with different populations that predict transitions. The findings provide an interpretable description of changing coordination; predictive associations with switching do not by themselves establish that a population causally triggers a transition.
summary.tldr: A switching latent dynamical model identifies changing neural-population interactions and populations that predict transitions between behaviorally relevant states.

title: Recurrent Switching Dynamical Systems Models for Multiple Interacting Neural Populations

abstract: Many real-world systems, such as moving planets, can be considered as multi-agent dynamic systems, where objects interact with each other and co-evolve along with the time. Such dynamics is usually difficult to capture, and understanding and predicting the dynamics based on observed trajectories of objects become a critical research problem in many domains. Most existing algorithms, however, assume the observations are regularly sampled and all the objects can be fully observed at each sampling time, which is impractical for many applications. In this paper, we pro-pose to learn system dynamics from irregularly-sampled and partial observations with underlying graph structure for the first time. To tackle the above challenge, we present LG-ODE, a latent ordinary differential equation generative model for modeling multi-agent dynamic system with known graph structure. It can simultaneously learn the embedding of high dimensional trajectories and infer continuous latent system dynamics. Our model employs a novel encoder parameterized by a graph neural network that can infer initial states in an unsupervised way from irregularly-sampled partial observations of structural objects and utilizes neuralODE to infer arbitrarily complex continuous-time latent dynamics. Experiments on motion capture, spring system, and charged particle datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach.

paragraphs: Many dynamic systems contain interacting objects whose states evolve together. Learning that evolution becomes difficult when measurements arrive at uneven times and some objects are missing from individual observations. This paper addresses those conditions instead of requiring complete snapshots at regular intervals.

The proposed LG-ODE model assumes a known graph describing the system's structure. A graph neural network encoder uses the irregular, partial observations to infer initial states without supervision. A neural ordinary differential equation then models continuous evolution in a latent representation, allowing the model to learn both a compact representation of trajectories and the dynamics within that representation.

The continuous-time formulation fits the problem's uneven observation times, while the graph encoder incorporates structural relationships among objects. Experiments on motion capture, spring systems, and charged particles demonstrate the approach's effectiveness. The results support combining graph-based inference with latent differential equations for partially observed systems, with knowledge of the underlying graph remaining an explicit part of the model's setup.
summary.tldr: LG-ODE combines graph-based state inference with continuous latent dynamics to learn from irregular, partial observations.

title: Learning Continuous System Dynamics from Irregularly-Sampled Partial Observations

abstract: Bayesian optimization is a sequential decision making framework for optimizing expensive-to-evaluate black-box functions. Computing a full lookahead policy amounts to solving a highly intractable stochastic dynamic program. Myopic approaches, such as expected improvement, are often adopted in practice, but they ignore the long-term impact of the immediate decision. Existing nonmyopic approaches are mostly heuristic and/or computationally expensive. In this paper, we provide the first efficient implementation of general multi-step lookahead Bayesian optimization, formulated as a sequence of nested optimization problems within a multi-step scenario tree. Instead of solving these problems in a nested way, we equivalently optimize all decision variables in the full tree jointly, in a "one-shot" fashion. Combining this with an efficient method for implementing multi-step Gaussian process "fantasization," we demonstrate that multi-step expected improvement is computationally tractable and exhibits performance superior to existing methods on a wide range of benchmarks.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization chooses evaluations of an expensive black-box function sequentially. A choice can matter both for its immediate result and for the later decisions it enables. Common myopic methods focus on the immediate step, while a full lookahead policy requires solving a highly intractable stochastic dynamic program. This paper seeks a computationally practical way to consider several steps ahead.

Instead, they optimize all decision variables in the tree jointly through an equivalent one-shot formulation. Efficient multi-step Gaussian process fantasization supplies the imagined future observations used in the lookahead computation.

The authors demonstrate that this combination makes multi-step expected improvement computationally tractable. Across a wide range of benchmarks, it outperforms existing methods. The result shows that a suitable reformulation can make longer-term evaluation planning practical within the studied framework, providing an alternative to choosing each evaluation solely for its immediate expected benefit.
summary.tldr: Joint optimization of scenario-tree decisions makes multi-step Bayesian optimization tractable and improves performance across the reported benchmarks.

title: Efficient Nonmyopic Bayesian Optimization via One-Shot Multi-Step Trees

abstract: In studying the expressiveness of neural networks, an important question is whether there are functions which can only be approximated by sufficiently deep networks, assuming their size is bounded. However, for constant depths, existing results are limited to depths $2$ and $3$, and achieving results for higher depths has been an important open question. In this paper, we focus on feedforward ReLU networks, and prove fundamental barriers to proving such results beyond depth $4$, by reduction to open problems and natural-proof barriers in circuit complexity. To show this, we study a seemingly unrelated problem of independent interest: Namely, whether there are polynomially-bounded functions which require super-polynomial weights in order to approximate with constant-depth neural networks. We provide a negative and constructive answer to that question, by showing that if a function can be approximated by a polynomially-sized, constant depth $k$ network with arbitrarily large weights, it can also be approximated by a polynomially-sized, depth $3k+3$ network, whose weights are polynomially bounded.

To show this, we study a seemingly unrelated problem of independent interest: Namely, whether there are polynomially-bounded functions which require super-polynomial weights in order to approximate with constant-depth neural networks. paragraphs: Depth-separation research asks whether some functions require sufficiently deep networks when network size is bounded. For constant depths, existing results discussed in the paper concern depths two and three. This work investigates why extending such results to greater depths is difficult for feedforward ReLU networks.

The authors establish barriers to proving depth-separation results beyond depth four by relating the task to open problems and natural-proof barriers in circuit complexity. This is a statement about obstacles to obtaining proofs, rather than a claim that deeper networks cannot have stronger approximation capabilities. It connects the neural-network question to established difficulties in another area of theoretical computation.

The argument uses a constructive result about weight size. For polynomially bounded functions, any approximation by a polynomial-size, constant-depth k network with arbitrarily large weights can also be achieved by a polynomial-size network of depth 3k+3 with polynomially bounded weights. Thus, in this setting, additional constant depth can replace the need for extremely large weights. That tradeoff is both an independent expressiveness result and a tool for establishing the proof barriers.
summary.tldr: The paper links higher-depth separation proofs to circuit-complexity barriers and shows how extra constant depth can replace arbitrarily large weights.

title: Neural Networks with Small Weights and Depth-Separation Barriers

abstract: The effectiveness of machine learning algorithms arises from being able to extract useful features from large amounts of data. As model and dataset sizes increase, dataset distillation methods that compress large datasets into significantly smaller yet highly performant ones will become valuable in terms of training efficiency and useful feature extraction. To that end, we apply a novel distributed kernel-based meta-learning framework to achieve state-of-the-art results for dataset distillation using infinitely wide convolutional neural networks. For instance, using only 10 datapoints (0.02% of original dataset), we obtain over 65% test accuracy on CIFAR-10 image classification task, a dramatic improvement over the previous best test accuracy of 40%. Our state-of-the-art results extend across many other settings for MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and SVHN. Furthermore, we perform some preliminary analyses of our distilled datasets to shed light on how they differ from naturally occurring data.

The challenge is to retain useful predictive information despite removing most of the original data volume. This paper approaches that challenge using infinitely wide convolutional neural networks within a distributed, kernel-based meta-learning framework.

On CIFAR-10, a distilled dataset containing just ten data points—0.02% of the original dataset—supports test accuracy above 65%. The abstract contrasts this with a previous best of 40%, illustrating how much predictive value a very small distilled collection can retain in this setup.

The reported improvements extend across settings involving MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and SVHN. The authors also conduct preliminary analyses of how distilled examples differ from naturally occurring data. These findings make dataset compression relevant to training efficiency while emphasizing that the small dataset is optimized for its learning role. The analyses begin to examine what information such compressed collections contain.
summary.tldr: A distributed kernel-based framework distills image datasets into tiny collections with strong reported classification performance.

title: Dataset Distillation with Infinitely Wide Convolutional Networks

abstract: A precise understanding of why units in an artificial network respond to certain stimuli would constitute a big step towards explainable artificial intelligence. One widely used approach towards this goal is to visualize unit responses via activation maximization. These feature visualizations are purported to provide humans with precise information about the image features that cause a unit to be activated - an advantage over other alternatives like strongly activating dataset samples. If humans indeed gain causal insight from visualizations, this should enable them to predict the effect of an intervention, such as how occluding a certain patch of the image (say, a dog's head) changes a unit's activation. Here, we test this hypothesis by asking humans to decide which of two square occlusions causes a larger change to a unit's activation.Both a large-scale crowdsourced experiment and measurements with experts show that on average the extremely activating feature visualizations by Olah et al. (2017) indeed help humans on this task ($68 \pm 4$% accuracy; baseline performance without any visualizations is $60 \pm 3$%). However, they do not provide any substantial advantage over other visualizations (such as e.g. dataset samples), which yield similar performance ($66\pm3$% to $67 \pm3$% accuracy). Taken together, we propose an objective psychophysical task to quantify the benefit of unit-level interpretability methods for humans, and find no evidence that a widely-used feature visualization method provides humans with better "causal understanding" of unit activations than simple alternative visualizations.

paragraphs: Feature visualizations synthesize images that strongly activate particular network units. This paper tests that interpretation through a concrete prediction task: can people judge which of two square image occlusions will change a unit's activation more?

Activation-maximizing visualizations help on average, producing 68 ± 4% accuracy compared with 60 ± 3% without visualizations. The study therefore finds useful assistance from visualization, but no evidence of a substantial causal-understanding advantage for the particular activation-maximization method tested. Its broader contribution is an objective human task for evaluating unit-level interpretability: an explanation should help people anticipate the consequences of an intervention. This makes the claimed benefit measurable through predictions about changes to images, rather than through how convincing a visualization appears.
summary.tldr: Activation-maximizing visualizations help people predict occlusion effects, but show no substantial advantage over simpler visual examples.

title: How Well do Feature Visualizations Support Causal Understanding of CNN Activations?

abstract: Domain adaptation (DA) attempts to transfer the knowledge from a labeled source domain to an unlabeled target domain that follows different distribution from the source. To achieve this, DA methods include a source classification objective to extract the source knowledge and a domain alignment objective to diminish the domain shift, ensuring knowledge transfer. Typically, former DA methods adopt some weight hyper-parameters to linearly combine the training objectives to form an overall objective. However, the gradient directions of these objectives may conflict with each other due to domain shift. Under such circumstances, the linear optimization scheme might decrease the overall objective value at the expense of damaging one of the training objectives, leading to restricted solutions. In this paper, we rethink the optimization scheme for DA from a gradient-based perspective. We propose a Pareto Domain Adaptation (ParetoDA) approach to control the overall optimization direction, aiming to cooperatively optimize all training objectives. Specifically, to reach a desirable solution on the target domain, we design a surrogate loss mimicking target classification. To improve target-prediction accuracy to support the mimicking, we propose a target-prediction refining mechanism which exploits domain labels via Bayes’ theorem. On the other hand, since prior knowledge of weighting schemes for objectives is often unavailable to guide optimization to approach the optimal solution on the target domain, we propose a dynamic preference mechanism to dynamically guide our cooperative optimization by the gradient of the surrogate loss on a held-out unlabeled target dataset. Our theoretical analyses show that the held-out data can guide but will not be over-fitted by the optimization. Extensive experiments on image classification and semantic segmentation benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of ParetoDA

The paper points out that their gradients can conflict: improving a weighted sum may still damage one component, limiting the solutions reached by ordinary combined-objective optimization.

ParetoDA controls the overall update direction to encourage cooperative progress across objectives. To guide that progress toward useful target predictions, it introduces a surrogate loss that imitates target classification. A prediction-refinement mechanism uses domain labels through Bayes' theorem to support this surrogate, despite the absence of target class labels.

The method also dynamically adjusts its optimization preference using the surrogate-loss gradient on held-out, unlabeled target data. This supplies guidance when an appropriate weighting scheme is not known beforehand. The theoretical analysis establishes that the held-out data can guide optimization without being overfitted by it. Experiments on image classification and semantic segmentation demonstrate effectiveness. The central contribution is treating adaptation as a problem of coordinating competing update directions, with target-oriented guidance throughout training.
summary.tldr: ParetoDA coordinates conflicting adaptation objectives using gradient control and a target-oriented surrogate derived from unlabeled target data.

title: Pareto Domain Adaptation

abstract: Surrogate risk minimization is an ubiquitous paradigm in supervised machine learning, wherein a target problem is solved by minimizing a surrogate loss on a dataset. Surrogate regret bounds, also called excess risk bounds, are a common tool to prove generalization rates for surrogate risk minimization. While surrogate regret bounds have been developed for certain classes of loss functions, such as proper losses, general results are relatively sparse. We provide two general results. The first gives a linear surrogate regret bound for any polyhedral (piecewise-linear and convex) surrogate, meaning that surrogate generalization rates translate directly to target rates. The second shows that for sufficiently non-polyhedral surrogates, the regret bound is a square root, meaning fast surrogate generalization rates translate to slow rates for the target. Together, these results suggest polyhedral surrogates are optimal in many cases.

paragraphs: Supervised learning often optimizes a convenient surrogate loss instead of the target loss that defines success. A surrogate regret bound describes how excess error on that training objective translates into excess error on the target task. This paper develops general results about that translation for different kinds of surrogate functions.

The first result gives a linear regret bound for polyhedral surrogates, whose functions are convex and piecewise linear. A linear relationship means that rates of improvement in surrogate generalization transfer directly to target rates. This provides a broad connection between the geometry of the training loss and the guarantees available for the actual task.

The second result concerns sufficiently non-polyhedral surrogates, for which the regret relationship is a square root. In that case, fast surrogate rates translate into slower target rates. Together, the results suggest that polyhedral surrogates are optimal in many cases. The conclusion concerns how guarantees transfer between objectives, with the non-polyhedral result explicitly restricted to the sufficiently non-polyhedral class.
summary.tldr: Polyhedral surrogates admit linear regret transfer, while sufficiently non-polyhedral surrogates incur a square-root relationship that slows target rates.

title: Surrogate Regret Bounds for Polyhedral Losses

abstract: Many modern machine learning tasks require models with high tail performance, i.e. high performance over the worst-off samples in the dataset. This problem has been widely studied in fields such as algorithmic fairness, class imbalance, and risk-sensitive decision making. A popular approach to maximize the model's tail performance is to minimize the CVaR (Conditional Value at Risk) loss, which computes the average risk over the tails of the loss. However, for classification tasks where models are evaluated by the zero-one loss, we show that if the classifiers are deterministic, then the minimizer of the average zero-one loss also minimizes the CVaR zero-one loss, suggesting that CVaR loss minimization is not helpful without additional assumptions. We circumvent this negative result by minimizing the CVaR loss over randomized classifiers, for which the minimizers of the average zero-one loss and the CVaR zero-one loss are no longer the same, so minimizing the latter can lead to better tail performance. To learn such randomized classifiers, we propose the Boosted CVaR Classification framework which is motivated by a direct relationship between CVaR and a classical boosting algorithm called LPBoost. Based on this framework, we design an algorithm called $\alpha$-AdaLPBoost. We empirically evaluate our proposed algorithm on four benchmark datasets and show that it achieves higher tail performance than deterministic model training methods.

A common objective is Conditional Value at Risk, or CVaR, which averages losses in the unfavorable tail. The authors identify a specific obstacle when classifiers are deterministic and evaluation uses zero-one loss.

Under those conditions, a classifier minimizing average zero-one loss also minimizes CVaR zero-one loss. Consequently, changing to the CVaR objective does not by itself provide the hoped-for benefit without additional assumptions. They develop Boosted CVaR Classification from a direct connection between CVaR and LPBoost, then introduce an algorithm called α-AdaLPBoost. On four benchmark datasets, it achieves higher tail performance than deterministic training methods. The contribution combines a precise negative result with a constructive alternative: randomization makes CVaR optimization potentially useful in the classification setting studied.
summary.tldr: Randomized boosted classifiers make CVaR optimization useful for improving tail performance where deterministic zero-one classification faces an obstacle.

title: Boosted CVaR Classification

abstract: Discrete-time diffusion-based generative models and score matching methods have shown promising results in modeling high-dimensional image data. Recently, Song et al. (2021) show that diffusion processes that transform data into noise can be reversed via learning the score function, i.e. the gradient of the log-density of the perturbed data. They propose to plug the learned score function into an inverse formula to define a generative diffusion process. Despite the empirical success, a theoretical underpinning of this procedure is still lacking. In this work, we approach the (continuous-time) generative diffusion directly and derive a variational framework for likelihood estimation, which includes continuous-time normalizing flows as a special case, and can be seen as an infinitely deep variational autoencoder. Under this framework, we show that minimizing the score-matching loss is equivalent to maximizing a lower bound of the likelihood of the plug-in reverse SDE proposed by Song et al. (2021), bridging the theoretical gap.

paragraphs: Diffusion generation starts from a process that gradually turns data into noise, then seeks to reverse it. One approach learns the score: the gradient of the perturbed data's log density. Inserting this learned quantity into a reverse diffusion formula produces a generative process, but empirical success alone does not explain what likelihood objective that training procedure serves.

The paper addresses this question by developing a variational framework directly for continuous-time generative diffusion. The framework provides a way to estimate likelihood through a lower bound. It also contains continuous-time normalizing flows as a special case and admits an interpretation as a variational autoencoder with infinitely many layers.

Within this framework, minimizing the score-matching objective is equivalent to maximizing a likelihood lower bound for the plug-in reverse stochastic differential equation. This establishes a precise connection between learning the score and training a probabilistic generative model. The equivalence concerns a lower bound on likelihood, preserving the distinction between the training objective and exact likelihood maximization.
summary.tldr: A variational framework shows that score matching maximizes a likelihood lower bound for a continuous-time reverse diffusion model.

title: A Variational Perspective on Diffusion-Based Generative Models and Score Matching

abstract: Rematerialization and offloading are two well known strategies to save memory during the training phase of deep neural networks, allowing data scientists to consider larger models, batch sizes or higher resolution data. Rematerialization trades memory for computation time, whereas Offloading trades memory for data movements. As these two resources are independent, it is appealing to consider the simultaneous combination of both strategies to save even more memory. We precisely model the costs and constraints corresponding to Deep Learning frameworks such as PyTorch or Tensorflow, we propose optimal algorithms to find a valid sequence of memory-constrained operations and finally, we evaluate the performance of proposed algorithms on realistic networks and computation platforms. Our experiments show that the possibility to offload can remove one third of the overhead of rematerialization, and that together they can reduce the memory used for activations by a factor 4 to 6, with an overhead below 20%.

paragraphs: Training deep networks requires memory for intermediate activations. Two established ways to reduce that demand make different tradeoffs: rematerialization recomputes values when needed, while offloading moves them out of the constrained memory. This paper investigates how to coordinate both strategies so that computation and data movement can jointly reduce memory use.

The authors model the costs and constraints associated with frameworks such as PyTorch and TensorFlow. They then propose optimal algorithms for finding valid sequences of operations under memory constraints. The scheduling problem matters because decisions about retaining, moving, and recomputing activations interact; combining the strategies requires accounting for those interactions.

Experiments on realistic networks and computing platforms show that allowing offloading can eliminate one-third of rematerialization’s overhead. Together, the strategies reduce activation memory by a factor of four to six with overhead below 20% in the reported experiments. These results indicate that carefully coordinated memory management can make larger models, batches, or higher-resolution inputs more feasible, while keeping the additional training cost relatively modest in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Jointly scheduling activation recomputation and offloading substantially reduces training memory with limited overhead in the reported experiments.

title: Efficient Combination of Rematerialization and Offloading for Training DNNs

abstract: We challenge a common assumption underlying most supervised deep learning: that a model makes a prediction depending only on its parameters and the features of a single input. To this end, we introduce a general-purpose deep learning architecture that takes as input the entire dataset instead of processing one datapoint at a time. Our approach uses self-attention to reason about relationships between datapoints explicitly, which can be seen as realizing non-parametric models using parametric attention mechanisms. However, unlike conventional non-parametric models, we let the model learn end-to-end from the data how to make use of other datapoints for prediction. Empirically, our models solve cross-datapoint lookup and complex reasoning tasks unsolvable by traditional deep learning models. We show highly competitive results on tabular data, early results on CIFAR-10, and give insight into how the model makes use of the interactions between points.

paragraphs: Most supervised neural networks predict from one input together with their learned parameters. This paper explores an alternative in which the model receives the entire dataset and explicitly reasons about relationships among examples. The aim is to let information in other data points contribute directly to a particular prediction.

The architecture uses self-attention between data points and learns end to end how those interactions should be used. It resembles a nonparametric model because predictions can depend on other observations, while the attention mechanisms themselves have learned parameters. This combines access to the dataset with a trainable procedure for deciding which cross-example relationships matter.

Empirically, the models solve cross-data-point lookup and complex reasoning tasks that the traditional deep-learning models considered cannot solve. The paper also reports highly competitive results on tabular data and preliminary results on CIFAR-10, alongside analysis of how interactions between points are used. These findings support making relationships among examples part of the prediction computation, particularly for tasks whose relevant information extends beyond a single input.
summary.tldr: A dataset-wide attention architecture learns to use relationships between examples when making predictions.

title: Self-Attention Between Datapoints: Going Beyond Individual Input-Output Pairs in Deep Learning

abstract: Consider learning a generative model for time-series data. The sequential setting poses a unique challenge: Not only should the generator capture the *conditional* dynamics of (stepwise) transitions, but its open-loop rollouts should also preserve the *joint* distribution of (multi-step) trajectories. On one hand, autoregressive models trained by MLE allow learning and computing explicit transition distributions, but suffer from compounding error during rollouts. On the other hand, adversarial models based on GAN training alleviate such exposure bias, but transitions are implicit and hard to assess. In this work, we study a generative framework that seeks to combine the strengths of both: Motivated by a moment-matching objective to mitigate compounding error, we optimize a local (but forward-looking) *transition policy*, where the reinforcement signal is provided by a global (but stepwise-decomposable) *energy model* trained by contrastive estimation. At training, the two components are learned cooperatively, avoiding the instabilities typical of adversarial objectives. At inference, the learned policy serves as the generator for iterative sampling, and the learned energy serves as a trajectory-level measure for evaluating sample quality. By expressly training a policy to imitate sequential behavior of time-series features in a dataset, this approach embodies "*generation by imitation*". Theoretically, we illustrate the correctness of this formulation and the consistency of the algorithm. Empirically, we evaluate its ability to generate predictively useful samples from real-world datasets, verifying that it performs at the standard of existing benchmarks.

paragraphs: Generating a time series requires both plausible next steps and coherent trajectories across many steps. Models trained to predict individual transitions can accumulate errors when generating their own sequences. Adversarial methods can reduce this exposure problem, but their implicit transitions are harder to assess. The paper seeks to combine strengths of both approaches.

Its framework learns a transition policy together with an energy model. The policy chooses local transitions while looking ahead, and the energy model supplies a trajectory-level learning signal that can be decomposed across steps. Contrastive estimation trains the energy model, while a moment-matching motivation guides the effort to reduce compounding errors. The two components learn cooperatively, avoiding the adversarial training instabilities targeted by the approach.

During generation, the policy produces samples iteratively, and the energy model provides a measure of whole-trajectory quality. The authors give theoretical support for the formulation's correctness and the algorithm's consistency. Experiments on real-world datasets find that generated samples are predictively useful and perform at the level of existing benchmarks, supporting imitation as a framework for sequential generation.
summary.tldr: A cooperatively trained transition policy and contrastive energy model generate time series while accounting for whole-trajectory behavior.

title: Time-series Generation by Contrastive Imitation

abstract: Promoting behavioural diversity is of critical importance in multi-agent reinforcement learning, since it helps the agent population maintain robust performance when encountering unfamiliar opponents at test time, or, when the game is highly non-transitive in the strategy space (e.g., Rock-Paper-Scissor). While a myriad of diversity metrics have been proposed, there are no widely accepted or unified definitions in the literature, making the consequent diversity-aware learning algorithms difficult to evaluate and the insights elusive. In this work, we propose a novel metric called the Unified Diversity Measure (UDM) that offers a unified view for existing diversity metrics. Based on UDM, we design the UDM-Fictitious Play (UDM-FP) and UDM-Policy Space Response Oracle (UDM-PSRO) algorithms as efficient solvers for normal-form games and open-ended games. In theory, we prove that UDM-based methods can enlarge the gamescape by increasing the response capacity of the strategy pool, and have convergence guarantee to two-player Nash equilibrium. We validate our algorithms on games that show strong non-transitivity, and empirical results show that our algorithms achieve better performances than strong PSRO baselines in terms of the exploitability and population effectivity.

paragraphs: In multiagent reinforcement learning, a population of different strategies can help against unfamiliar opponents. Diversity is especially useful when strategies form cycles of advantage, as in Rock-Paper-Scissors. However, competing definitions of diversity make it difficult to compare learning methods or explain which kinds of variation improve a strategy population.

The paper introduces the Unified Diversity Measure, or UDM, to provide a common perspective on existing diversity metrics. It then builds two learning algorithms around that measure: UDM-Fictitious Play for normal-form games and UDM-Policy Space Response Oracle for open-ended games. Diversity therefore becomes part of the procedure for developing the strategy pool, rather than only a quantity measured afterward.

On games with strong non-transitivity, the proposed algorithms outperform strong PSRO baselines on exploitability and population effectivity. These findings connect the diversity measure to both strategic coverage and observed competitive performance.
summary.tldr: A unified diversity measure supports strategy-population algorithms with theoretical guarantees and improved results on strongly non-transitive games.

title: A Unified Diversity Measure for Multiagent Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Image reconstruction enhanced by regularizers, e.g., to enforce sparsity, low rank or smoothness priors on images, has many successful applications in vision tasks such as computer photography, biomedical and spectral imaging. It has been well accepted that non-convex regularizers normally perform better than convex ones in terms of the reconstruction quality. But their convergence analysis is only established to a critical point, rather than the global optima. To mitigate the loss of guarantees for global optima, we propose to apply the concept of invexity and provide the first list of proved invex regularizers for improving image reconstruction. Moreover, we establish convergence guarantees to global optima for various advanced image reconstruction techniques after being improved by such invex regularization. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first practical work applying invex regularization to improve imaging with global optima guarantees. To demonstrate the effectiveness of invex regularization, numerical experiments are conducted for various imaging tasks using benchmark datasets.

Those guarantees apply to the analyzed constructions rather than to non-convex regularization in general.
summary.tldr: Proved invex regularizers improve image reconstruction while enabling global-optimum convergence guarantees for the analyzed methods.

title: Improved Imaging by Invex Regularizers with Global Optima Guarantees

abstract: Fine-tuning pretrained language models (LMs) without making any architectural changes has become a norm for learning various language downstream tasks. However, for non-language downstream tasks, a common practice is to employ task-specific designs for input, output layers, and loss functions. For instance, it is possible to fine-tune an LM into an MNIST classifier by replacing the word embedding layer with an image patch embedding layer, the word token output layer with a 10-way output layer, and the word prediction loss with a 10-way classification loss, respectively. A natural question arises: Can LM fine-tuning solve non-language downstream tasks without changing the model architecture or loss function? To answer this, we propose Language-Interfaced Fine-Tuning (LIFT) and study its efficacy and limitations by conducting an extensive empirical study on a suite of non-language classification and regression tasks. LIFT does not make any changes to the model architecture or loss function, and it solely relies on the natural language interface, enabling "no-code machine learning with LMs." We find that LIFT performs comparably well across a wide range of low-dimensional classification and regression tasks, matching the performances of the best baselines in many cases, especially for the classification tasks. We also report experimental results on the fundamental properties of LIFT, including inductive bias, robustness, and sample complexity. We also analyze the effect of pretraining on LIFT and a few properties/techniques specific to LIFT, e.g., context-aware learning via appropriate prompting, calibrated predictions, data generation, and two-stage fine-tuning. Our code is available at https://github.com/UW-Madison-Lee-Lab/LanguageInterfacedFineTuning.

title: LIFT: Language-Interfaced Fine-Tuning for Non-language Machine Learning Tasks

abstract: Group Testing (GT) is about learning a (hidden) subset $K$, of size $k$, of some large domain $N$, of size $n \gg k$, using a sequence of queries. A result of a query provides some information about the intersection of the query with the unknown set $K$. The goal is to design efficient (polynomial time) and scalable (polylogarithmic number of queries per element in $K$) algorithms for constructing queries that allow to decode every hidden set $K$ based on the results of the queries. A vast majority of the previous work focused on randomized algorithms minimizing the number of queries; however, in case of large domains N, randomization may result in asignificant deviation from the expected precision of learning the set $K$. Others assumed unlimited computational power (existential results) or adaptiveness of queries (next query could be constructed taking into account the results of the previous queries) – the former approach is less practical due to non-efficiency, and the latter has several drawbacks including non-parallelization. To avoid all the abovementioned drawbacks, for Quantitative Group Testing (QGT) where query result is the size of its intersection with the hidden set, we present the first efficient and scalable non-adaptive deterministic algorithms for constructing queries and decoding a hidden set K from the results of the queries – these solutions do not use any randomization, adaptiveness or unlimited computational power.

paragraphs: Group testing seeks a small hidden subset within a much larger collection by querying groups of elements. This paper studies quantitative group testing, where each answer gives the number of hidden elements inside the queried group. The objective is to construct informative queries and recover every possible hidden subset efficiently.

The proposed algorithms are deterministic and non-adaptive: they use no random choices, and all queries can be specified without waiting for earlier answers. This avoids dependence on randomized outcomes and removes the sequential dependency of adaptive query construction. The contribution covers both building the query set and decoding the hidden subset from the resulting counts.

The authors claim the first algorithms for this setting that combine polynomial-time computation with scalability measured by a polylogarithmic number of queries per hidden element. These requirements distinguish an executable construction from a proof that a suitable query set merely exists. The result brings computational efficiency, controlled query growth, and deterministic recovery together under the quantitative-answer model.
summary.tldr: The paper gives efficient deterministic quantitative group-testing algorithms whose queries are fixed in advance and scale polylogarithmically per hidden element.

title: Scalable and Efficient Non-adaptive Deterministic Group Testing

abstract: The intensive computations in convolutional neural networks (CNNs) pose challenges for resource-constrained devices; eliminating redundant computations from convolution is essential. This paper gives a principled method to detect and avoid transient redundancy, a type of redundancy existing in input data or activation maps and hence changing across inferences. By introducing a new form of convolution (TREC), this new method makes transient redundancy detection and avoidance an inherent part of the CNN architecture, and the determination of the best configurations for redundancy elimination part of CNN backward propagation. We provide a rigorous proof of the robustness and convergence of TREC-equipped CNNs. TREC removes over 96% computations and achieves 3.51x average speedups on microcontrollers with minimal (about 0.7%) accuracy loss.
