paragraphs: Convolutional neural networks can require too much computation for resource-constrained devices. This paper focuses on transient redundancy: redundant information in inputs or activation maps that changes from one inference to another. Because the redundancy varies with the data being processed, detecting and avoiding it must account for each inference.

TREC introduces a form of convolution that makes redundancy detection and avoidance part of the network architecture. It also makes choosing configurations for eliminating redundancy part of backward propagation. This brings the decision about how to exploit changing redundancy into the learning process, connecting the architecture’s computational behavior to training.

The authors provide proofs of robustness and convergence for networks equipped with TREC. They report removal of more than 96% of computations and an average 3.51-fold speedup on microcontrollers, with approximately 0.7% accuracy loss. The results show substantial practical acceleration in the evaluated setting, while also distinguishing the reduction in counted computations from the smaller, measured improvement in execution speed.
summary.tldr: TREC learns to detect and avoid input-dependent convolution redundancy, yielding reported microcontroller speedups with a small accuracy loss.

title: TREC: Transient Redundancy Elimination-based Convolution

abstract: The graph retrieval problem is to search in a large corpus of graphs for ones that are most similar to a query graph. A common consideration for scoring similarity is the maximum common subgraph (MCS) between the query and corpus graphs, usually counting the number of common edges (i.e., MCES). In some applications, it is also desirable that the common subgraph be connected, i.e., the maximum common connected subgraph (MCCS). Finding exact MCES and MCCS is intractable, but may be unnecessary if ranking corpus graphs by relevance is the goal. We design fast and trainable neural functions that approximate MCES and MCCS well. Late interaction methods compute dense representations for the query and corpus graph separately, and compare these representations using simple similarity functions at the last stage, leading to highly scalable systems. Early interaction methods combine information from both graphs right from the input stages, are usually considerably more accurate, but slower. We propose both late and early interaction neural MCES and MCCS formulations. They are both based on a continuous relaxation of a node alignment matrix between query and corpus nodes. For MCCS, we propose a novel differentiable network for estimating the size of the largest connected common subgraph. Extensive experiments with seven data sets show that our proposals are superior among late interaction models in terms of both accuracy and speed. Our early interaction models provide accuracy competitive with the state of the art, at substantially greater speeds.

paragraphs: Graph retrieval ranks stored graphs by similarity to a query. A useful measure is the size of their largest shared subgraph, sometimes with the additional requirement that it be connected. Computing these quantities exactly is intractable, but approximate scores may be sufficient when the objective is to rank candidates.

The authors develop neural approximations for both common-edge and connected-common-subgraph measures. Their formulations use a continuous relaxation of the alignment between nodes in the two graphs. Late interaction models represent each graph separately before comparing them, supporting scalability. Early interaction models exchange information between the graphs from the input stages. Experiments on seven datasets show that the proposed late interaction models outperform other late interaction methods in both accuracy and speed. The early interaction models achieve accuracy competitive with the state of the art at substantially higher speeds. The paper thus offers alternatives for different retrieval needs while retaining a similarity objective grounded in shared graph structure.
summary.tldr: Neural approximations of maximum common subgraphs enable fast graph retrieval with competitive accuracy in both early and late interaction models.

title: Maximum Common Subgraph Guided Graph Retrieval: Late and Early Interaction Networks

abstract: Among the most striking features of retinal organization is the grouping of its output neurons, the retinal ganglion cells (RGCs), into a diversity of functional types. Each of these types exhibits a mosaic-like organization of receptive fields (RFs) that tiles the retina and visual space. Previous work has shown that many features of RGC organization, including the existence of ON and OFF cell types, the structure of spatial RFs, and their relative arrangement, can be predicted on the basis of efficient coding theory. This theory posits that the nervous system is organized to maximize information in its encoding of stimuli while minimizing metabolic costs. Here, we use efficient coding theory to present a comprehensive account of mosaic organization in the case of natural videos as the retinal channel capacity---the number of simulated RGCs available for encoding---is varied. We show that mosaic density increases with channel capacity up to a series of critical points at which, surprisingly, new cell types emerge. Each successive cell type focuses on increasingly high temporal frequencies and integrates signals over larger spatial areas. In addition, we show theoretically and in simulation that a transition from mosaic alignment to anti-alignment across pairs of cell types is observed with increasing output noise and decreasing input noise. Together, these results offer a unified perspective on the relationship between retinal mosaics, efficient coding, and channel capacity that can help to explain the stunning functional diversity of retinal cell types.

paragraphs: Retinal ganglion cells form distinct functional types, each arranging its receptive fields into a mosaic that covers visual space. This paper asks how those mosaics could emerge from efficient coding: the principle that neural systems preserve information about stimuli while limiting metabolic costs. The authors study natural videos while varying the number of simulated output cells available for encoding.

As this channel capacity increases, existing mosaics become denser until critical points are reached and additional cell types appear. Successive types respond to increasingly high temporal frequencies and combine signals across larger spatial areas. The model thus links the available number of cells to both the density of visual coverage and the emergence of functional diversity.

Theory and simulations show a transition from alignment to anti-alignment as output noise increases and input noise decreases. Together, these findings provide an efficient-coding account of how capacity and noise can shape retinal organization, offering a possible explanation for the diversity of retinal cell types.
summary.tldr: An efficient-coding model links retinal capacity and noise to mosaic density, the emergence of cell types, and their spatial arrangement.

title: Efficient coding, channel capacity, and the emergence of retinal mosaics

abstract: The impossibility theorem of fairness is a foundational result in the algorithmic fairness literature. It states that outside of special cases, one cannot exactly and simultaneously satisfy all three common and intuitive definitions of fairness - demographic parity, equalized odds, and predictive rate parity. This result has driven most works to focus on solutions for one or two of the metrics. Rather than follow suit, in this paper we present a framework that pushes the limits of the impossibility theorem in order to satisfy all three metrics to the best extent possible. We develop an integer-programming based approach that can yield a certifiably optimal post-processing method for simultaneously satisfying multiple fairness criteria under small violations. We show experiments demonstrating that our post-processor can improve fairness across the different definitions simultaneously with minimal model performance reduction. We also discuss applications of our framework for model selection and fairness explainability, thereby attempting to answer the question: Who's the fairest of them all?

This incompatibility often leads researchers to optimize only one or two criteria. The paper instead asks how closely a prediction system can satisfy all three when small violations are allowed.

Their framework can produce a certifiably optimal solution for simultaneously addressing multiple fairness criteria within that formulation. Allowing small departures from exact fairness creates room to search for joint improvements without contradicting the impossibility result about exact simultaneous satisfaction.

Experiments show that the post-processor can improve multiple fairness definitions at once while reducing model performance only minimally. The authors also discuss using the framework to compare models and explain their fairness properties. The contribution turns a general incompatibility into an optimization problem about achievable compromises, with certificates of optimality available for the proposed formulation.
summary.tldr: An integer-programming framework seeks certifiably optimal compromises among fairness criteria by allowing small violations of exact fairness.

title: Pushing the limits of fairness impossibility: Who's the fairest of them all?

abstract: Multi-task learning (MTL) jointly learns a set of tasks by sharing parameters among tasks. It is a promising approach for reducing storage costs while improving task accuracy for many computer vision tasks. The effective adoption of MTL faces two main challenges. The first challenge is to determine what parameters to share across tasks to optimize for both memory efficiency and task accuracy. The second challenge is to automatically apply MTL algorithms to an arbitrary CNN backbone without requiring time-consuming manual re-implementation and significant domain expertise. This paper addresses the challenges by developing the first programming framework AutoMTL that automates efficient MTL model development for vision tasks. AutoMTL takes as inputs an arbitrary backbone convolutional neural network (CNN) and a set of tasks to learn, and automatically produces a multi-task model that achieves high accuracy and small memory footprint simultaneously. Experiments on three popular MTL benchmarks (CityScapes, NYUv2, Tiny-Taskonomy) demonstrate the effectiveness of AutoMTL over state-of-the-art approaches as well as the generalizability of AutoMTL across CNNs. AutoMTL is open-sourced and available at https://github.com/zhanglijun95/AutoMTL.

paragraphs: Multi-task learning lets several prediction tasks share model parameters, potentially reducing storage while improving accuracy. Making this work requires deciding which parameters should be shared. It also creates an engineering burden: applying a multi-task method to a different convolutional backbone can require substantial manual implementation and expertise.

AutoMTL addresses both issues through a programming framework. Its inputs are a convolutional neural network backbone and the tasks to learn. It automatically produces a multi-task model intended to combine high task accuracy with a small memory footprint. This makes the choice of parameter sharing part of an automated development process.

Experiments on CityScapes, NYUv2, and Tiny-Taskonomy demonstrate the framework's effectiveness relative to state-of-the-art approaches and its ability to work across different convolutional networks. The contribution matters because efficient sharing and ease of adoption are connected: a useful sharing strategy becomes more accessible when developers can apply it to their backbone without repeatedly rebuilding the method by hand.
summary.tldr: AutoMTL automates the construction of shared multi-task vision models that combine strong accuracy with a small memory footprint.

title: AutoMTL: A Programming Framework for Automating Efficient Multi-Task Learning

abstract: Despite the success of cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning algorithms, most of them focus on a single team composition, which prevents them from being used in more realistic scenarios where dynamic team composition is possible. While some studies attempt to solve this problem via multi-task learning in a fixed set of team compositions, there is still a risk of overfitting to the training set, which may lead to catastrophic performance when facing dramatically varying team compositions during execution. To address this problem, we propose to use mutual information (MI) as an augmented reward to prevent individual policies from relying too much on team-related information and encourage agents to learn policies that are robust in different team compositions. Optimizing this MI-augmented objective in an off-policy manner can be intractable due to the existence of dynamic marginal distribution. To alleviate this problem, we first propose a multi-agent policy iteration algorithm with a fixed marginal distribution and prove its convergence and optimality. Then, we propose to employ the Blahut–Arimoto algorithm and an imaginary team composition distribution for optimization with approximate marginal distribution as the practical implementation. Empirically, our method demonstrates strong zero-shot generalization to dynamic team compositions in complex cooperative tasks.

paragraphs: Cooperative agents trained with one team composition can struggle when their teammates change. Even training on several fixed compositions may leave policies overly dependent on those particular teams. This paper augments the reward with a mutual-information term designed to discourage excessive reliance on team-related information and encourage behavior that works across different compositions.

Optimizing that objective off-policy is difficult because it involves a marginal distribution that changes during learning. The authors first analyze a version with a fixed marginal distribution, proving convergence and optimality for its policy-iteration algorithm. For practical training, they then use the Blahut–Arimoto algorithm and an imaginary distribution over team compositions to work with an approximate marginal.

Experiments show strong zero-shot generalization to changing team compositions in complex cooperative tasks. The theoretical result belongs to the fixed-marginal formulation, while the practical implementation uses approximation to address the harder optimization problem. Together, the results provide a principled objective for reducing dependence on familiar teams and empirical evidence that its implementation can improve adaptability.
summary.tldr: Mutual-information regularization encourages cooperative policies that generalize to changing teams, with guarantees for a fixed-marginal formulation.

title: Mutual-Information Regularized Multi-Agent Policy Iteration

abstract: Handling out-of-distribution (OOD) samples has become a major stake in the real-world deployment of machine learning systems. This work explores the use of self-supervised contrastive learning to the simultaneous detection of two types of OOD samples: unseen classes and adversarial perturbations. First, we pair self-supervised contrastive learning with the maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) two-sample test. This approach enables us to robustly test whether two independent sets of samples originate from the same distribution, and we demonstrate its effectiveness by discriminating between CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-10.1 with higher confidence than previous work. Motivated by this success, we introduce CADet (Contrastive Anomaly Detection), a novel method for OOD detection of single samples. CADet draws inspiration from MMD, but leverages the similarity between contrastive transformations of a same sample. CADet outperforms existing adversarial detection methods in identifying adversarially perturbed samples on ImageNet and achieves comparable performance to unseen label detection methods on two challenging benchmarks: ImageNet-O and iNaturalist. Significantly, CADet is fully self-supervised and requires neither labels for in-distribution samples nor access to OOD examples.

paragraphs: A deployed model may encounter unfamiliar categories or inputs altered by adversarial perturbations. This paper explores detecting both kinds of unusual input through self-supervised contrastive learning. Its approach does not require labels for the ordinary training samples or examples of the out-of-distribution inputs it will later try to identify.

The authors first combine contrastive representations with the maximum mean discrepancy two-sample test. This tests whether two independent collections of observations come from the same distribution. They report distinguishing CIFAR-10 from CIFAR-10.1 with higher confidence than previous work. Building on this result, they introduce CADet for detecting anomalies one sample at a time, using similarities between contrastive transformations of that sample.

CADet outperforms existing adversarial-detection methods on adversarially perturbed ImageNet samples. For unfamiliar categories, it performs comparably to unseen-label detection methods on ImageNet-O and iNaturalist. These results support using contrastive representations for both group-level distribution testing and individual anomaly detection, while keeping the different reported outcomes clear: improved adversarial detection and comparable unseen-category detection.
summary.tldr: CADet uses self-supervised contrastive similarities to detect unfamiliar and adversarial inputs without labeled training data or OOD examples.

title: CADet: Fully Self-Supervised Out-Of-Distribution Detection With Contrastive Learning

abstract: A fundamental problem in many sciences is the learning of causal structure underlying a system, typically through observation and experimentation. Commonly, one even collects data across multiple domains, such as gene sequencing from different labs, or neural recordings from different species. Although there exist methods for learning the equivalence class of causal diagrams from observational and experimental data, they are meant to operate in a single domain. In this paper, we develop a fundamental approach to structure learning in non-Markovian systems (i.e. when there exist latent confounders) leveraging observational and interventional data collected from multiple domains. Specifically, we start by showing that learning from observational data in multiple domains is equivalent to learning from interventional data with unknown targets in a single domain. But there are also subtleties when considering observational and experimental data. Using causal invariances derived from do-calculus, we define a property called S-Markov that connects interventional distributions from multiple-domains to graphical criteria on a selection diagram. Leveraging the S-Markov property, we introduce a new constraint-based causal discovery algorithm, S-FCI, that can learn from observational and interventional data from different domains. We prove that the algorithm is sound and subsumes existing constraint-based causal discovery algorithms.

This paper develops an approach that also allows latent confounders: unobserved factors that can influence multiple measured variables.

summary.tldr: S-FCI uses a new causal invariance property to soundly combine observational and experimental evidence across domains with latent confounders.

title: Causal discovery from observational and interventional data across multiple environments

abstract: In this paper, we propose a novel data-pruning approach called moving-one-sample-out (MoSo), which aims to identify and remove the least informative samples from the training set. The core insight behind MoSo is to determine the importance of each sample by assessing its impact on the optimal empirical risk. This is achieved by measuring the extent to which the empirical risk changes when a particular sample is excluded from the training set. Instead of using the computationally expensive leaving-one-out-retraining procedure, we propose an efficient first-order approximator that only requires gradient information from different training stages. The key idea behind our approximation is that samples with gradients that are consistently aligned with the average gradient of the training set are more informative and should receive higher scores, which could be intuitively understood as follows: if the gradient from a specific sample is consistent with the average gradient vector, it implies that optimizing the network using the sample will yield a similar effect on all remaining samples. Experimental results demonstrate that MoSo effectively mitigates severe performance degradation at high pruning ratios and achieves satisfactory performance across various settings. Experimental results demonstrate that MoSo effectively mitigates severe performance degradation at high pruning ratios and outperforms state-of-the-art methods by a large margin across various settings.

paragraphs: Training-data pruning requires deciding which examples contribute enough to keep. Moving-one-Sample-out, or MoSo, defines importance through an example's effect on the optimal training objective: how much would empirical risk change if that example were removed? This ties the pruning decision to the sample's contribution to learning across the remaining dataset.

Directly answering that question by retraining after every possible removal would be expensive. MoSo instead uses a first-order approximation based on gradients collected at different training stages. Examples receive higher scores when their gradients consistently point in a similar direction to the average training gradient, indicating agreement with the dataset's overall optimization direction.

The underlying intuition is that training on an aligned example should have an effect similar to training on the other examples. The reported experiments show that MoSo reduces severe performance losses when a large fraction of training data is removed and outperforms state-of-the-art pruning methods across various settings. Its contribution is therefore both a sample-importance criterion and an efficient approximation that makes that criterion usable.
summary.tldr: MoSo uses gradient alignment across training to identify informative examples and reduce performance losses from aggressive data pruning.

title: Data Pruning via Moving-one-Sample-out

abstract: Classification is a fundamental problem in machine learning, and considerable efforts have been recently devoted to the demanding long-tailed setting due to its prevalence in nature. Departure from the Bayesian framework, this paper rethinks classification from a matching perspective by studying the matching probability between samples and labels with optimal transport (OT) formulation. Specifically, we first propose a new variant of optimal transport, called Relative Entropic Optimal Transport (RE-OT), which guides the coupling solution to a known prior information matrix. We gives some theoretical results and their proof for RE-OT and surprisingly find RE-OT can help to deblur for barycenter images. Then we adopt inverse RE-OT for training long-tailed data and find that the loss derived from RE-OT has a similar form to Softmax-based cross-entropy loss, indicating a close connection between optimal transport and classification and the potential for transferring concepts between these two academic fields, such as barycentric projection in OT, which can map the labels back to the feature space. We further derive an epoch-varying RE-OT loss, and do the experiments on unbalanced image classification, molecule classification, instance segmentation and representation learning. Experimental results show its effectiveness.

paragraphs: The paper views classification as a matching problem between examples and labels. This perspective is especially relevant to long-tailed data, where some classes appear much more often than others. The authors develop Relative Entropic Optimal Transport, or RE-OT, which guides the transport coupling toward information supplied in a known prior matrix.

They establish theoretical results for this transport formulation and find that it can also help deblur barycenter images. For classification, they use inverse RE-OT to derive a training loss for long-tailed data. The loss resembles softmax cross-entropy, exposing a connection between a familiar classification objective and an optimal-transport matching formulation.

That connection suggests ways to transfer ideas between the two areas. One example is barycentric projection, which can map labels back into feature space. The authors further develop a version of the RE-OT loss that varies across training epochs. Experiments on unbalanced image classification, molecule classification, instance segmentation, and representation learning support its effectiveness. The contribution combines a prior-aware transport method with a new route to constructing classification losses.
summary.tldr: RE-OT uses prior-aware optimal transport to derive classification losses and connect long-tailed learning with sample-label matching.

title: Relative Entropic Optimal Transport: a (Prior-aware) Matching Perspective to (Unbalanced) Classification

abstract: Clustering is an important technique for identifying structural information in large-scale data analysis, where the underlying dataset may be too large to store. In many applications, recent data can provide more accurate information and thus older data past a certain time is expired. The sliding window model captures these desired properties and thus there has been substantial interest in clustering in the sliding window model. In this paper, we give the first algorithm that achieves near-optimal $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximation to $(k,z)$-clustering in the sliding window model. Our algorithm uses $\frac{k}{\min(\varepsilon^4,\varepsilon^{2+z})}\,\text{polylog}\frac{n\Delta}{\varepsilon}$ words of space when the points are from $[\Delta]^d$, thus significantly improving on works by Braverman et. al. (SODA 2016), Borassi et. al. (NeurIPS 2021), and Epasto et. al. (SODA 2022).Along the way, we develop a data structure for clustering called an online coreset, which outputs a coreset not only for the end of a stream, but also for all prefixes of the stream. Our online coreset samples $\frac{k}{\min(\varepsilon^4,\varepsilon^{2+z})}\,\text{polylog}\frac{n\Delta}{\varepsilon}$ points from the stream. We then show that any online coreset requires $\Omega\left(\frac{k}{\varepsilon^2}\log n\right)$ samples, which shows a separation between the problem of constructing an offline coreset, i.e., constructing online coresets is strictly harder. Our results also extend to general metrics on $[\Delta]^d$ and are near-optimal in light of a $\Omega\left(\frac{k}{\varepsilon^{2+z}}\right)$ lower bound for the size of an offline coreset.

The sliding-window model captures this by expiring older points while limiting storage. This paper gives an algorithm for general (k,z)-clustering in that model with a near-optimal approximation guarantee.

The algorithm achieves a (1+ε)-approximation, meaning its clustering objective stays within that multiplicative factor of the optimum. For points in the specified discrete coordinate domain, its space bound scales with k, an accuracy-dependent factor, and polylogarithmic terms. A key ingredient is an online coreset: a sampled summary that supports clustering for every prefix of the stream, rather than only its final state.

The authors also prove a lower bound on the samples required by any online coreset. This establishes that constructing summaries valid across stream prefixes is strictly harder than constructing an offline coreset. The results extend to general metrics on the stated domain, and offline coreset lower bounds support their near-optimality. The paper therefore combines an efficient streaming construction with evidence about the resources such summaries inherently require.
summary.tldr: The paper develops near-optimal sliding-window clustering using online coresets and proves lower bounds on the storage such summaries require.

title: Near-Optimal $k$-Clustering in the Sliding Window Model

abstract: Recent text-to-image generation models like DreamBooth have made remarkable progress in generating highly customized images of a target subject, by fine-tuning an ``expert model'' for a given subject from a few examples.However, this process is expensive, since a new expert model must be learned for each subject. In this paper, we present SuTI, a Subject-driven Text-to-Image generator that replaces subject-specific fine tuning with {in-context} learning.Given a few demonstrations of a new subject, SuTI can instantly generate novel renditions of the subject in different scenes, without any subject-specific optimization.SuTI is powered by {apprenticeship learning}, where a single apprentice model is learned from data generated by a massive number of subject-specific expert models. Specifically, we mine millions of image clusters from the Internet, each centered around a specific visual subject. We adopt these clusters to train a massive number of expert models, each specializing in a different subject. The apprentice model SuTI then learns to imitate the behavior of these fine-tuned experts. SuTI can generate high-quality and customized subject-specific images 20x faster than optimization-based SoTA methods. On the challenging DreamBench and DreamBench-v2, our human evaluation shows that SuTI significantly outperforms existing models like InstructPix2Pix, Textual Inversion, Imagic, Prompt2Prompt, Re-Imagen and DreamBooth.

paragraphs: Personalized image generators can learn a subject from a few examples, but training a separate expert for every subject is expensive. SuTI aims to make a new subject usable immediately through in-context examples. Given a few demonstrations, it generates new renditions in different scenes without performing subject-specific optimization.

The method obtains this ability through apprenticeship learning. The authors mine millions of image clusters from the Internet, each organized around a visual subject, and use them to train many subject-specific experts. A single apprentice model then learns to imitate those experts from the data they generate. The work of learning individual experts thus supplies training experience for a reusable generator.

The authors report customized image generation twenty times faster than optimization-based state-of-the-art methods. Human evaluations on DreamBench and DreamBench-v2 also show significant improvements over the compared models, including DreamBooth. These findings support learning a shared model from many specialists as a way to provide subject customization at use time through examples, while retaining the benefits of extensive expert-based training beforehand.
summary.tldr: SuTI learns from many subject-specific experts to personalize image generation from examples without optimizing a new model for each subject.

title: Subject-driven Text-to-Image Generation via Apprenticeship Learning

abstract: In many real-world scenarios it is crucial to be able to reliably and efficiently reason under uncertainty while capturing complex relationships in data. Probabilistic circuits (PCs), a prominent family of tractable probabilistic models, offer a remedy to this challenge by composing simple, tractable distributions into a high-dimensional probability distribution. However, learning PCs on heterogeneous data is challenging and densities of some parametric distributions are not available in closed form, limiting their potential use. We introduce characteristic circuits (CCs), a family of tractable probabilistic models providing a unified formalization of distributions over heterogeneous data in the spectral domain. The one-to-one relationship between characteristic functions and probability measures enables us to learn high-dimensional distributions on heterogeneous data domains and facilitates efficient probabilistic inference even when no closed-form density function is available. We show that the structure and parameters of CCs can be learned efficiently from the data and find that CCs outperform state-of-the-art density estimators for heterogeneous data domains on common benchmark data sets.

paragraphs: Probabilistic circuits represent complex distributions by combining simpler distributions in ways that keep reasoning computationally manageable. However, learning them becomes challenging when data contain heterogeneous types, and some useful distributions lack a closed-form density. Characteristic circuits address these issues by changing the mathematical representation used to describe the distributions.

The proposed models operate in the spectral domain through characteristic functions. Because a characteristic function uniquely corresponds to a probability measure, this representation can describe a distribution even when a convenient density formula is unavailable. The paper uses that relationship to provide a unified treatment of high-dimensional heterogeneous data while supporting efficient probabilistic inference.

The authors show that both the structure and parameters of characteristic circuits can be learned efficiently from data. On common benchmark datasets involving heterogeneous domains, the models outperform state-of-the-art density estimators. The significance is that tractable uncertainty modeling need not depend on every component distribution having an explicit density: a different representation can preserve useful inference and learning capabilities.
summary.tldr: Characteristic circuits use characteristic functions to learn tractable distributions over heterogeneous data, including cases without closed-form densities.

title: Characteristic Circuits

abstract: Exploring in environments with high-dimensional observations is hard. One promising approach for exploration is to use intrinsic rewards, which often boils down to estimating "novelty" of states, transitions, or trajectories with deep networks. Prior works have shown that conditional prediction objectives such as masked autoencoding can be seen as stochastic estimation of pseudo-likelihood. We show how this perspective naturally leads to a unified view on existing intrinsic reward approaches: they are special cases of conditional prediction, where the estimation of novelty can be seen as pseudo-likelihood estimation with different mask distributions. From this view, we propose a general framework for deriving intrinsic rewards -- Masked Input Modeling for Exploration (MIMEx) -- where the mask distribution can be flexibly tuned to control the difficulty of the underlying conditional prediction task. We demonstrate that MIMEx can achieve superior results when compared against competitive baselines on a suite of challenging sparse-reward visuomotor tasks.

paragraphs: Exploration becomes difficult when an agent receives high-dimensional observations and useful external rewards are rare. Intrinsic rewards encourage exploration by estimating how novel a state, transition, or trajectory is. This paper connects such novelty estimates to conditional prediction: predicting missing information from whatever parts of an observation or sequence remain visible.

The authors use the perspective that masked prediction objectives can estimate pseudo-likelihood, a probability-related quantity built from conditional predictions. They show that existing intrinsic reward approaches can be understood as special cases using different masking distributions. Their framework, Masked Input Modeling for Exploration, or MIMEx, makes that distribution a flexible design choice.

Changing which information is hidden controls the difficulty of the underlying prediction task and therefore how novelty is estimated. On a suite of challenging sparse-reward visuomotor tasks, MIMEx can outperform competitive baselines. The contribution is both a common explanation for existing exploration rewards and a way to derive new ones by adjusting the conditional prediction problem.
summary.tldr: MIMEx derives exploration rewards from masked prediction tasks whose difficulty can be adjusted through the masking distribution.

title: MIMEx: Intrinsic Rewards from Masked Input Modeling

abstract: In computational neuroscience, there has been an increased interest in developing machine learning algorithms that leverage brain imaging data to provide estimates of "brain age" for an individual. Importantly, the discordance between brain age and chronological age (referred to as "brain age gap") can capture accelerated aging due to adverse health conditions and therefore, can reflect increased vulnerability towards neurological disease or cognitive impairments. However, widespread adoption of brain age for clinical decision support has been hindered due to lack of transparency and methodological justifications in most existing brain age prediction algorithms. In this paper, we leverage coVariance neural networks (VNN) to propose an explanation-driven and anatomically interpretable framework for brain age prediction using cortical thickness features. Specifically, our brain age prediction framework extends beyond the coarse metric of brain age gap in Alzheimer’s disease (AD) and we make two important observations: (i) VNNs can assign anatomical interpretability to elevated brain age gap in AD by identifying contributing brain regions, (ii) the interpretability offered by VNNs is contingent on their ability to exploit specific eigenvectors of the anatomical covariance matrix. Together, these observations facilitate an explainable and anatomically interpretable perspective to the task of brain age prediction.

paragraphs: Brain-age prediction uses imaging data to estimate an individual’s apparent brain age. A difference between that estimate and chronological age can reflect accelerated aging and increased vulnerability to neurological disease or cognitive impairment. The paper addresses an interpretability problem: a single age-gap value provides little anatomical explanation for the model’s estimate.

The authors build a framework using coVariance neural networks and cortical thickness features. Their aim is to connect predictions to identifiable brain regions. In the Alzheimer’s disease setting they study, the networks can identify anatomical regions contributing to an elevated predicted brain-age gap, adding an explanation to the overall age estimate.

A second observation links that interpretability to the model’s use of specific eigenvectors of the anatomical covariance matrix. These eigenvectors describe particular patterns within the covariance structure, and exploiting them is a condition for the reported interpretability. The contribution therefore connects a regional explanation of brain-age predictions with a mathematical property of the network’s representation, extending the analysis beyond the coarse age-gap measurement.
summary.tldr: CoVariance neural networks connect elevated brain-age predictions in Alzheimer’s disease to contributing brain regions through specific covariance patterns.

title: Explainable Brain Age Prediction using coVariance Neural Networks

abstract: Despite recent progress in reinforcement learning (RL) from raw pixel data, sample inefficiency continues to present a substantial obstacle. Prior works have attempted to address this challenge by creating self-supervised auxiliary tasks, aiming to enrich the agent's learned representations with control-relevant information for future state prediction.However, these objectives are often insufficient to learn representations that can represent the optimal policy or value function, and they often consider tasks with small, abstract discrete action spaces and thus overlook the importance of action representation learning in continuous control.In this paper, we introduce $\texttt{TACO}$: $\textbf{T}$emporal $\textbf{A}$ction-driven $\textbf{CO}$ntrastive Learning, a simple yet powerful temporal contrastive learning approach that facilitates the concurrent acquisition of latent state and action representations for agents. $\texttt{TACO}$ simultaneously learns a state and an action representation by optimizing the mutual information between representations of current states paired with action sequences and representations of the corresponding future states. Theoretically, $\texttt{TACO}$ can be shown to learn state and action representations that encompass sufficient information for control, thereby improving sample efficiency.For online RL, $\texttt{TACO}$ achieves 40% performance boost after one million environment interaction steps on average across nine challenging visual continuous control tasks from Deepmind Control Suite. In addition, we show that $\texttt{TACO}$ can also serve as a plug-and-play module adding to existing offline visual RL methods to establish the new state-of-the-art performance for offline visual RL across offline datasets with varying quality.

paragraphs: TACO addresses the large amount of interaction data needed to learn control from images. The paper argues that auxiliary prediction tasks can fail to retain enough information for optimal policies or value functions. It also emphasizes action representations, which deserve particular attention when controls are continuous rather than a small set of discrete choices.

The method jointly learns latent representations of states and actions through temporal contrastive learning. Its objective increases mutual information between a current state paired with an action sequence and the corresponding future state. The authors provide a theoretical account showing that the learned representations can contain sufficient information for control, linking this learning objective to sample efficiency.

For online learning, TACO delivers an average 40% performance improvement after one million environment interactions across nine challenging visual continuous-control tasks from DeepMind Control Suite. It also works as an added module for existing offline visual reinforcement-learning methods, achieving reported state-of-the-art performance across datasets of varying quality. These findings support learning action and state representations together in both evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: TACO jointly learns state and action representations through temporal contrastive learning, improving online and offline visual control performance.

title: $\texttt{TACO}$: Temporal Latent Action-Driven Contrastive Loss for Visual Reinforcement Learning

abstract: We study an abstract framework for interactive learning called interactive estimation in which the goal is to estimate a target from its ``similarity'' to points queried by the learner.We introduce a combinatorial measure called Dissimilarity dimension which largely captures learnability in our model.We present a simple, general, and broadly-applicable algorithm, for which we obtain both regret and PAC generalization bounds that are polynomial in the new dimension. We show that our framework subsumes and thereby unifies two classic learning models:statistical-query learning and structured bandits. We also delineate how the Dissimilarity dimension is related to well-known parameters for both frameworks, in some cases yielding significantly improved analyses.

paragraphs: This paper studies learning through interaction: a learner queries points and receives information about their similarity to an unknown target. The goal is to estimate that target from the responses. By expressing the interaction abstractly, the authors seek a common account of learning problems that are usually analyzed through separate mathematical frameworks.

They introduce a combinatorial measure called Dissimilarity dimension, which largely captures learnability in this setting. They also give a general algorithm whose regret and PAC generalization bounds depend polynomially on this dimension. These bounds connect a structural property of the problem to both performance during interaction and the quality of the resulting estimate.

The framework includes statistical-query learning and structured bandits as special cases. The authors explain how their dimension relates to established parameters in both areas, obtaining substantially improved analyses in some cases. The contribution is therefore both a shared language for these learning models and a way to analyze their difficulty through the same structural measure.
summary.tldr: Interactive estimation unifies statistical-query learning and structured bandits through a new dimension that supports polynomial learning guarantees.

title: A Unified Model and Dimension for Interactive Estimation

abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) are the de facto standard deep learning architectures for machine learning on graphs. This has led to a large body of work analyzing the capabilities and limitations of these models, particularly pertaining to their representation and extrapolation capacity. We offer a novel theoretical perspective on the representation and extrapolation capacity of GNNs, by answering the question: how do GNNs behave as the number of graph nodes become very large? Under mild assumptions, we show that when we draw graphs of increasing size from the Erdős–Rényi model, the probability that such graphs are mapped to a particular output by a class of GNN classifiers tends to either zero or one. This class includes the popular graph convolutional network architecture. The result establishes `zero-one laws' for these GNNs, and analogously to other convergence laws, entails theoretical limitations on their capacity. We empirically verify our results, observing that the theoretical asymptotic limits are evident already on relatively small graphs.

The result concerns particular architectures and random-graph distributions; it does not say every graph neural network produces a constant answer on every family of large real-world graphs.
summary.tldr: Certain graph neural classifiers approach deterministic outputs on growing Erdős–Rényi graphs.

title: Zero-One Laws of Graph Neural Networks

abstract: Embedding tables are used by machine learning systems to work with categorical features.In modern Recommendation Systems, these tables can be very large, necessitating the development of new methods for fitting them in memory, even during training.We suggest Clustered Compositional Embeddings (CCE) which combines clustering-based compression like quantization to codebooks with dynamic methods like The Hashing Trick and Compositional Embeddings [Shi et al., 2020].Experimentally CCE achieves the best of both worlds: The high compression rate of codebook-based quantization, but \emph{dynamically} like hashing-based methods, so it can be used during training.Theoretically, we prove that CCE is guaranteed to converge to the optimal codebook and give a tight bound for the number of iterations required.

paragraphs: Embedding tables let machine learning systems represent categorical features. In recommendation systems, these tables can become large enough that fitting them into memory is difficult even during training. Compression therefore needs to address the training process as well as the size of a completed model.

The paper proposes Clustered Compositional Embeddings, or CCE. It combines clustering-based compression, including quantization into codebooks, with dynamic techniques such as hashing and compositional embeddings. The aim is to retain the strong compression available from codebooks while gaining the ability to operate dynamically as training proceeds.

The experiments report that CCE achieves this combination: high compression associated with codebook methods together with the training-time flexibility of hashing-based methods. The authors also prove convergence to the optimal codebook and provide a tight bound on the iterations required. That guarantee specifically concerns the codebook optimization. The overall contribution is a way to bring clustering-based compression into the changing setting of embedding-table training, where memory pressure already matters before training finishes.
summary.tldr: CCE combines codebook compression with dynamic embedding methods to reduce table memory during training.

title: Clustering the Sketch: Dynamic Compression for Embedding Tables

abstract: Exquisite demand exists for customizing the pretrained large text-to-image model, $e.g.$ Stable Diffusion, to generate innovative concepts, such as the users themselves. However, the newly-added concept from previous customization methods often shows weaker combination abilities than the original ones even given several images during training. We thus propose a new personalization method that allows for the seamless integration of a unique individual into the pre-trained diffusion model using just $one\ facial\ photograph$ and only $1024\ learnable\ parameters$ under $3\ minutes$. So we can effortlessly generate stunning images of this person in any pose or position, interacting with anyone and doing anything imaginable from text prompts. To achieve this, we first analyze and build a well-defined celeb basis from the embedding space of the pre-trained large text encoder. Then, given one facial photo as the target identity, we generate its own embedding by optimizing the weight of this basis and locking all other parameters. Empowered by the proposed celeb basis, the new identity in our customized model showcases a better concept combination ability than previous personalization methods. Besides, our model can also learn several new identities at once and interact with each other where the previous customization model fails to. Project page is at: http://celeb-basis.github.io. Code is at: https://github.com/ygtxr1997/CelebBasis.

paragraphs: Personalizing a text-to-image model requires more than teaching it a person's appearance. The new identity also needs to combine effectively with other concepts in text prompts. This paper targets that combination ability, which the authors describe as weaker for identities added by previous customization methods than for concepts already present in the pretrained model.

Their method builds a celebrity-based basis within the pretrained text encoder's embedding space. Given one facial photograph, it learns weights over that basis to produce an embedding for the target identity. All other parameters stay fixed. The reported customization uses 1,024 learnable parameters and takes less than three minutes.

The authors report better combination of the new identity with other concepts than previous personalization methods. They also demonstrate learning several identities together and generating interactions among them. The approach matters because it places a new identity within an existing representational space, supporting prompted combinations while requiring only a small amount of identity-specific training and a single input photograph.
summary.tldr: Celeb Basis personalizes a diffusion model from one facial photo by learning a compact identity embedding with improved concept-combination ability.

title: Inserting Anybody in Diffusion Models via Celeb Basis

abstract: A core aim in theoretical and systems neuroscience is to develop models which help us better understand biological intelligence. Such models range broadly in both complexity and biological plausibility. One widely-adopted example is task-optimized recurrent neural networks (RNNs), which have been used to generate hypotheses about how the brain’s neural dynamics may organize to accomplish tasks. However, task-optimized RNNs typically have a fixed weight matrix representing the synaptic connectivity between neurons. From decades of neuroscience research, we know that synaptic weights are constantly changing, controlled in part by chemicals such as neuromodulators. In this work we explore the computational implications of synaptic gain scaling, a form of neuromodulation, using task-optimized low-rank RNNs.In our neuromodulated RNN (NM-RNN) model, a neuromodulatory subnetwork outputs a low-dimensional neuromodulatory signal that dynamically scales the low-rank recurrent weights of an output-generating RNN. In empirical experiments, we find that the structured flexibility in the NM-RNN allows it to both train and generalize with a higher degree of accuracy than low-rank RNNs on a set of canonical tasks.Additionally, via theoretical analyses we show how neuromodulatory gain scaling endows networks with gating mechanisms commonly found in artificial RNNs. We end by analyzing the low-rank dynamics of trained NM-RNNs, to show how task computations are distributed.

paragraphs: Task-trained recurrent neural networks are used to investigate how neural dynamics might support behavior, but they typically keep recurrent connection weights fixed. Biological synaptic connections can change under the influence of neuromodulators. This paper explores a structured version of that flexibility in low-rank recurrent networks, focusing on the computational effects of dynamically scaling connection strengths.

The proposed NM-RNN contains a neuromodulatory subnetwork that produces a low-dimensional control signal. That signal scales the low-rank recurrent weights of another network responsible for producing outputs. The arrangement allows connectivity to change in a constrained, organized way during computation, giving the model more flexibility while retaining a low-rank structure that the authors can analyze.

In experiments on canonical tasks, NM-RNNs train and generalize more accurately than the compared low-rank RNNs. Theoretical analysis also shows how neuromodulatory gain scaling produces gating mechanisms familiar from artificial recurrent networks. Further analysis of trained dynamics examines how task computations are distributed. Together, these results connect a biologically motivated form of changing connectivity with useful and interpretable computational mechanisms.
summary.tldr: A neuromodulatory subnetwork dynamically scales recurrent weights, improving tested task performance and providing a theoretical link to gating mechanisms.

title: Structured flexibility in recurrent neural networks via neuromodulation

abstract: Medical Vision-Language Pretraining (MedVLP) shows promise in learning generalizable and transferable visual representations from paired and unpaired medical images and reports. MedVLP can provide useful features to downstream tasks and facilitate adapting task-specific models to new setups using fewer examples. However, existing MedVLP methods often differ in terms of datasets, preprocessing, and finetuning implementations. This pose great challenges in evaluating how well a MedVLP method generalizes to various clinically-relevant tasks due to the lack of unified, standardized, and comprehensive benchmark. To fill this gap, we propose BenchX, a unified benchmark framework that enables head-to-head comparison and systematical analysis between MedVLP methods using public chest X-ray datasets. Specifically, BenchX is composed of three components: 1) Comprehensive datasets covering nine datasets and four medical tasks; 2) Benchmark suites to standardize data preprocessing, train-test splits, and parameter selection; 3) Unified finetuning protocols that accommodate heterogeneous MedVLP methods for consistent task adaptation in classification, segmentation, and report generation, respectively. Utilizing BenchX, we establish baselines for nine state-of-the-art MedVLP methods and found that the performance of some early MedVLP methods can be enhanced to surpass more recent ones, prompting a revisiting of the developments and conclusions from prior works in MedVLP. Our code are available at https://github.com/yangzhou12/BenchX.

paragraphs: Medical vision-language pretraining learns representations from medical images and reports that can support later tasks. Comparing these methods is difficult when studies use different datasets, preprocessing steps, or adaptation procedures. BenchX addresses this evaluation problem by providing a shared framework for comparing methods on public chest X-ray data.

The framework brings together nine datasets covering four medical tasks. It standardizes preprocessing, training and testing splits, and parameter selection. It also provides common fine-tuning procedures that accommodate different pretrained methods for classification, segmentation, and report generation. These controls make comparisons more informative by reducing differences introduced by the surrounding evaluation setup.

The authors establish results for nine existing MedVLP methods using BenchX. They find that improved evaluation and adaptation configurations can allow some earlier methods to outperform newer ones. This finding suggests that reported progress can depend substantially on implementation choices. BenchX therefore contributes both an evaluation resource and evidence that some previous conclusions about relative method quality deserve reconsideration.
summary.tldr: BenchX standardizes chest X-ray pretraining evaluations and shows that some older methods can outperform newer ones under improved configurations.

title: BenchX: A Unified Benchmark Framework for Medical Vision-Language Pretraining on Chest X-Rays

abstract: Link prediction, which aims to forecast unseen connections in graphs, is a fundamental task in graph machine learning. Heuristic methods, leveraging a range of different pairwise measures such as common neighbors and shortest paths, often rival the performance of vanilla Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). Therefore, recent advancements in GNNs for link prediction (GNN4LP) have primarily focused on integrating one or a few types of pairwise information. In this work, we reveal that different node pairs within the same dataset necessitate varied pairwise information for accurate prediction and models that only apply the same pairwise information uniformly could achieve suboptimal performance.As a result, we propose a simple mixture of experts model Link-MoE for link prediction. Link-MoE utilizes various GNNs as experts and strategically selects the appropriate expert for each node pair based on various types of pairwise information. Experimental results across diverse real-world datasets demonstrate substantial performance improvement from Link-MoE. Notably, Link-Mo achieves a relative improvement of 18.71% on the MRR metric for the Pubmed dataset and 9.59% on the Hits@100 metric for the ogbl-ppa dataset, compared to the best baselines. The code is available at https://github.com/ml-ml/Link-MoE/.

paragraphs: Link prediction estimates which connections are missing or may occur in a graph. Simple pairwise measures, including shared neighbors and shortest paths, can compete with standard graph neural networks. This paper argues that the useful information varies between node pairs even within one dataset, making a uniform choice of pairwise information potentially suboptimal.

Link-MoE addresses that variation with a mixture of experts. Different graph neural networks act as experts, and the system selects an appropriate expert for each node pair using several types of pairwise information. The selection mechanism makes the prediction method responsive to the particular relationship being assessed.

Experiments across real-world datasets show substantial improvements over the compared methods. The authors report relative gains of 18.71% in MRR on Pubmed and 9.59% in Hits@100 on ogbl-ppa against the best baselines. These findings support choosing predictive expertise at the node-pair level, allowing different graph relationships to benefit from different sources of structural information.
summary.tldr: Link-MoE improves graph link prediction by selecting different graph-network experts for node pairs with different informational needs.

title: Mixture of Link Predictors on Graphs

abstract: Residual networks, as discrete approximations of Ordinary Differential Equations (ODEs), have inspired significant advancements in neural network design, including multistep methods, high-order methods, and multi-particle dynamical systems. The precision of the solution to ODEs significantly affects parameter optimization, thereby impacting model performance. In this work, we present a series of advanced explorations of Transformer architecture design to minimize the error compared to the true ``solution.'' First, we introduce a predictor-corrector learning framework to minimize truncation errors, which consists of a high-order predictor and a multistep corrector. Second, we propose an exponential moving average-based coefficient learning method to strengthen our higher-order predictor. Extensive experiments on large-scale machine translation, abstractive summarization, language modeling, and natural language understanding benchmarks demonstrate the superiority of our approach. On the WMT'14 English-German and English-French tasks, our model achieved BLEU scores of 30.95 and 44.27, respectively. Furthermore, on the OPUS multilingual machine translation task, our model surpasses a robust 3.8B DeepNet by an average of 2.9 SacreBLEU, using only 1/3 parameters. Notably, it also beats LLama models by 5.7 accuracy points on the LM Harness Evaluation.

paragraphs: Residual networks can be viewed as discrete approximations to ordinary differential equations. This perspective suggests that errors introduced by the approximation can affect optimization and model performance. The paper uses that connection to redesign transformer computations, seeking a more accurate approximation to the underlying continuous solution.

Its framework combines a high-order predictor with a multistep corrector to reduce truncation error. The predictor supplies an initial update, and the corrector refines it using the multistep formulation. An additional coefficient-learning method based on an exponential moving average strengthens the higher-order predictor. Together, these components bring numerical-solution ideas into the transformer architecture.

Experiments span machine translation, abstractive summarization, language modeling, and natural language understanding. Reported translation scores are 30.95 BLEU for WMT'14 English-German and 44.27 for English-French. It also exceeds the compared Llama models by 5.7 accuracy points on LM Harness Evaluation, supporting the architecture across the tested language tasks.
summary.tldr: A transformer design using predictor-corrector updates and moving-average coefficient learning improves performance across the reported language benchmarks.

title: Predictor-Corrector Enhanced Transformers with Exponential Moving Average Coefficient Learning

abstract: Sequential recommender systems (SRS) aim to predict users' subsequent choices based on their historical interactions and have found applications in diverse fields such as e-commerce and social media. However, in real-world systems, most users interact with only a handful of items, while the majority of items are seldom consumed. These two issues, known as the long-tail user and long-tail item challenges, often pose difficulties for existing SRS. These challenges can adversely affect user experience and seller benefits, making them crucial to address. Though a few works have addressed the challenges, they still struggle with the seesaw or noisy issues due to the intrinsic scarcity of interactions. The advancements in large language models (LLMs) present a promising solution to these problems from a semantic perspective. As one of the pioneers in this field, we propose the Large Language Models Enhancement framework for Sequential Recommendation (LLM-ESR). This framework utilizes semantic embeddings derived from LLMs to enhance SRS without adding extra inference load. To address the long-tail item challenge, we design a dual-view modeling framework that combines semantics from LLMs and collaborative signals from conventional SRS. For the long-tail user challenge, we propose a retrieval augmented self-distillation method to enhance user preference representation using more informative interactions from similar users. To verify the effectiveness and versatility of our proposed enhancement framework, we conduct extensive experiments on three real-world datasets using three popular SRS models. The results consistently show that our method surpasses existing baselines. The implementation code is available in Supplementary Material.

Experiments combine three real-world datasets with three popular sequential recommendation models. The authors report consistent improvements over existing baselines, supporting both effectiveness and versatility across the evaluated combinations. The approach matters because it introduces semantic knowledge and information from related users into established recommenders while preserving the stated absence of additional inference burden.
summary.tldr: LLM-ESR enhances sparse sequential recommendation with language-model semantics and information from similar users without extra inference load.

title: LLM-ESR: Large Language Models Enhancement for Long-tailed Sequential Recommendation

abstract: We introduce a benchmark to directly evaluate the alignment between human observers and vision models on a 3D shape inference task. We leverage an experimental design from the cognitive sciences: given a set of images, participants identify which contain the same/different objects, despite considerable viewpoint variation. We draw from a diverse range of images that include common objects (e.g., chairs) as well as abstract shapes (i.e., procedurally generated 'nonsense' objects). After constructing over 2000 unique image sets, we administer these tasks to human participants, collecting 35K trials of behavioral data from over 500 participants. This includes explicit choice behaviors as well as intermediate measures, such as reaction time and gaze data. We then evaluate the performance of common vision models (e.g., DINOv2, MAE, CLIP). We find that humans outperform all models by a wide margin. Using a multi-scale evaluation approach, we identify underlying similarities and differences between models and humans: while human-model performance is correlated, humans allocate more time/processing on challenging trials. All images, data, and code can be accessed via our project page.

paragraphs: This paper builds a benchmark for comparing how humans and vision models infer object identity across changes in viewpoint. Given several images, participants decide whether they show the same object or different objects. The images include familiar categories such as chairs and procedurally generated abstract shapes, so the task covers more than recognition of familiar objects.

The researchers construct over 2,000 image sets and collect 35,000 behavioral trials from more than 500 people. They record choices along with reaction times and gaze information. These additional measurements help characterize how people handle the task, extending the comparison beyond a single accuracy score. Models evaluated include DINOv2, MAE, and CLIP.

Humans outperform every tested model by a wide margin. At the same time, human and model performance are correlated, indicating some shared pattern in which cases are difficult. The analysis also finds that humans devote more time or processing to challenging trials. The benchmark thus reveals both overlap in task difficulty and a substantial gap in successful recognition across viewpoints, while providing behavioral data for studying that gap.
summary.tldr: Humans substantially outperform tested vision models at recognizing objects across viewpoints, despite correlated patterns of difficulty.

title: Evaluating Multiview Object Consistency in Humans and Image Models

abstract: The validation of global climate models is crucial to ensure the accuracy and efficacy of model output. We introduce the spherical convolutional Wasserstein distance to more comprehensively measure differences between climate models and reanalysis data. This new similarity measure accounts for spatial variability using convolutional projections and quantifies local differences in the distribution of climate variables. We apply this method to evaluate the historical model outputs of the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project (CMIP) members by comparing them to observational and reanalysis data products. Additionally, we investigate the progression from CMIP phase 5 to phase 6 and find modest improvements in the phase 6 models regarding their ability to produce realistic climatologies.

paragraphs: Validating a global climate model requires comparing its outputs with observational and reanalysis data. This paper introduces spherical convolutional Wasserstein distance as a way to make that comparison more spatially informative. The measure is designed to account for geographic variability while quantifying differences in the local distributions of climate variables.

The method uses convolutional projections to incorporate spatial information into the comparison. Its focus on local distributions makes the assessment sensitive to how climate variables differ across locations. This provides a framework for examining discrepancies between model output and reference data while retaining information about their spatial structure.

The authors apply the measure to historical outputs from members of the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project and compare phase 5 with phase 6. They find modest improvements in phase 6 models' ability to reproduce realistic climatologies. The result provides evidence of incremental progress under this evaluation, alongside a new distribution-based tool for assessing global climate-model output.
summary.tldr: A spatially informed distributional distance evaluates climate models and finds modest climatology improvements from CMIP5 to CMIP6.

title: Validating Climate Models with Spherical Convolutional Wasserstein Distance

abstract: Tracking points in video frames is essential for understanding video content. However, the task is fundamentally hindered by the computation demands for brute-force correspondence matching across the frames. As the current models down-sample the frame resolutions to mitigate this challenge, they fall short in accurately representing point trajectories due to information truncation. Instead, we address the challenge by pruning the search space for point tracking and let the model process only the important regions of the frames without down-sampling. Our first key idea is to identify the object instance and its trajectory over the frames, then prune the regions of the frame that do not contain the instance. Concretely, to estimate the instance’s trajectory, we track a group of points on the instance and aggregate their motion trajectories. Furthermore, to deal with the occlusions in complex scenes, we propose to compensate for the occluded points while tracking. To this end, we introduce a unified framework that jointly performs point tracking and segmentation, providing synergistic effects between the two tasks. For example, the segmentation results enable a tracking model to avoid the occluded points referring to the instance mask, and conversely, the improved tracking results can help to produce more accurate segmentation masks. Our framework can be easily incorporated with various tracking models, and we demonstrate its efficacy for enhanced point tracking throughout extensive experiments. For example, on the recent TAP-Vid benchmark, our framework consistently improves all baselines, e.g., up to 13.5% improvement on the average Jaccard metric.

summary.tldr: TrackIME uses object motion and segmentation to narrow point-tracking searches while retaining image detail and handling occlusion.

title: TrackIME: Enhanced Video Point Tracking via Instance Motion Estimation

abstract: Sequential recommender systems are designed to capture users' evolving interests over time. Existing methods typically assume a uniform time interval among consecutive user interactions and may not capture users' continuously evolving behavior in the short and long term. In reality, the actual time intervals of user interactions vary dramatically. Consequently, as the time interval between interactions increases, so does the uncertainty in user behavior. Intuitively, it is beneficial to establish a correlation between the interaction time interval and the model uncertainty to provide effective recommendations. To this end, we formulate a novel Evidential Neural Stochastic Differential Equation (*E-NSDE*) to seamlessly integrate NSDE and evidential learning for effective time-aware sequential recommendations. The NSDE enables the model to learn users' fine-grained time-evolving behavior by capturing continuous user representation while evidential learning quantifies both aleatoric and epistemic uncertainties considering interaction time interval to provide model confidence during prediction. Furthermore, we derive a mathematical relationship between the interaction time interval and model uncertainty to guide the learning process. Experiments on real-world data demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method compared to the SOTA methods.

paragraphs: Sequential recommendation tries to follow how a user's interests change across interactions. Many methods effectively treat successive interactions as equally spaced, even though real gaps vary considerably. The paper focuses on the associated uncertainty: as more time passes without an interaction, the user's behavior becomes less certain. It aims to make that timing relevant to both predictions and confidence.

The proposed E-NSDE combines a neural stochastic differential equation with evidential learning. The differential equation models a continuously evolving user representation, allowing behavior to change between observed interactions. Evidential learning estimates uncertainty associated with behavior and with the model's knowledge, taking the time gap into account when assigning confidence to a prediction.

The authors also derive a mathematical relationship between elapsed interaction time and model uncertainty, which guides learning. Experiments on real-world data show the method's effectiveness relative to state-of-the-art approaches. The contribution brings temporal evolution and uncertainty estimation into a single recommendation framework, making the spacing of observations part of how the model reasons about changing interests.
summary.tldr: E-NSDE models continuously changing user interests and links prediction uncertainty to the time between interactions.

title: Evidential Stochastic Differential Equations for Time-Aware Sequential Recommendation

abstract: The aim of this paper is to address the challenge of gradual domain adaptation within a class of manifold-constrained data distributions. In particular, we consider a sequence of $T\ge2$ data distributions $P_1,\ldots,P_T$ undergoing a gradual shift, where each pair of consecutive measures $P_i,P_{i+1}$ are close to each other in Wasserstein distance. We have a supervised dataset of size $n$ sampled from $P_0$, while for the subsequent distributions in the sequence, only unlabeled i.i.d. samples are available. Moreover, we assume that all distributions exhibit a known favorable attribute, such as (but not limited to) having intra-class soft/hard margins. In this context, we propose a methodology rooted in Distributionally Robust Optimization (DRO) with an adaptive Wasserstein radius. We theoretically show that this method guarantees the classification error across all $P_i$s can be suitably bounded. Our bounds rely on a newly introduced {\it {compatibility}} measure, which fully characterizes the error propagation dynamics along the sequence. Specifically, for inadequately constrained distributions, the error can exponentially escalate as we progress through the gradual shifts. Conversely, for appropriately constrained distributions, the error can be demonstrated to be linear or even entirely eradicated. We have substantiated our theoretical findings through several experimental results.

paragraphs: Gradual domain adaptation asks whether a classifier can follow a sequence of changing data distributions using labels only from an initial distribution. Here, successive distributions must be close in Wasserstein distance, and later samples are unlabeled and independently drawn. The analysis also assumes that every distribution has a known favorable property, such as a soft or hard within-class margin.

The authors propose distributionally robust optimization with an adaptive Wasserstein radius. This radius controls the distributional neighborhood considered during optimization. They establish bounds on classification error throughout the sequence and introduce a compatibility measure that characterizes how errors propagate from one distribution to the next.

The central conclusion is conditional on the constraints imposed on the distributions. With inadequate constraints, errors can grow exponentially even though individual shifts are gradual. With appropriate constraints, the analysis can establish linear error behavior or even eliminate the error. Experimental results support the theoretical findings. The work explains why small successive changes alone do not settle whether adaptation will remain reliable over a long sequence.
summary.tldr: An adaptive robust optimization method bounds error across gradual distribution shifts, with error propagation governed by the distributions' structural compatibility.

title: Gradual Domain Adaptation via Manifold-Constrained Distributionally Robust Optimization

abstract: Open-vocabulary semantic segmentation (OVSS) aims to segment unseen classes without corresponding labels. Existing Vision-Language Model (VLM)-based methods leverage VLM's rich knowledge to enhance additional explicit segmentation-specific networks, yielding competitive results, but at the cost of extensive training cost. To reduce the cost, we attempt to enable VLM to directly produce the segmentation results without any segmentation-specific networks. Prompt learning offers a direct and parameter-efficient approach, yet it falls short in guiding VLM for pixel-level visual classification. Therefore, we propose the ${\bf R}$elationship ${\bf P}$rompt ${\bf M}$odule (${\bf RPM}$), which generates the relationship prompt that directs VLM to extract pixel-level semantic embeddings suitable for OVSS. Moreover, RPM integrates with VLM to construct the ${\bf R}$elationship ${\bf P}$rompt ${\bf N}$etwork (${\bf RPN}$), achieving OVSS without any segmentation-specific networks. RPN attains state-of-the-art performance with merely about ${\bf 3M}$ trainable parameters (2\% of total parameters).
