paragraphs: Open-vocabulary semantic segmentation assigns class labels to image pixels, including classes without corresponding training labels. Existing approaches use the broad knowledge of vision-language models alongside additional segmentation-specific networks. Although effective, those extra networks introduce substantial training cost. This paper asks whether a vision-language model can directly produce the segmentation result.

Ordinary prompt learning offers a parameter-efficient way to adapt a model, but the authors find it insufficient for guiding pixel-level classification. They introduce the Relationship Prompt Module, which generates prompts that guide the vision-language model toward pixel-level semantic embeddings suitable for segmentation. Combining this module with the vision-language model produces the Relationship Prompt Network.

The resulting system performs open-vocabulary segmentation without an additional segmentation-specific network. It reports state-of-the-art performance while training about three million parameters, approximately 2% of the total. The finding supports a focused adaptation strategy: prompts designed for pixel-level representations can make a pretrained vision-language model useful for dense prediction with a small trainable portion.
summary.tldr: Relationship prompts enable direct open-vocabulary segmentation with a vision-language model, achieving reported state-of-the-art performance with about three million trainable parameters.

title: Relationship Prompt Learning is Enough for Open-Vocabulary Semantic Segmentation

abstract: We propose using mechanistic interpretability -- techniques for reverse engineering model weights into human-interpretable algorithms -- to derive and compactly prove formal guarantees on model performance.We prototype this approach by formally proving accuracy lower bounds for a small transformer trained on Max-of-$K$, validating proof transferability across 151 random seeds and four values of $K$.We create 102 different computer-assisted proof strategies and assess their length and tightness of bound on each of our models.Using quantitative metrics, we find that shorter proofs seem to require and provide more mechanistic understanding.Moreover, we find that more faithful mechanistic understanding leads to tighter performance bounds.We confirm these connections by qualitatively examining a subset of our proofs.Finally, we identify compounding structureless errors as a key challenge for using mechanistic interpretability to generate compact proofs on model performance.

paragraphs: This paper explores whether understanding a neural network's internal algorithm can help produce compact formal guarantees about its performance. It uses mechanistic interpretability to translate model weights into human-interpretable computations, then uses that understanding to construct proofs. The prototype establishes accuracy lower bounds for small transformers trained on the Max-of-K task.

The authors develop 102 computer-assisted proof strategies and compare both proof length and how tightly each proof bounds model performance. They also test whether the proofs transfer across models trained with 151 random seeds and four values of K. This makes proof construction itself an object of study: different explanations of a model can lead to proofs with different lengths and strengths.

Their quantitative findings suggest that shorter proofs require and provide more mechanistic understanding, while more faithful understanding yields tighter performance bounds. Qualitative examination of selected proofs supports these connections. The paper also identifies accumulating, structureless errors as a central obstacle to compact proofs, highlighting why finding a clean internal algorithm does not automatically make every remaining contribution easy to bound.
summary.tldr: A small-transformer study connects faithful mechanistic understanding with tighter performance guarantees and suggests that compact proofs require deeper understanding.

title: Compact Proofs of Model Performance via Mechanistic Interpretability

abstract: Bayesian optimization (BO) is an attractive machine learning framework for performing sample-efficient global optimization of black-box functions. The optimization process is guided by an acquisition function that selects points to acquire in each round of BO. In batched BO, when multiple points are acquired in parallel, commonly used acquisition functions are often high-dimensional and intractable, leading to the use of sampling-based alternatives. We propose a statistical physics inspired acquisition function that can natively handle batches. Batched Energy-Entropy acquisition for BO (BEEBO) enables tight control of the explore-exploit trade-off of the optimization process and generalizes to heteroskedastic black-box problems. We demonstrate the applicability of BEEBO on a range of problems, showing competitive performance to existing acquisition functions.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization chooses which evaluations of a black-box function to perform next, aiming to find good solutions with relatively few evaluations. Choosing several evaluations together creates an additional challenge: the acquisition function that guides selection can become high-dimensional and difficult to handle. Existing approaches therefore often rely on sampling-based alternatives.

The paper introduces Batched Energy-Entropy acquisition for Bayesian Optimization, or BEEBO. Inspired by statistical physics, its acquisition function handles batches directly. It also provides control over the balance between exploring uncertain possibilities and exploiting promising ones. This makes the exploration decision an explicit part of selecting a group of evaluations.

BEEBO also extends to problems where observation noise varies across the search space. The authors demonstrate its applicability across a range of optimization problems and report performance competitive with existing acquisition functions. The stated contribution is a batch-native approach with a controllable exploration balance and support for varying noise, alongside empirical evidence that it can compete with established choices.
summary.tldr: BEEBO directly selects batches for Bayesian optimization while controlling exploration and exploitation and accommodating varying observation noise.

title: Batched Energy-Entropy acquisition for Bayesian Optimization

abstract: The remarkable instruction-following capability of large language models (LLMs) has sparked a growing interest in automatically finding good prompts, i.e., prompt optimization. Most existing works follow the scheme of selecting from a pre-generated pool of candidate prompts. However, these designs mainly focus on the generation strategy, while limited attention has been paid to the selection method. Especially, the cost incurred during the selection (e.g., accessing LLM and evaluating the responses) is rarely explicitly considered. To overcome this limitation, this work provides a principled framework, TRIPLE, to efficiently perform prompt selection under an explicit budget constraint. TRIPLE is built on a novel connection established between prompt optimization and fixed-budget best arm identification (BAI-FB) in multi-armed bandits (MAB); thus, it is capable of leveraging the rich toolbox from BAI-FB systematically and also incorporating unique characteristics of prompt optimization. Extensive experiments on multiple well-adopted tasks using various LLMs demonstrate the remarkable performance improvement of TRIPLE over baselines while satisfying the limited budget constraints. As an extension, variants of TRIPLE are proposed to efficiently select examples for few-shot prompts, also achieving superior empirical performance.

paragraphs: Automatic prompt optimization often starts with a collection of candidate prompts and then chooses one. The paper focuses on the cost of that choice: testing candidates requires model calls and evaluation of their responses. A strong candidate-generation method alone does not determine how efficiently a limited evaluation budget is spent.

TRIPLE treats prompt selection as fixed-budget best-arm identification, a problem from multi-armed bandits. In this connection, candidate prompts correspond to alternatives whose performance must be assessed before the budget runs out. The framework draws on methods developed for that problem while incorporating characteristics specific to prompt optimization. This makes the spending limit an explicit part of selection rather than an incidental practical concern.

Experiments across multiple tasks and language models show improved performance over baselines while respecting the imposed budgets. The authors also extend TRIPLE to selecting examples for few-shot prompts, with favorable empirical results. The contribution is therefore an approach to making better selection decisions with limited evaluations, covering both prompt candidates and the examples included in prompts.
summary.tldr: TRIPLE uses fixed-budget best-arm identification to select effective prompts and few-shot examples while explicitly limiting evaluation costs.

title: Efficient Prompt Optimization Through the Lens of Best Arm Identification

abstract: In recent years, the input context sizes of large language models (LLMs) have increased dramatically. However, existing evaluation methods have not kept pace, failing to comprehensively assess the efficiency of models in handling long contexts. To bridge this gap, we introduce the BABILong benchmark, designed to test language models' ability to reason across facts distributed in extremely long documents. BABILong includes a diverse set of 20 reasoning tasks, including fact chaining, simple induction, deduction, counting, and handling lists/sets. These tasks are challenging on their own, and even more demanding when the required facts are scattered across long natural text. Our evaluations show that popular LLMs effectively utilize only 10-20% of the context and their performance declines sharply with increased reasoning complexity. Among alternatives to in-context reasoning, Retrieval-Augmented Generation methods achieve a modest 60% accuracy on single-fact question answering, independent of context length. Among context extension methods, the highest performance is demonstrated by recurrent memory transformers after fine-tuning, enabling the processing of lengths up to 50 million tokens. The BABILong benchmark is extendable to any length to support the evaluation of new upcoming models with increased capabilities, and we provide splits up to 10 million token lengths.

paragraphs: BABILong evaluates whether language models can reason using facts scattered through very long documents. A large input capacity alone does not establish that a model can connect relevant information within it. The benchmark makes this distinction concrete through 20 tasks involving operations such as chaining facts, deduction, induction, counting, and working with lists or sets.

The necessary facts appear amid long stretches of natural text, combining the challenge of finding information with the challenge of reasoning over it. In the reported evaluations, popular language models effectively use only 10–20% of their context, and performance drops sharply as reasoning becomes more complex. Tested retrieval-augmented approaches achieve about 60% accuracy on single-fact questions, independently of context length.

Among the evaluated context-extension methods, fine-tuned recurrent memory transformers perform best and process sequences reaching 50 million tokens. The released benchmark splits extend to 10 million tokens, while the construction can support arbitrary lengths. The results distinguish nominal context capacity from demonstrated reasoning ability and provide a framework for testing both as models develop.
summary.tldr: BABILong tests reasoning over facts scattered through long documents and reveals substantial gaps between context capacity and effective use.

title: BABILong: Testing the Limits of LLMs with Long Context Reasoning-in-a-Haystack

abstract: Recent sequence modeling approaches using selective state space sequence models, referred to as Mamba models, have seen a surge of interest. These models allow efficient processing of long sequences in linear time and are rapidly being adopted in a wide range of applications such as language modeling, demonstrating promising performance. To foster their reliable use in real-world scenarios, it is crucial to augment their transparency. Our work bridges this critical gap by bringing explainability, particularly Layer-wise Relevance Propagation (LRP), to the Mamba architecture. Guided by the axiom of relevance conservation, we identify specific components in the Mamba architecture, which cause unfaithful explanations. To remedy this issue, we propose MambaLRP, a novel algorithm within the LRP framework, which ensures a more stable and reliable relevance propagation through these components. Our proposed method is theoretically sound and excels in achieving state-of-the-art explanation performance across a diverse range of models and datasets. Moreover, MambaLRP facilitates a deeper inspection of Mamba architectures, uncovering various biases and evaluating their significance. It also enables the analysis of previous speculations regarding the long-range capabilities of Mamba models.

paragraphs: Mamba models process long sequences with computation that grows linearly with sequence length, making them attractive for applications such as language modeling. This paper addresses a complementary need: explaining their predictions. It adapts Layer-wise Relevance Propagation, or LRP, to trace a model’s output back through its internal computations.

The authors use relevance conservation as a guiding principle, tracking how explanatory relevance is distributed through the network. They identify particular Mamba components that produce unfaithful explanations under relevance propagation. MambaLRP modifies the propagation procedure for these components to make the resulting explanations more stable and reliable.

They also use MambaLRP to inspect architectural biases and assess their significance. Another application examines earlier speculation about Mamba’s long-range capabilities. The contribution therefore includes both an explanation algorithm and a means of investigating model behavior, without the abstract claiming a particular resolution to every question about long-range processing.
summary.tldr: MambaLRP adapts relevance propagation to Mamba’s architecture, improving explanations and enabling closer study of biases and long-range behavior.

title: MambaLRP: Explaining Selective State Space Sequence Models

abstract: This paper explores the problem of class-generalizable anomaly detection, where the objective is to train one unified AD model that can generalize to detect anomalies in diverse classes from different domains without any retraining or fine-tuning on the target data. Because normal feature representations vary significantly across classes, this will cause the widely studied one-for-one AD models to be poorly classgeneralizable (i.e., performance drops dramatically when used for new classes). In this work, we propose a simple but effective framework (called ResAD) that can be directly applied to detect anomalies in new classes. Our main insight is to learn the residual feature distribution rather than the initial feature distribution. In this way, we can significantly reduce feature variations. Even in new classes, the distribution of normal residual features would not remarkably shift from the learned distribution. Therefore, the learned model can be directly adapted to new classes. ResAD consists of three components: (1) a Feature Converter that converts initial features into residual features; (2) a simple and shallow Feature Constraintor that constrains normal residual features into a spatial hypersphere for further reducing feature variations and maintaining consistency in feature scales among different classes; (3) a Feature Distribution Estimator that estimates the normal residual feature distribution, anomalies can be recognized as out-of-distribution. Despite the simplicity, ResAD can achieve remarkable anomaly detection results when directly used in new classes. The code is available at https://github.com/xcyao00/ResAD.

paragraphs: An anomaly detector trained for one class can perform poorly on another because normal examples have very different feature representations. ResAD targets a broader objective: a single detector that works across new classes and domains without retraining or fine-tuning on the target data. Its central move is to learn the distribution of residual features.

The framework has three components. A Feature Converter transforms initial features into residual features to reduce variation across classes. A shallow Feature Constraintor gathers normal residual features inside a spatial hypersphere, further reducing variation and keeping feature scales consistent. A Feature Distribution Estimator then learns how normal residual features are distributed and identifies anomalies as departures from that distribution.

The rationale is that normal residual features shift less across classes than the original features do. This makes the learned normality model more transferable to previously unseen classes. The authors report strong anomaly-detection results when applying ResAD directly to new classes, supporting residual representations as a practical basis for class-generalizable detection.
summary.tldr: ResAD learns normal residual-feature distributions to detect anomalies in new classes without target-specific retraining.

title: ResAD: A Simple Framework for Class Generalizable Anomaly Detection

abstract: Multi-task reinforcement learning aims to quickly identify solutions for new tasks with minimal or no additional interaction with the environment. Generalized Policy Improvement (GPI) addresses this by combining a set of base policies to produce a new one that is at least as good—though not necessarily optimal—as any individual base policy. Optimality can be ensured, particularly in the linear-reward case, via techniques that compute a Convex Coverage Set (CCS). However, these are computationally expensive and do not scale to complex domains. The Option Keyboard (OK) improves upon GPI by producing policies that are at least as good—and often better. It achieves this through a learned meta-policy that dynamically combines base policies. However, its performance critically depends on the choice of base policies. This raises a key question: is there an optimal set of base policies—an optimal *behavior basis*—that enables zero-shot identification of optimal solutions for *any* linear tasks? We solve this open problem by introducing a novel method that efficiently constructs such an optimal behavior basis. We show that it significantly reduces the number of base policies needed to ensure optimality in new tasks. We also prove that it is strictly more expressive than a CCS, enabling particular classes of *non-linear* tasks to be solved optimally. We empirically evaluate our technique in challenging domains and show that it outperforms state-of-the-art approaches, increasingly so as task complexity increases.

paragraphs: Multi-task reinforcement learning seeks to solve new tasks using behaviors learned previously, ideally without further interaction. Generalized Policy Improvement combines existing policies and guarantees performance at least as good as the individual policies, but that does not ensure an optimal solution. The Option Keyboard uses a learned meta-policy to combine behaviors dynamically, making the choice of its underlying policies especially important.

This paper provides a method for constructing an optimal behavior basis: a collection of base policies that enables the Option Keyboard to identify optimal solutions without additional interaction for any linear task in the considered framework. The method substantially reduces the number of policies needed to ensure optimality. This addresses the computational burden associated with constructing a Convex Coverage Set, another route to optimality for linear rewards.

The authors also prove that the resulting construction is strictly more expressive than a Convex Coverage Set, supporting optimal solutions for particular classes of nonlinear tasks. That extension does not cover every nonlinear task. Experiments in challenging domains show improvements over state-of-the-art approaches, with larger advantages as task complexity increases.
summary.tldr: An efficiently constructed behavior basis lets the Option Keyboard solve new linear tasks optimally and extends optimality to certain nonlinear tasks.

title: Constructing an Optimal Behavior Basis for the Option Keyboard

abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) such as CLIP demonstrate strong generalization in zero-shot classification but remain highly vulnerable to adversarial perturbations. Existing methods primarily focus on adversarial fine-tuning or prompt optimization, they often overlook the gaps in CLIP’s encoded features, which is shown as the text and image features lie far apart from each other. This misalignment is significantly amplified under adversarial perturbations, leading to severe degradation in classification performance. To address this problem, we propose **C**r**O**ss-moda**L**ity **A**lignment, dubbed **COLA**, an optimal transport-based framework that explicitly addresses adversarial misalignment by restoring both global image-text alignment and local structural consistency in the feature space. (1) COLA first projects adversarial image embeddings onto a subspace spanned by class text features, effectively filtering out non-semantic distortions while preserving discriminative information. (2) It then models images and texts as discrete distributions over multiple augmented views and refines their alignment via OT, with the subspace projection seamlessly integrated into the cost computation. This design ensures stable cross-modal alignment even under adversarial conditions. COLA is training-free and compatible with existing fine-tuned models. Extensive evaluations across 14 zero-shot classification benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of COLA, especially with an average improvement of 6.7% on ImageNet and its variants under PGD adversarial attacks, while maintaining high accuracy on clean samples.

paragraphs: CLIP classifies images by relating their representations to text representations, yet the two can lie far apart in its feature space. This paper finds that adversarial perturbations amplify that mismatch and damage classification. COLA addresses the mismatch directly through a training-free alignment procedure that can also work with already fine-tuned models.

The procedure first projects an adversarial image representation into the space spanned by class text features. This is designed to remove distortions unrelated to meaning while retaining information that distinguishes classes. It then treats multiple augmented image and text views as distributions and uses optimal transport to refine their alignment, incorporating the projection into the matching cost.

These steps address both overall image-text alignment and local structure among representations. Evaluation across 14 zero-shot classification benchmarks supports the method's effectiveness. On ImageNet and its variants, the authors report an average improvement of 6.7% under PGD adversarial attacks while retaining high accuracy on clean inputs. The findings show that adjusting cross-modal relationships can improve robustness without an additional training stage.
summary.tldr: COLA improves CLIP's adversarial robustness without training by projecting and realigning image and text representations.

title: Enhancing CLIP Robustness via Cross-Modality Alignment

abstract: In this work we consider generic Gaussian Multi-index models, in which the labels only depend on the (Gaussian) $d$-dimensional inputs through their projection onto a low-dimensional $r = O_d(1)$ subspace, and we study efficient agnostic estimation procedures for this hidden subspace. We introduce the *generative leap* exponent, a natural extension of the generative exponent from Damian et al. 2024 to the multi-index setting. We show that a sample complexity of $n=\Theta(d^{1 \vee k^\star/2})$ is necessary in the class of algorithms captured by the Low-Degree-Polynomial framework; and also sufficient, by giving a sequential estimation procedure based on a spectral U-statistic over appropriate Hermite tensors.

We introduce the *generative leap* exponent, a natural extension of the generative exponent from Damian et al. 2024 to the multi-index setting. We show that a sample complexity of $n=\Theta(d^{1 \vee k^\star/2})$ is necessary in the class of algorithms captured by the Low-Degree-Polynomial framework; and also sufficient, by giving a sequential estimation procedure based on a spectral U-statistic over appropriate Hermite tensors.

paragraphs: The paper studies Gaussian multi-index models, where labels depend on high-dimensional Gaussian inputs only through their projection onto a hidden low-dimensional subspace. The task is to estimate that subspace efficiently in an agnostic setting. Its dimension remains bounded as the ambient input dimension grows, making the relevant structure small relative to the full input.

The authors introduce a quantity called the generative leap exponent, extending a generative exponent to this multi-index setting. It determines the stated sample scaling: the required number of examples is proportional to d raised to the larger of 1 and half the generative leap exponent. The necessity result applies specifically to algorithms captured by the Low-Degree-Polynomial framework.

They also establish sufficiency by constructing a sequential estimator using a spectral U-statistic built from suitable Hermite tensors. The matching sample bounds connect an algorithmic limitation with an explicit estimation procedure at the same scaling. This characterizes how dimension and the generative leap jointly govern efficient subspace recovery within the paper's model and computational framework.
summary.tldr: The generative leap exponent characterizes matching sample bounds for Gaussian multi-index subspace estimation, with necessity established in the Low-Degree-Polynomial framework.

title: The Generative Leap: Tight Sample Complexity for Efficiently Learning Gaussian Multi-Index Models

abstract: Modern AI systems struggle most in environments where reliability is critical - scenes with smoke, poor visibility, and structural deformation. Each year, tens of thousands of firefighters are injured on duty, often due to breakdowns in situational perception. We introduce Fire360, a benchmark for evaluating perception and reasoning in safety-critical firefighting scenarios. The dataset includes 228 360° videos from professional training sessions under diverse conditions (e.g., low light, thermal distortion), annotated with action segments, object locations, and degradation metadata. Fire360 supports five tasks: Visual Question Answering, Temporal Action Captioning, Object Localization, Safety-Critical Reasoning, and Transformed Object Retrieval (TOR). TOR tests whether models can match pristine exemplars to fire-damaged counterparts in unpaired scenes, evaluating episodic memory under irreversible visual transformations. While human experts achieve 83.5% on TOR, models like GPT-4o lag significantly, exposing failures in reasoning under degradation. By releasing Fire360 and its evaluation suite, we aim to advance models that not only see, but also remember, reason, and act under uncertainty. The dataset is available at https://uofi.box.com/v/fire360dataset

paragraphs: Fire360 evaluates whether AI can interpret firefighting scenes when smoke, low light, heat-related distortion, and damage make visual evidence difficult to use. It contains 228 panoramic videos recorded during professional training sessions. Annotations describe actions, object locations, and visual degradation, allowing evaluation to account for the challenging conditions in each scene.

The benchmark covers visual question answering, descriptions of actions over time, object localization, safety-related reasoning, and a task called Transformed Object Retrieval. This last task asks a model to match an intact example of an object to a fire-damaged counterpart in an unpaired scene. It tests recognition across irreversible changes in appearance as an evaluation of episodic memory.

Human experts reach 83.5% on the retrieval task, while models including GPT-4o perform substantially worse. That gap exposes difficulties reasoning about degraded visual evidence and connecting altered objects to their earlier appearance. The benchmark and evaluation suite provide a way to study these capabilities together, extending evaluation beyond recognizing what is immediately visible.
summary.tldr: Fire360 tests perception, reasoning, and object memory in degraded firefighting videos, revealing a substantial model–expert gap.

title: Fire360: A Benchmark for Robust Perception and Episodic Memory in Degraded 360° Firefighting Video

abstract: Weight decay is a standard regularization technique for training large language models (LLMs). While it is common to assign a uniform decay rate to every layer, this approach overlooks the structural diversity of LLMs and the varying spectral properties across modules. In this paper, we introduce AlphaDecay, a simple yet effective method that adaptively assigns different weight decay strengths to each module of an LLM. Our approach is guided by Heavy-Tailed Self-Regularization (HT-SR) theory, which analyzes the empirical spectral density (ESD) of weight correlation matrices to quantify “heavy-tailedness.” Modules exhibiting more pronounced heavy-tailed ESDs, reflecting stronger feature learning, are assigned weaker decay, while modules with lighter-tailed spectra receive stronger decay. Our method leverages tailored weight decay assignments to balance the module-wise differences in spectral properties, leading to improved performance. Extensive pre-training tasks with various model sizes from 60M to 1B demonstrate that AlphaDecay achieves better perplexity and generalization than conventional uniform decay and other adaptive decay baselines. The code is available at https://github.com/hed-ucas/AlphaDecay.

paragraphs: Weight decay regularizes language-model training, but applying the same strength everywhere treats structurally different model components alike. AlphaDecay instead assigns decay strengths separately to individual modules. Its central idea is that the structure of learned weights can help determine how strongly each component should be regularized.

The method uses Heavy-Tailed Self-Regularization theory to examine the spectral distributions of weight correlation matrices. Within this framework, more pronounced heavy tails reflect stronger feature learning. AlphaDecay gives those modules weaker decay and gives modules with lighter-tailed distributions stronger decay. These assignments are intended to balance differences in spectral properties across the model.

The authors evaluate pretraining with models ranging from 60 million to one billion parameters. They report better perplexity and generalization than both uniform weight decay and other adaptive decay baselines. The findings support using module-specific weight statistics to guide regularization in the tested settings, showing that a common training ingredient can benefit from accounting for differences within a language model.
summary.tldr: AlphaDecay improves tested language-model pretraining by assigning weight decay separately according to each module’s spectral properties.

title: AlphaDecay: Module-wise Weight Decay for Heavy-Tailed Balancing in LLMs

abstract: The physical sciences are replete with dynamical systems that require the resolution of a wide range of length and time scales. This presents significant computational challenges since direct numerical simulation requires discretization at the finest relevant scales, leading to a high-dimensional state space. In this work, we propose an approach to learn stochastic multiscale models in the form of stochastic differential equations directly from observational data. Drawing inspiration from physics-based multiscale modeling approaches, we resolve the macroscale state on a coarse mesh while introducing a microscale latent state to explicitly model unresolved dynamics. We learn the parameters of the multiscale model using a simulator-free amortized variational inference method with a Product of Experts likelihood that enforces scale separation. We present detailed numerical studies to demonstrate that our learned multiscale models achieve superior predictive accuracy compared to under-resolved direct numerical simulation and closure-type models at equivalent resolution, as well as reduced-order modeling approaches.

paragraphs: Physical systems often evolve across widely separated spatial and temporal scales. Simulating every relevant detail requires a fine discretization and a large state space, which makes computation expensive. This paper learns stochastic differential-equation models directly from observations, aiming to retain useful fine-scale dynamics while representing the observable large-scale state on a coarse mesh.

The model includes a latent microscale state that explicitly describes dynamics unresolved by that mesh. Its parameters are learned through simulator-free amortized variational inference. A Product of Experts likelihood enforces separation between scales, making scale separation part of the learning formulation. The coarse and latent states together provide the multiscale description.

Detailed numerical studies report better predictive accuracy than under-resolved direct simulations and closure-type models at equivalent resolution, as well as reduced-order modeling approaches. These comparisons support the benefit of learning an explicit representation of unresolved dynamics. The result is a data-driven route to multiscale prediction in which coarse resolution need not mean discarding all information about the smaller-scale processes influencing the system.
summary.tldr: The method learns stochastic models that combine coarse physical states with latent fine-scale dynamics to improve prediction.

title: Learning Stochastic Multiscale Models

abstract: The whole-slide pathology images (WSIs) are widely recognized as the golden standard for cancer survival analysis. However, due to the high-resolution of WSIs, the existing studies require dividing WSIs into patches and identify key components before building the survival prediction system, which is time-consuming and cannot reflect the overall spatial organization of WSIs. Inspired by the fact that the spatial interactions among different tumor microenvironment (TME) components in WSIs are associated with the cancer prognosis, some studies attempt to capture the complex interactions among different TME components to improve survival predictions. However, they require extra efforts for building the TME segmentation model, which involves substantial annotation workloads on different TME components and is independent to the construction of the survival prediction model. To address the above issues, we propose ZTSurv, a novel end-to-end cancer survival analysis framework via efficient zero-shot TME segmentation on low-resolution WSIs. Specifically, by leveraging tumor infiltrating lymphocyte (TIL) maps on the 50x down-sampled WSIs, ZTSurv enables zero-shot segmentation on other two important TME components (i.e., tumor and stroma) that can reduce the annotation efforts from the pathologists. Then, based on the visual and semantic information extracted from different TME components, we construct a heterogeneous graph to capture their spatial intersections for clinical outcome prediction. We validate ZTSurv across four cancer cohorts derived from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA), and the experimental results indicate that our method can not only achieve superior prediction results but also significantly reduce the computational costs in comparison with the state-of-the-art methods.

The findings support the usefulness of low-resolution tissue organization for this prediction task. The approach matters because it connects efficient component segmentation with explicit spatial modeling, addressing both annotation demands and the cost of processing whole slides.
summary.tldr: ZTSurv uses low-resolution tissue segmentation and spatial graphs to improve reported cancer survival predictions while reducing computation.

title: Cancer Survival Analysis via Zero-shot Tumor Microenvironment Segmentation on Low-resolution Whole Slide Pathology Images

abstract: In this work, we introduce Erasure of Language Memory (ELM), a principled approach to concept-level unlearning that operates by matching distributions defined by the model's own introspective classification capabilities. Our key insight is that effective unlearning should leverage the model's ability to evaluate its own knowledge, using the language model itself as a classifier to identify and reduce the likelihood of generating content related to undesired concepts. ELM applies this framework to create targeted low-rank updates that reduce generation probabilities for concept-specific content while preserving the model's broader capabilities. We demonstrate ELM's efficacy on biosecurity, cybersecurity, and literary domain erasure tasks. Comparative evaluation reveals that ELM-modified models achieve near-random performance on assessments targeting erased concepts, while simultaneously preserving generation coherence, maintaining benchmark performance on unrelated tasks, and exhibiting strong robustness to adversarial attacks.

paragraphs: Erasure of Language Memory, or ELM, addresses concept-level unlearning: reducing a language model's ability to generate material associated with selected concepts while retaining its broader abilities. Its central idea is to use the model's own classification capabilities to judge whether content relates to the knowledge being targeted.

ELM turns those judgments into distributions that guide the unlearning process. It then applies targeted low-rank updates to reduce generation probabilities for concept-specific content. The approach links the model's ability to recognize a concept with changes to its tendency to produce that concept, making its own assessments part of the mechanism for selective removal.

The authors evaluate erasure in biosecurity, cybersecurity, and literary domains. Modified models perform near chance on assessments of the targeted concepts, while preserving coherent generation and benchmark performance on unrelated tasks. They also show strong robustness to adversarial attacks in the reported evaluation. These findings provide evidence that targeted concept suppression can coexist with retained general capability, with the erasure claim grounded in the assessments and attacks tested.
summary.tldr: ELM uses a language model's own concept judgments to guide targeted updates that suppress selected knowledge while preserving broader capabilities.

title: Erasing Conceptual Knowledge from Language Models

abstract: Visual tokens consume substantial computational resources in multi-modal large models (MLLMs), significantly compromising their efficiency. Recent works have attempted to improve efficiency by compressing visual tokens during training, either through modifications to model components or by introducing additional parameters. However, they often overlook the increased learning difficulty caused by such compression, as the model’s parameter space struggles to quickly adapt to the substantial perturbations in the feature space induced by token compression. In this work, we propose to develop Efficient MLLMs via Progressive Consistency Distillation (EPIC), a progressive learning framework. Specifically, by decomposing the feature space perturbations introduced by token compression along the token-wise and layer-wise dimensions, we introduce token consistency distillation and layer consistency distillation, respectively, aiming to reduce the training difficulty by leveraging guidance from a teacher model and following a progressive learning trajectory. Extensive experiments demonstrate the superior effectiveness, robustness, and generalization capabilities of our proposed framework.

paragraphs: Visual tokens account for substantial computation in multimodal language models, making compression an appealing route to efficiency. However, compression also changes the features that the model must process. The authors argue that existing approaches often underestimate this learning problem: model parameters may struggle to adapt quickly when the visual representation changes substantially.

EPIC addresses adaptation through a progressive training framework guided by a teacher model. It separates the disturbances caused by compression into two dimensions: differences across tokens and differences across layers. Token consistency distillation and layer consistency distillation provide corresponding forms of guidance, helping the compressed model follow a more gradual learning trajectory.

The contribution is therefore about how a model learns to operate with compressed visual information, as well as the computational motivation for using fewer tokens. Extensive experiments report superior effectiveness, robustness, and generalization for the proposed framework. These findings support the authors' argument that managing the transition to compressed representations is an important part of building efficient multimodal models, rather than assuming that ordinary training will readily absorb the change.
summary.tldr: EPIC uses progressive teacher guidance across tokens and layers to help multimodal models adapt to visual-token compression.

title: Efficient Multi-modal Large Language Models via Progressive Consistency Distillation

abstract: The established redundancy in visual tokens within large vision–language models (LVLMs) allows for pruning to effectively reduce their substantial computational demands. Empirical evidence from previous works indicates that visual tokens in later decoder stages receive less attention than shallow layers. Then, previous methods typically employ heuristics layer-specific pruning strategies where, although the number of tokens removed may differ across decoder layers, the overall pruning schedule is fixed and applied uniformly to all input samples and tasks, failing to align token elimination with the model’s holistic reasoning trajectory. Cognitive science indicates that human visual processing often begins with broad exploration to accumulate evidence before narrowing focus as the target becomes distinct. Our experiments reveal an analogous pattern in LVLMs. This observation strongly suggests that neither a fixed pruning schedule nor a heuristics layer-wise strategy can optimally accommodate the diverse complexities inherent in different inputs. To overcome this limitation, we introduce Complexity-Adaptive Pruning (AutoPrune), which is a training-free, plug-and-play framework that tailors pruning policies to varying sample and task complexities. Specifically, AutoPrune quantifies the mutual information between visual and textual tokens, and then projects this signal to a budget-constrained logistic retention curve. Each such logistic curve, defined by its unique shape, is shown to effectively correspond with the specific complexity of different tasks, and can easily guarantee adherence to a pre-defined computational constraints. We evaluate AutoPrune not only on standard vision-language tasks but also on Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models for autonomous driving. Notably, when applied to LLaVA-1.5-7B, our method prunes 89% of visual tokens and reduces inference FLOPs by 76.8%, but still retaining 96.7% of the original accuracy averaged over all tasks. This corresponds to a 9.1% improvement over the recent work PDrop (CVPR'2025), demonstrating the effectivenes. Code is available at https://github.com/AutoLab-SAI-SJTU/AutoPrune.

This paper observes a pattern of broad initial exploration followed by narrower focus, suggesting that token retention should adapt to input complexity.

It measures mutual information between visual and textual tokens and maps this signal to a logistic retention curve under a computational budget. The curve determines how token retention changes through the model, allowing different samples and tasks to receive different pruning policies while respecting the specified budget.

The authors evaluate the approach on vision-language tasks and vision-language-action models for autonomous driving. For LLaVA-1.5-7B, it removes 89% of visual tokens and reduces inference FLOPs by 76.8%, while retaining 96.7% of original accuracy averaged across tasks. These results show that substantial computational savings can coexist with much of the original performance in the reported evaluation.
summary.tldr: AutoPrune adapts visual-token pruning to sample and task complexity, substantially reducing computation while retaining most accuracy in the reported evaluation.

title: Each Complexity Deserves a Pruning Policy

abstract: Network traffic classification is essential for network management and security. In recent years, deep learning (DL) algorithms have emerged as essential tools for classifying complex traffic. However, they rely heavily on high-quality labeled training data. In practice, traffic data is often noisy due to human error or inaccurate automated labeling, which could render classification unreliable and lead to severe consequences. Although some studies have alleviated the label noise issue in specific scenarios, they are difficult to generalize to general traffic classification tasks due to the inherent semantic complexity of traffic data. In this paper, we propose FlowRefiner, a robust and general traffic classification framework against label noise. FlowRefiner consists of three core components: a traffic semantics-driven noise detector, a confidence-guided label correction mechanism, and a cross-granularity robust classifier. First, the noise detector utilizes traffic semantics extracted from a pre-trained encoder to identify mislabeled flows. Next, the confidence-guided label correction module fine-tunes a label predictor to correct noisy labels and construct refined flows. Finally, the cross-granularity robust classifier learns generalized patterns of both flow-level and packet-level, improving classification robustness against noisy labels. We evaluate our method on four traffic datasets with various classification scenarios across varying noise ratios. Experimental results demonstrate that FlowRefiner mitigates the impact of label noise and consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines by a large margin. The code is available at https://github.com/NSSL-SJTU/FlowRefiner.

title: FlowRefiner: A Robust Traffic Classification Framework against Label Noise

abstract: Solving bilevel optimization (BLO) problems to global optimality is generally intractable. A common surrogate is to compute a hyper-stationary point—a stationary point of the hyper-objective function obtained by minimizing or maximizing the upper-level objective over the lower-level solution set. Existing methods, however, either provide weak notions of stationarity or require restrictive assumptions to guarantee the smoothness of hyper-objective functions. In this paper, we eliminate these impractical assumptions and show that strong (Clarke) hyper-stationarity remains computable even when the hyper-objective is nonsmooth. Our key ingredient is a new structural property, called set smoothness, which captures the variational dependence of the lower-level solution set on the upper-level variable. We prove that this property holds for a broad class of BLO problems and ensures weak convexity (resp. concavity) of pessimistic (resp. optimistic) hyper-objective functions. Building on this foundation, we show that a zeroth-order algorithm that computes approximate Clarke hyper-stationary points with non-asymptotic convergence guarantees. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first computational guarantee for Clarke-type stationarity in nonsmooth BLO. Beyond this specific application, the set smoothness property emerges as a structural concept of independent interest, with potential to inform the analysis of broader classes of optimization and variational problems.

paragraphs: Bilevel optimization places one optimization problem inside another. The upper-level objective may depend on choosing among several lower-level solutions, producing a hyper-objective that can be nonsmooth. Because finding global optima is generally intractable, researchers seek stationary points. Existing guarantees often use weaker stationarity notions or restrictive assumptions that make the hyper-objective smooth.

The paper introduces set smoothness, a property describing how the lower-level solution set varies with the upper-level variable. The authors prove it holds for a broad class of problems. It ensures weak convexity for pessimistic hyper-objectives and weak concavity for optimistic ones, providing useful structure even when ordinary smoothness is absent.

Using this structure, the authors establish non-asymptotic convergence guarantees for a zeroth-order algorithm computing approximate Clarke hyper-stationary points. This supplies a stronger stationarity guarantee in the nonsmooth setting without the earlier smoothness requirements. The authors describe it as the first computational guarantee of this kind and suggest that set smoothness could also inform broader optimization and variational analysis.
summary.tldr: Set smoothness enables guaranteed computation of approximate Clarke hyper-stationary points for a broad class of nonsmooth bilevel problems.

title: Set Smoothness Unlocks Clarke Hyper-stationarity in Bilevel Optimization

abstract: Large language model (LLM) evaluation is increasingly costly, prompting interest in methods that speed up evaluation by shrinking benchmark datasets. Benchmark prediction (also called efficient LLM evaluation) aims to select a small subset of evaluation points and predict overall benchmark performance from that subset. In this paper, we systematically assess the strengths and limitations of 11 benchmark prediction methods across 19 diverse benchmarks. First, we identify a highly competitive baseline: Take a random sample and fit a regression model on the sample to predict missing entries. Outperforming most existing methods, this baseline challenges the assumption that careful subset selection is necessary for benchmark prediction. Second, we discover that all existing methods crucially depend on model similarity. They work best when interpolating scores among similar models. The effectiveness of benchmark prediction sharply declines when new models have higher accuracy than previously seen models. In this setting of extrapolation, none of the previous methods consistently beat a simple average over random samples. To improve over the sample average, we introduce a new method inspired by augmented inverse propensity weighting. This method consistently outperforms the random sample average even for extrapolation. However, its performance still relies on model similarity and the gains are modest in general. This shows that benchmark prediction fails just when it is most needed: at the evaluation frontier, where the goal is to evaluate new models of unknown capabilities.

paragraphs: Benchmark prediction estimates a language model’s full evaluation score from a small subset of questions. The paper compares 11 methods across 19 benchmarks to investigate when this cost-saving strategy works. A strong baseline simply samples questions randomly and uses regression to predict unobserved results, outperforming most existing methods.

The central finding is that success depends heavily on similarity between models. Predicting scores among models resembling those already observed works better than predicting results for newly stronger models. In that extrapolation setting, none of the previous methods consistently improves on the average score from a random sample. This challenges both sophisticated subset selection and reliance on patterns learned from earlier models.

Its gains are generally modest, however, and it still depends on model similarity. The study therefore identifies a practical weakness at the evaluation frontier, where unfamiliar capabilities make reliable score prediction especially valuable.
summary.tldr: Predicting benchmark scores from small subsets becomes unreliable for newly stronger models, and a proposed improvement offers only modest gains.

title: How Benchmark Prediction from Fewer Data Misses the Mark

abstract: Color plays an important role in human perception and usually provides critical clues in visual reasoning. However, it is unclear whether and how vision-language models (VLMs) can perceive, understand, and leverage color as humans.This paper introduces ColorBench, an innovative benchmark meticulously crafted to assess the capabilities of VLMs in color understanding, including color perception, reasoning, and robustness. By curating a suite of diverse test scenarios, with grounding in real applications, ColorBench evaluates how these models perceive colors, infer meanings from color-based cues, and maintain consistent performance under varying color transformations. Through an extensive evaluation of 32 VLMs with varying language models and vision encoders, our paper reveals some undiscovered findings: (i) The scaling law (larger models are better) still holds on ColorBench, while the language model plays a more important role than the vision encoder. (ii) However, the performance gaps across models are relatively small, indicating that color understanding has been largely neglected by existing VLMs. (iii) CoT reasoning improves color understanding accuracies and robustness, though they are vision-centric tasks. (iv) Color clues are indeed leveraged by VLMs on ColorBench but they can also mislead models in some tasks.These findings highlight the critical limitations of current VLMs and underscore the need to enhance color comprehension. Our ColorBench can serve as a foundational tool for advancing the study of human-level color understanding of multimodal AI.

paragraphs: Color can identify an object, convey meaning, or provide a clue needed to answer a visual question. ColorBench investigates whether vision-language models use this information effectively. It separates color understanding into perceiving colors, reasoning from color cues, and remaining reliable when colors undergo transformations, using varied scenarios grounded in applications.

The authors evaluate 32 models with different language components and vision encoders. Larger models generally perform better on this benchmark, and the language component plays a greater role than the vision encoder. Nevertheless, differences between models are relatively small. The authors interpret this limited separation as evidence that existing model development has paid insufficient attention to color understanding.

Step-by-step reasoning improves both accuracy and robustness, even though the tasks center on visual information. The evaluation also finds that models do use color clues, but those same clues can mislead them on some tasks. Together, these results show why color understanding needs several kinds of tests: using color information and using it appropriately are distinct capabilities.
summary.tldr: ColorBench evaluates 32 vision-language models and finds that color cues support reasoning but can also mislead models.

title: ColorBench: Can VLMs See and Understand the Colorful World? A Comprehensive Benchmark for Color Perception, Reasoning, and Robustness

abstract: Open-Vocabulary semantic segmentation (OVSS) and domain generalization in semantic segmentation (DGSS) highlight a subtle complementarity that motivates Open-Vocabulary Domain-Generalized Semantic Segmentation (OV-DGSS). OV-DGSS aims to generate pixel-level masks for unseen categories while maintaining robustness across unseen domains, a critical capability for real-world scenarios such as autonomous driving in adverse conditions. We introduce Vireo, a novel single-stage framework for OV-DGSS that unifies the strengths of OVSS and DGSS for the first time. Vireo builds upon the frozen Visual Foundation Models (VFMs) and incorporates scene geometry via Depth VFMs to extract domain-invariant structural features. To bridge the gap between visual and textual modalities under domain shift, we propose three key components: (1) GeoText Query, which align geometric features with language cues and progressively refine VFM encoder representations; (2) Coarse Mask Prior Embedding (CMPE) for enhancing gradient flow for faster convergence and stronger textual influence; and (3) the Domain-Open-Vocabulary Vector Embedding Head (DOV-VEH), which fuses refined structural and semantic features for robust prediction. Comprehensive evaluation on these components demonstrates the effectiveness of our designs. Our proposed Vireo achieves the state-of-the-art performance and surpasses existing methods by a large margin in both domain generalization and open-vocabulary recognition, offering a unified and scalable solution for robust visual understanding in diverse and dynamic environments. Code is available at https://github.com/SY-Ch/Vireo.

paragraphs: Semantic segmentation assigns categories to individual image pixels. This paper combines two challenges: producing masks for categories not seen during training and remaining reliable in unfamiliar visual domains. Its Vireo framework brings open-vocabulary recognition and domain generalization together in a single-stage system, using both language and scene geometry.

GeoText Query aligns geometric features with language cues while progressively refining encoder representations. Coarse Mask Prior Embedding strengthens textual influence and improves gradient flow for faster convergence. A final embedding head combines the refined structural and semantic information to make pixel-level predictions.

The geometric component is intended to supply structural features that remain useful across domain changes, while the language connection supports recognition beyond a fixed training vocabulary. Component evaluations support the proposed design, and the authors report state-of-the-art results with large improvements in both domain generalization and open-vocabulary recognition. The findings support addressing these capabilities together through representations that connect scene structure with category meaning.
summary.tldr: Vireo combines depth geometry and language to segment unseen categories while generalizing across unfamiliar visual domains.

title: Leveraging Depth and Language for Open-Vocabulary Domain-Generalized Semantic Segmentation

abstract: Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) have recently demonstrated remarkable performance in visual generation tasks, surpassing traditional U-Net-based diffusion models by significantly improving image and video generation quality and scalability. However, the large model size and iterative denoising process introduce substantial computational and memory overhead, limiting their deployment in real-world applications. Post-training quantization (PTQ) is a promising solution that compresses models and accelerates inference by converting weights and activations to low-bit representations. Despite its potential, PTQ faces significant challenges when applied to DiTs, often resulting in severe degradation of generative quality. To address these issues, we propose VETA-DiT (**V**ariance-**E**qualized and **T**emporal **A**daptation for **Di**ffusion **T**ransformers), a dedicated quantization framework for DiTs. Our method first analyzes the sources of quantization error from the perspective of inter-channel variance and introduces a Karhunen–Loève Transform enhanced alignment to equalize variance across channels, facilitating effective quantization under low bit-widths. Furthermore, to handle the temporal variation of activation distributions inherent in the iterative denoising steps of DiTs, we design an incoherence-aware adaptive method that identifies and properly calibrates timesteps with high quantization difficulty. We validate VETA-DiT on extensive image and video generation tasks, preserving acceptable visual quality under the more aggressive W4A4 configuration. Specifically, VETA-DiT reduces FID by 33.65 on the DiT-XL/2 model and by 45.76 on the PixArt-$\Sigma$ model compared to the baseline under W4A4, demonstrating its strong quantization capability and generative performance. Code is available at: https://github.com/xululi0223/VETA-DiT.

Its framework addresses both differences across channels and changes across denoising steps.

title: VETA-DiT: Variance-Equalized and Temporally Adaptive Quantization for Efficient 4-bit Diffusion Transformers

abstract: Sampling from constrained statistical distributions is a fundamental task in various fields including Bayesian statistics, computational chemistry, and statistical physics. This article considers the cases where the constrained distribution is described by an unconstrained density, as well as additional equality and/or inequality constraints, which often make the constraint set nonconvex. Existing methods for nonconvex constraint set $\Sigma \subset \mathbb{R}^d$ defined by equality or inequality constraints commonly rely on costly projection steps. Moreover, they cannot handle equality and inequality constraints simultaneously as each method only specialized in one case. In addition, rigorous and quantitative convergence guarantee is often lacking. In this paper, we introduce Overdamped Langevin with LAnding (OLLA), a new framework that can design overdamped Langevin dynamics accommodating both equality and inequality constraints. The proposed dynamics also deterministically corrects trajectories along the normal direction of the constraint surface, thus obviating the need for explicit projections. We show that, under suitable regularity conditions on the target density and $\Sigma$, OLLA converges exponentially fast in $W_2$ distance to the constrained target density $\rho_\Sigma(x) \propto \exp(-f(x))d\sigma_\Sigma$. Lastly, through experiments, we demonstrate the efficiency of OLLA compared to projection-based constrained Langevin algorithms and their slack variable variants, highlighting its favorable computational cost and reasonable empirical mixing.

paragraphs: Sampling becomes difficult when a probability distribution must obey equality and inequality constraints, especially when the allowed region is nonconvex. Existing approaches discussed in the paper often require expensive projections back onto that region. They also tend to specialize in one constraint type, and rigorous quantitative convergence guarantees are often unavailable.

Overdamped Langevin with Landing, or OLLA, provides a framework for dynamics that accommodate both kinds of constraints. Alongside the stochastic sampling process, it deterministically corrects trajectories in the direction normal to the constraint surface. This correction removes the need for explicit projection steps while directing the dynamics toward the constrained target distribution.

Under suitable regularity conditions on the density and constraint set, the authors prove exponential convergence in Wasserstein-2 distance, a measure of discrepancy between distributions. Experiments compare OLLA with projection-based constrained Langevin algorithms and slack-variable variants, showing favorable computational cost and reasonable empirical mixing. The theoretical result is conditional on the stated regularity requirements, while the experiments assess how efficiently the method explores the tested distributions.
summary.tldr: OLLA samples under equality and inequality constraints without explicit projections and has exponential convergence guarantees under suitable regularity conditions.

title: Fast Non-Log-Concave Sampling under Nonconvex Equality and Inequality Constraints with Landing

abstract: The remarkable progress of Large Language Models (LLMs) presents promising opportunities for Verilog code generation which is significantly important for automated circuit design. The lacking of meaningful functional rewards hinders the preference optimization based on Reinforcement Learning (RL) for producing functionally correct Verilog code. In this paper, we propose Signal-Aware Learning for Verilog code generation (QiMeng-SALV) by leveraging code segments of functionally correct output signal to optimize RL training. Considering Verilog code specifies the structural interconnection of hardware gates and wires so that different output signals are independent, the key insight of QiMeng-SALV is to extract verified signal-aware implementations in partially incorrect modules, so as to enhance the extraction of meaningful functional rewards. Roughly, we verify the functional correctness of signals in generated module by comparing with that of reference module in the training data. Then abstract syntax tree (AST) is employed to identify signal-aware code segments which can provide meaningful functional rewards from erroneous modules. Finally, we introduce signal-aware DPO which is optimized on the correct signal-level code segments, thereby preventing noise and interference from incorrect signals. The proposed QiMeng-SALV underscores the paradigm shift from conventional module-level to fine-grained signal-level optimization in Verilog code generation, addressing the issue of insufficient functional rewards. Experiments demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on VerilogEval and RTLLM, with a 7B parameter model matching the performance of the DeepSeek v3 671B model and significantly outperforming the leading open-source model CodeV trained on the same dataset.

paragraphs: A generated Verilog module can be partly wrong while still implementing some output signals correctly. Evaluating only whether the entire module works discards that useful partial success. QiMeng-SALV uses correctly implemented signals inside otherwise incorrect modules to obtain more meaningful functional feedback for training code-generating language models.

The method compares generated signals with a reference module from the training data to verify their behavior. It then uses the code's abstract syntax tree to identify the segments associated with correct signals. A signal-aware form of direct preference optimization trains on those segments, avoiding noise and interference from incorrect outputs.

The main contribution is a finer unit of optimization: functional signal implementations rather than whole modules. This makes partially successful generations useful training evidence. Experiments report state-of-the-art performance on VerilogEval and RTLLM. A 7B-parameter model matches the performance of DeepSeek v3's 671B model in the reported evaluation and significantly outperforms CodeV trained on the same dataset, supporting the value of more precise functional feedback.
summary.tldr: QiMeng-SALV improves Verilog generation by training on verified signal-level code extracted from partially incorrect modules.

title: QiMeng-SALV: Signal-Aware Learning for Verilog Code Generation

abstract: This paper investigates the dynamical properties of tokens in pre-trained transformer models and explores their application to improving Transformers. To this end, we analyze the dynamical system governing the continuous-time limit of the pre-trained model and characterize the asymptotic behavior of its solutions. Specifically, we characterize when tokens move closer to or farther from one another over time, depending on the model parameters. We provide sufficient conditions, based on these parameters, to identify scenarios where tokens either converge to zero or diverge to infinity. Unlike prior works, our conditions are broader in scope and more applicable to real-world models. Furthermore, we investigate how different forms of positional encoding - specifically absolute and rotary - affect these dynamical regimes. Empirical evidence reveals that the convergence scenario adversely impacts model performance. Motivated by these insights, we propose simple refinements to Transformer architectures that mitigate convergence behavior in models with absolute or rotary positional encoding. These findings support theoretical foundations and design principles for improving Transformer models.
originalAbstract: This paper investigates the dynamical properties of tokens in pre-trained transformer models and explores their application to improving Transformers. To this end, we analyze the dynamical system governing the continuous-time limit of the pre-trained model and characterize the asymptotic behavior of its solutions. Specifically, we characterize when tokens move closer to or farther from one another over time, depending on the model parameters. We provide sufficient conditions, based on these parameters, to identify scenarios where tokens either converge to zero or diverge to infinity. Unlike prior works, our conditions are broader in scope and more applicable to real-world models. Furthermore, we investigate how different forms of positional encoding - specifically absolute and rotary - affect these dynamical regimes. Empirical evidence reveals that the convergence scenario adversely impacts model performance. Motivated by these insights, we propose simple refinements to Transformer architectures that mitigate convergence behavior in models with absolute or rotary positional encoding. These findings support theoretical foundations and design principles for improving Transformer models.

paragraphs: This paper examines transformer token representations as objects that evolve under a dynamical system. It analyzes a continuous-time limit of a pretrained model to understand how representations behave over time. The central questions concern whether tokens move closer together or farther apart, and how those tendencies depend on model parameters.

The analysis gives sufficient parameter-based conditions for two extreme behaviors: representations converging to zero or diverging to infinity. Sufficient conditions identify cases where a behavior follows; they do not establish that every case with that behavior must meet those conditions. The authors describe their conditions as broader and more applicable to real models than earlier results. They also examine how absolute and rotary positional encodings affect these regimes.

Empirical evidence links the convergence scenario to poorer model performance. Motivated by that finding, the authors propose simple architectural refinements that mitigate convergence in transformers using either positional encoding. The contribution connects a mathematical account of representation dynamics with concrete design changes, using the observed performance consequences to guide architectural choices.
summary.tldr: An analysis of transformer token dynamics identifies sufficient conditions for convergence or divergence and motivates architectural changes that mitigate harmful convergence.

title: Dynamical Properties of Tokens in Self-Attention and Effects of Positional Encoding

abstract: Zeroth-order methods are extensively used in machine learning applications where gradients are infeasible or expensive to compute, such as black-box attacks, reinforcement learning, and language model fine-tuning. Existing optimization theory focuses on convergence to an arbitrary stationary point, but less is known on the implicit regularization that provides a fine-grained characterization on which particular solutions are finally reached. We show that zeroth-order optimization with the standard two-point estimator favors solutions with small trace of Hessian, which is widely used in previous work to distinguish between sharp and flat minima. We further provide convergence rates of zeroth-order optimization to approximate flat minima for convex and sufficiently smooth functions, where flat minima are defined as the minimizers that achieve the smallest trace of Hessian among all optimal solutions. Experiments on binary classification tasks with convex losses and language model fine-tuning support our theoretical findings.

paragraphs: Zeroth-order optimization uses function evaluations when gradients are unavailable or expensive. Much of its theory asks whether optimization reaches a stationary point. This paper instead examines which solutions the method tends to favor, investigating an implicit preference that arises from the optimization procedure without an explicitly added regularization objective.

The authors show that the standard two-point estimator favors solutions with a small Hessian trace, a curvature measure used to distinguish flatter from sharper minima. They also provide convergence rates toward approximate flat minima for convex, sufficiently smooth functions. In that result, flat minima are defined specifically as optimal solutions with the smallest Hessian trace among all optimal solutions.

Experiments on binary classification with convex losses and on language-model fine-tuning support the theoretical findings. The result offers a more detailed picture than convergence alone: the gradient-free estimator can influence the geometry of the solution reached. The formal convergence guarantee depends on convexity and sufficient smoothness, while the language-model experiments provide empirical support in a different application setting.
summary.tldr: Zeroth-order optimization with a two-point estimator favors low-curvature solutions, with flat-minimum convergence guarantees for convex, sufficiently smooth functions.

title: Zeroth-Order Optimization Finds Flat Minima

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) and Foundation Models (FMs) have recently become prevalent for time series forecasting tasks. While fine-tuning LLMs enables domain adaptation, they often struggle to generalize across diverse and unseen datasets. Moreover, existing Time Series Foundation Models (TSFMs) still face challenges in handling non-stationary dynamics and distribution shifts, largely due to the lack of effective mechanisms for adaptation. To this end, we present TS-RAG, a retrieval-augmented generation framework for time series forecasting that enhances the generalization and interpretability of TSFMs. Specifically, TS-RAG leverages pre-trained time series encoders to retrieve semantically relevant segments from a dedicated knowledge base, enriching the contextual representation of the input query. Furthermore, we propose an Adaptive Retrieval Mixer (ARM) module that dynamically fuses the retrieved patterns with the TSFM's internal representation, improving forecasting accuracy without requiring task-specific fine-tuning. Thorough empirical studies on seven public benchmark datasets demonstrate that TS-RAG achieves state-of-the-art zero-shot forecasting performance, outperforming the existing TSFMs by up to 6.84\% across diverse domains while also providing desirable interpretability. Our code and data are available at: https://github.com/UConn-DSIS/TS-RAG.

paragraphs: Time-series foundation models must forecast sequences whose behavior may change across domains or over time. The paper argues that existing models lack effective adaptation mechanisms for these shifts. TS-RAG adds retrieval so a forecasting model can draw on relevant examples without requiring task-specific fine-tuning.

The framework uses pretrained time-series encoders to find semantically relevant segments in a dedicated knowledge base. These segments enrich the context available for the current input. An Adaptive Retrieval Mixer then dynamically combines the retrieved patterns with the foundation model's internal representation, connecting external examples to the model's existing forecasting capabilities.

Across seven public benchmark datasets, the authors report state-of-the-art zero-shot forecasting performance and improvements of up to 6.84% over existing time-series foundation models. They also report useful interpretability from the retrieval-based framework. The findings support retrieval as a way to improve generalization across the evaluated domains while making the contextual patterns informing a forecast more accessible, without adapting the model separately to each target task.
summary.tldr: TS-RAG retrieves relevant time-series patterns and adaptively mixes them into foundation-model representations to improve zero-shot forecasts.

title: TS-RAG: Retrieval-Augmented Generation based Time Series Foundation Models are Stronger Zero-Shot Forecaster

abstract: Multi-task learning (MTL) is a widely explored paradigm that enables the simultaneous learning of multiple tasks using a single model. Despite numerous solutions, the key issues of optimization conflict and task imbalance remain under-addressed, limiting performance. Unlike existing optimization-based approaches that typically reweight task losses or gradients to mitigate conflicts or promote progress, we propose a novel approach based on Continual Optimization with Symmetry Teleportation (COST). During MTL optimization, when an optimization conflict arises, we seek an alternative loss-equivalent point on the loss landscape to reduce conflict. Specifically, we utilize a low-rank adapter (LoRA) to facilitate this practical teleportation by designing convergent, loss-invariant objectives. Additionally, we introduce a historical trajectory reuse strategy to continually leverage the benefits of advanced optimizers. Extensive experiments on multiple mainstream datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach. COST is a plug-and-play solution that enhances a wide range of existing MTL methods. When integrated with state-of-the-art methods, COST achieves superior performance.
