paragraphs: A single model learning several tasks can encounter conflicting optimization directions and uneven progress across tasks. Many approaches respond by changing the weights assigned to task losses or gradients. COST instead explores whether moving to a different parameter configuration with an equivalent loss can make subsequent optimization less conflicted.

When a conflict arises, the method searches for such an alternative point on the loss landscape. It implements this symmetry-based movement using a low-rank adapter, or LoRA, and objectives designed to converge while preserving loss. The purpose is to change the optimization situation without first requiring an improvement in the loss value.

COST also reuses historical optimization trajectories to retain the benefits of advanced optimizers over continued training. Experiments on multiple mainstream datasets demonstrate improvements across a broad range of existing multi-task methods, including superior results when combined with state-of-the-art approaches. Its plug-and-play design matters because the proposed movement can augment established training methods, providing another way to address conflict within a shared model.
summary.tldr: COST reduces multi-task optimization conflict by moving between loss-equivalent parameter configurations and reusing optimization history.

title: Continual Optimization with Symmetry Teleportation for Multi-Task Learning

abstract: Although discriminative learning in graphical models generally improves classification results, the generative semantics of the model are compromised. In this paper, we introduce a novel approach of hybrid generative-discriminative learning for Bayesian networks. We use an SVM-type large margin formulation for discriminative training, introducing a likelihood-weighted \ell^1-norm for the SVM-norm-penalization. This simultaneously optimizes the data likelihood and therefore partly maintains the generative character of the model. For many network structures, our method can be formulated as a convex problem, guaranteeing a globally optimal solution. In terms of classification, the resulting models outperform state-of-the art generative and discriminative learning methods for Bayesian networks, and are comparable with linear and kernelized SVMs. Furthermore, the models achieve likelihoods close to the maximum likelihood solution and show robust behavior in classification experiments with missing features.

paragraphs: Bayesian networks can describe how data are generated as well as support classification. Training them primarily to separate classes often improves predictions but weakens their generative interpretation. This paper proposes a hybrid training method intended to obtain strong classification while retaining part of the model’s ability to explain the observed data probabilistically.

The method uses a large-margin formulation similar to a support vector machine, with a likelihood-weighted L1 penalty. This construction simultaneously optimizes data likelihood, helping preserve the model’s generative character. For many network structures, the objective can be formulated as a convex problem, which guarantees a globally optimal solution in those cases.

The reported models outperform leading generative and discriminative Bayesian-network training methods in classification and perform comparably to linear and kernelized support vector machines. They also achieve likelihoods close to the maximum-likelihood solution and behave robustly in classification experiments with missing features. These results support the proposed compromise: discriminative performance can improve while substantial generative quality remains, rather than being entirely sacrificed during training.
summary.tldr: Likelihood-weighted large-margin training improves Bayesian-network classification while partly preserving generative quality.

title: The Most Generative Maximum Margin Bayesian Networks

abstract: We analyze ’Distribution to Distribution regression’ where one is regressing a mapping where both the covariate (inputs) and response (outputs) are distributions. No parameters on the input or output distributions are assumed, nor are any strong assumptions made on the measure from which input distributions are drawn from. We develop an estimator and derive an upper bound for the L2 risk; also, we show that when the effective dimension is small enough (as measured by the doubling dimension), then the risk converges to zero with a polynomial rate.
originalAbstract: We analyze ’Distribution to Distribution regression’ where one is regressing a mapping where both the covariate (inputs) and response (outputs) are distributions. No parameters on the input or output distributions are assumed, nor are any strong assumptions made on the measure from which input distributions are drawn from. We develop an estimator and derive an upper bound for the L2 risk; also, we show that when the effective dimension is small enough (as measured by the doubling dimension), then the risk converges to zero with a polynomial rate.

paragraphs: This paper studies regression in which both the input and the output are probability distributions. The learning task is therefore to estimate a mapping between distributions, rather than a relationship between ordinary numerical inputs and responses. It treats the distributions themselves as the objects whose relationship must be learned.

The analysis does not assume a parametric form for either the input or output distributions. It also avoids strong assumptions about the measure that generates input distributions. Within this setting, the authors construct an estimator and derive an upper bound on its L2 risk, providing a theoretical account of the estimator's prediction error.

A more specific convergence result depends on effective dimension, measured through doubling dimension. When that dimension is sufficiently small, the risk approaches zero at a polynomial rate. The result identifies a condition under which learning a mapping between distributions remains statistically feasible, while preserving the distinction between broad distributional flexibility and the dimensional condition needed for this rate.
summary.tldr: An estimator learns mappings between distributions with an L2 risk bound and polynomial convergence when the effective dimension is sufficiently small.

title: Distribution to Distribution Regression

abstract: We consider a discriminative learning (regression) problem, whereby the regression function is a convex combination of k linear classifiers. Existing approaches are based on the EM algorithm, or similar techniques, without provable guarantees. We develop a simple method based on spectral techniques and a ‘mirroring’ trick, that discovers the subspace spanned by the classifiers’ parameter vectors. Under a probabilistic assumption on the feature vector distribution, we prove that this approach has nearly optimal statistical efficiency.
originalAbstract: We consider a discriminative learning (regression) problem, whereby the regression function is a convex combination of k linear classifiers. Existing approaches are based on the EM algorithm, or similar techniques, without provable guarantees. We develop a simple method based on spectral techniques and a ‘mirroring’ trick, that discovers the subspace spanned by the classifiers’ parameter vectors. Under a probabilistic assumption on the feature vector distribution, we prove that this approach has nearly optimal statistical efficiency.

paragraphs: This paper considers a regression function formed by combining k linear classifiers with nonnegative weights that sum to one. The learning problem therefore involves several classifier parameter vectors contributing to a single function. Existing approaches use EM or related procedures, but the abstract identifies a lack of provable guarantees for those approaches.

The authors develop a simple method that combines spectral techniques with a construction they call mirroring. Its stated output is the subspace spanned by the classifiers' parameter vectors. Recovering this subspace identifies the collection of directions containing those vectors, which is a precise structural target within the mixture-learning problem.

Under a probabilistic assumption about the distribution of feature vectors, the authors prove nearly optimal statistical efficiency. This means their method uses an amount of data close to the best achievable for the stated recovery task. The result gives a conditional theoretical foundation for learning this shared parameter subspace, tying the guarantee explicitly to the assumed feature distribution.
summary.tldr: A spectral method with a mirroring construction recovers a classifier mixture's parameter subspace with nearly optimal statistical efficiency under a feature-distribution assumption.

title: Learning Mixtures of Linear Classifiers

abstract: We present the hierarchical Dirichlet scaling process (HDSP), a Bayesian nonparametric mixed membership model for multi-labeled data. We construct the HDSP based on the gamma representation of the hierarchical Dirichlet process (HDP) which allows scaling the mixture components. With such construction, HDSP allocates a latent location to each label and mixture component in a space, and uses the distance between them to guide membership probabilities. We develop a variational Bayes algorithm for the approximate posterior inference of the HDSP. Through experiments on synthetic datasets as well as datasets of newswire, medical journal articles, and Wikipedia, we show that the HDSP results in better predictive performance than HDP, labeled LDA and partially labeled LDA.
originalAbstract: We present the hierarchical Dirichlet scaling process (HDSP), a Bayesian nonparametric mixed membership model for multi-labeled data. We construct the HDSP based on the gamma representation of the hierarchical Dirichlet process (HDP) which allows scaling the mixture components. With such construction, HDSP allocates a latent location to each label and mixture component in a space, and uses the distance between them to guide membership probabilities. We develop a variational Bayes algorithm for the approximate posterior inference of the HDSP. Through experiments on synthetic datasets as well as datasets of newswire, medical journal articles, and Wikipedia, we show that the HDSP results in better predictive performance than HDP, labeled LDA and partially labeled LDA.

paragraphs: The hierarchical Dirichlet scaling process is a Bayesian nonparametric mixed membership model for data carrying multiple labels. Mixed membership allows an observation to be associated with several latent components. The paper's aim is to use the labels to guide those memberships through the model's construction.

The authors build on the gamma representation of the hierarchical Dirichlet process, which permits mixture components to be scaled. Each label and each mixture component receives a latent location in a shared space. Distances between these locations influence membership probabilities, giving the model a geometric way to connect observed labels with latent components.

A variational Bayes algorithm provides approximate posterior inference. Experiments include synthetic data and collections of newswire, medical journal articles, and Wikipedia content. The proposed model achieves better predictive performance than the hierarchical Dirichlet process, labeled LDA, and partially labeled LDA in these evaluations. The findings support the usefulness of incorporating label-component relationships into the mixture structure.
summary.tldr: The hierarchical Dirichlet scaling process uses latent distances between labels and mixture components to guide memberships and improve prediction in reported experiments.

title: Hierarchical Dirichlet Scaling Process

abstract: A non-parametric approach to the problem of testing the independence of two random processes is developed. The test statistic is the Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion (HSIC), which was used previously in testing independence for i.i.d. pairs of variables. The asymptotic behaviour of HSIC is established when computed from samples drawn from random processes. It is shown that earlier bootstrap procedures which worked in the i.i.d. case will fail for random processes, and an alternative consistent estimate of the p-values is proposed. Tests on artificial data and real-world forex data indicate that the new test procedure discovers dependence which is missed by linear approaches, while the earlier bootstrap procedure returns an elevated number of false positives.

The test statistic is the Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion (HSIC), which was used previously in testing independence for i.i.d. pairs of variables. The asymptotic behaviour of HSIC is established when computed from samples drawn from random processes. It is shown that earlier bootstrap procedures which worked in the i.i.d. case will fail for random processes, and an alternative consistent estimate of the p-values is proposed. Tests on artificial data and real-world forex data indicate that the new test procedure discovers dependence which is missed by linear approaches, while the earlier bootstrap procedure returns an elevated number of false positives.

paragraphs: The paper develops a test for whether two random processes are independent. Its starting point is the Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion, or HSIC, which had already been used for independent and identically distributed pairs of observations. The challenge is to extend that approach to observations drawn from processes, where the sampling structure changes the statistical analysis.

The authors establish the asymptotic behavior of HSIC in this setting. They also show that earlier bootstrap procedures suitable for independent observations fail for random processes. This matters because a test needs more than a statistic that measures dependence: it also needs a reliable way to judge whether the observed value provides evidence against independence.

The proposed procedure supplies an alternative, consistent estimate of p-values. Experiments with artificial data and foreign exchange data indicate that it detects dependence missed by linear approaches. The earlier bootstrap procedure produces elevated false positives in these tests, illustrating why adapting the significance calculation is central to making HSIC useful for process data.
summary.tldr: The paper adapts HSIC independence testing to random processes with a consistent p-value procedure that accounts for the failure of earlier bootstrap methods.

title: A Kernel Independence Test for Random Processes

abstract: Many machine learning methods are given as parameterized optimization problems. Important examples of such parameters are regularization- and kernel hyperparameters. These parameters have to be tuned carefully since the choice of their values can have a significant impact on the statistical performance of the learning methods. In most cases the parameter space does not carry much structure and parameter tuning essentially boils down to exploring the whole parameter space. The case when there is only one parameter received quite some attention over the years. First, algorithms for tracking an optimal solution for several machine learning optimization problems over regularization- and hyperparameter intervals had been developed, but since these algorithms can suffer from numerical problems more robust and efficient approximate path tracking algorithms have been devised and analyzed recently. By now approximate path tracking algorithms are known for regularization-and kernel hyperparameter paths with optimal path complexities that depend only on the prescribed approximation error. Here we extend the work on approximate path tracking algorithms with approximation guarantees to multi-dimensional parameter domains. We show a lower bound on the complexity of approximately exploring a multi-dimensional parameter domain that is the product of the corresponding path complexities. We also show a matching upper bound that can be turned into a theoretically and practically efficient algorithm. Experimental results for kernelized support vector machines and the elastic net confirm the theoretical complexity analysis.

paragraphs: Many learning methods require solving an optimization problem whose solution changes with regularization or kernel hyperparameters. Selecting those parameters can require exploring a broad domain. This paper extends approximate solution tracking from a single parameter interval to domains with multiple parameter dimensions, while retaining guarantees on approximation quality.

The authors establish a lower bound on the complexity of approximate exploration. It is the product of the corresponding one-dimensional path complexities, capturing how the work compounds across parameter dimensions. They also prove a matching upper bound and turn it into an algorithm intended to be efficient both theoretically and practically.

The matching bounds show that the algorithm’s complexity meets the established limit in the analyzed setting. This makes the contribution more than a procedure for searching several parameters: it also explains the cost of that exploration relative to simpler paths. Experiments with kernelized support vector machines and the elastic net confirm the theoretical complexity analysis, connecting the guarantees to two parameterized learning problems.
summary.tldr: Approximate solution tracking extends to multidimensional hyperparameter domains with matching lower and upper complexity bounds.

title: Tracking Approximate Solutions of Parameterized Optimization Problems over Multi-Dimensional (Hyper-)Parameter Domains

abstract: The robust principal component analysis (robust PCA) problem has been considered in many machine learning applications, where the goal is to decompose the data matrix as a low rank part plus a sparse residual. While current approaches are developed by only considering the low rank plus sparse structure, in many applications, side information of row and/or column entities may also be given, and it is still unclear to what extent could such information help robust PCA. Thus, in this paper, we study the problem of robust PCA with side information, where both prior structure and features of entities are exploited for recovery. We propose a convex problem to incorporate side information in robust PCA and show that the low rank matrix can be exactly recovered via the proposed method under certain conditions. In particular, our guarantee suggests that a substantial amount of low rank matrices, which cannot be recovered by standard robust PCA, become recoverable by our proposed method. The result theoretically justifies the effectiveness of features in robust PCA. In addition, we conduct synthetic experiments as well as a real application on noisy image classification to show that our method also improves the performance in practice by exploiting side information.

paragraphs: Robust PCA separates a data matrix into a low-rank component and a sparse residual. The paper asks how additional information about row or column entities can help this recovery. Such features provide information beyond the matrix's low-rank-plus-sparse structure, but their theoretical value needs to be established.

The authors formulate a convex optimization problem incorporating this side information together with the structural assumptions. Under certain conditions, they prove exact recovery of the low-rank matrix. Their guarantee suggests that a substantial collection of matrices unrecoverable by standard robust PCA becomes recoverable through the proposed method.

This establishes a conditional theoretical reason to use entity features in robust PCA: they can change which low-rank components are recoverable. Synthetic experiments and a noisy-image-classification application also show practical performance improvements from using side information. The contribution connects additional descriptive information to both recovery theory and observed results, while keeping the exact-recovery claim tied to the conditions of the analysis.
summary.tldr: A convex robust-PCA method uses entity features to enable exact recovery under stated conditions and improves performance in reported experiments.

title: Robust Principal Component Analysis with Side Information

abstract: We consider the problem of online prediction in changing environments. In this framework the performance of a predictor is evaluated as the loss relative to an arbitrarily changing predictor, whose individual components come from a base class of predictors. Typical results in the literature consider different base classes (experts, linear predictors on the simplex, etc.) separately. Introducing an arbitrary mapping inside the mirror decent algorithm, we provide a framework that unifies and extends existing results. As an example, we prove new shifting regret bounds for matrix prediction problems.

In this framework the performance of a predictor is evaluated as the loss relative to an arbitrarily changing predictor, whose individual components come from a base class of predictors. Typical results in the literature consider different base classes (experts, linear predictors on the simplex, etc.) separately. Introducing an arbitrary mapping inside the mirror decent algorithm, we provide a framework that unifies and extends existing results. As an example, we prove new shifting regret bounds for matrix prediction problems.

paragraphs: Online prediction in a changing environment calls for a benchmark that can change too. This paper evaluates a predictor against an arbitrarily changing sequence of predictors drawn from a base class. The resulting shifting-regret perspective measures loss relative to an adaptable comparator, reflecting a setting where one fixed predictor may be an inadequate reference.

Earlier results typically handle different base classes separately, including experts and linear predictors on the simplex. The authors introduce an arbitrary mapping within mirror descent to create a common framework. This modification gives them a way to unify and extend results that had been developed for distinct prediction settings.

As a concrete application, the paper proves new shifting-regret bounds for matrix prediction problems. These bounds extend the framework beyond the separately treated examples motivating the work. The contribution is primarily a general analytical and algorithmic construction: it brings changing-comparator guarantees into a shared mirror-descent formulation and demonstrates its reach through new results for matrix-valued prediction.
summary.tldr: A modified mirror-descent framework unifies shifting-regret analyses and yields new bounds for matrix prediction.

title: Shifting Regret, Mirror Descent, and Matrices

abstract: We propose a novel deep neural network that is both lightweight and effectively structured for model parallelization. Our network, which we name as SplitNet, automatically learns to split the network weights into either a set or a hierarchy of multiple groups that use disjoint sets of features, by learning both the class-to-group and feature-to-group assignment matrices along with the network weights. This produces a tree-structured network that involves no connection between branched subtrees of semantically disparate class groups. SplitNet thus greatly reduces the number of parameters and requires significantly less computations, and is also embarrassingly model parallelizable at test time, since the network evaluation for each subnetwork is completely independent except for the shared lower layer weights that can be duplicated over multiple processors. We validate our method with two deep network models (ResNet and AlexNet) on two different datasets (CIFAR-100 and ILSVRC 2012) for image classification, on which our method obtains networks with significantly reduced number of parameters while achieving comparable or superior classification accuracies over original full deep networks, and accelerated test speed with multiple GPUs.

This produces a tree-structured network that involves no connection between branched subtrees of semantically disparate class groups. SplitNet thus greatly reduces the number of parameters and requires significantly less computations, and is also embarrassingly model parallelizable at test time, since the network evaluation for each subnetwork is completely independent except for the shared lower layer weights that can be duplicated over multiple processors. We validate our method with two deep network models (ResNet and AlexNet) on two different datasets (CIFAR-100 and ILSVRC 2012) for image classification, on which our method obtains networks with significantly reduced number of parameters while achieving comparable or superior classification accuracies over original full deep networks, and accelerated test speed with multiple GPUs.

paragraphs: SplitNet addresses two connected costs of deep networks: storing many parameters and coordinating computation across processors. It learns to organize a network into groups, or a hierarchy of groups, that use disjoint feature sets. The grouping is learned alongside the network weights through assignments linking classes and features to groups.

The resulting network has a tree structure with no connections between branched subtrees serving semantically different class groups. Removing those connections reduces parameters and computation. At prediction time, the subnetworks can be evaluated independently, apart from shared lower-layer weights that can be copied across processors. This structure makes model parallelization straightforward.

The authors evaluate the approach with ResNet and AlexNet on CIFAR-100 and ILSVRC 2012. They report substantially fewer parameters while maintaining comparable or better classification accuracy than the original full networks, along with faster testing using multiple GPUs. The findings show that learned class-and-feature organization can serve both model compression and parallel execution, rather than treating those goals as separate modifications.
summary.tldr: SplitNet learns independent semantic branches that reduce network size and enable parallel prediction while retaining strong classification accuracy.

title: SplitNet: Learning to Semantically Split Deep Networks for Parameter Reduction and Model Parallelization

abstract: The optimization of expensive-to-evaluate black-box functions over combinatorial structures is an ubiquitous task in machine learning, engineering and the natural sciences. The combinatorial explosion of the search space and costly evaluations pose challenges for current techniques in discrete optimization and machine learning, and critically require new algorithmic ideas. This article proposes, to the best of our knowledge, the first algorithm to overcome these challenges, based on an adaptive, scalable model that identifies useful combinatorial structure even when data is scarce. Our acquisition function pioneers the use of semidefinite programming to achieve efficiency and scalability. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that this algorithm consistently outperforms other methods from combinatorial and Bayesian optimization.

paragraphs: The paper studies optimization over combinatorial structures when evaluating a candidate is expensive and the objective is available only as a black box. Two difficulties interact: the number of possible structures can grow enormously, and collecting information about their quality requires costly evaluations. An effective method therefore needs to use limited observations efficiently.

The proposed Bayesian optimization algorithm uses an adaptive, scalable model designed to identify useful combinatorial structure even with little data. The model supports the decision about which candidate to evaluate next. For this selection step, the authors introduce an acquisition function that uses semidefinite programming, making that optimization technique part of their approach to efficiency and scalability.

Experimental evaluations report that the algorithm consistently outperforms the compared methods from combinatorial optimization and Bayesian optimization. The stated result supports the combination of learning structure from scarce observations and efficiently selecting further evaluations. Its significance lies in addressing both the cost of learning about the objective and the difficulty of searching a large discrete space.
summary.tldr: The proposed Bayesian optimization method learns combinatorial structure from scarce data and uses semidefinite programming to select evaluations efficiently.

title: Bayesian Optimization of Combinatorial Structures

abstract: What makes humans so good at solving seemingly complex video games? Unlike computers, humans bring in a great deal of prior knowledge about the world, enabling efficient decision making. This paper investigates the role of human priors for solving video games. Given a sample game, we conduct a series of ablation studies to quantify the importance of various priors on human performance. We do this by modifying the video game environment to systematically mask different types of visual information that could be used by humans as priors. We find that removal of some prior knowledge causes a drastic degradation in the speed with which human players solve the game, e.g. from 2 minutes to over 20 minutes. Furthermore, our results indicate that general priors, such as the importance of objects and visual consistency, are critical for efficient game-play. Videos and the game manipulations are available at https://rach0012.github.io/humanRL_website/

This paper investigates how much that prior knowledge contributes to efficient play. It focuses on visual information that allows players to bring useful expectations to a sample game.

The researchers modify the game environment to systematically mask different kinds of visual information. These ablation studies test how human performance changes when particular sources of prior knowledge become harder to use. The approach links changes in available information to changes in how quickly people solve the game.

Removing some information produces a large slowdown, with one reported example increasing solution time from two minutes to more than twenty. The results indicate that general expectations concerning objects and visual consistency are critical for efficient play in the investigated setting. The contribution is evidence that human game-solving speed depends substantially on prior knowledge supported by the presentation of the environment, rather than solely on learning through play.
summary.tldr: Masking visual cues in a sample game shows that human priors about objects and visual consistency can strongly affect solving speed.

title: Investigating Human Priors for Playing Video Games

abstract: State-action value functions (i.e., Q-values) are ubiquitous in reinforcement learning (RL), giving rise to popular algorithms such as SARSA and Q-learning. We propose a new notion of action value defined by a Gaussian smoothed version of the expected Q-value. We show that such smoothed Q-values still satisfy a Bellman equation, making them learnable from experience sampled from an environment. Moreover, the gradients of expected reward with respect to the mean and covariance of a parameterized Gaussian policy can be recovered from the gradient and Hessian of the smoothed Q-value function. Based on these relationships we develop new algorithms for training a Gaussian policy directly from a learned smoothed Q-value approximator. The approach is additionally amenable to proximal optimization by augmenting the objective with a penalty on KL-divergence from a previous policy. We find that the ability to learn both a mean and covariance during training leads to significantly improved results on standard continuous control benchmarks.

paragraphs: An action-value function estimates the expected reward associated with taking an action in a state. This paper introduces a version that smooths expected Q-values with a Gaussian distribution. The aim is to build a value representation that connects directly to learning a Gaussian policy, whose behavior depends on both its mean and covariance.

The authors show that the smoothed values satisfy a Bellman equation, so they can be learned from environmental experience. They also establish that derivatives of expected reward with respect to the policy's mean and covariance can be recovered from the gradient and Hessian of the smoothed value function. These relationships provide the basis for algorithms that train the policy from a learned value approximator.

The approach also supports proximal optimization by penalizing KL divergence from a previous policy. Experiments on standard continuous-control benchmarks report significant improvements from learning both mean and covariance during training. The result highlights the value of adapting the policy's distribution, with the smoothing construction providing a mathematical route to those updates.
summary.tldr: Gaussian-smoothed Q-values provide derivatives for learning both the mean and covariance of Gaussian policies, improving tested continuous-control performance.

title: Smoothed Action Value Functions for Learning Gaussian Policies

abstract: In reinforcement learning, it is common to let an agent interact for a fixed amount of time with its environment before resetting it and repeating the process in a series of episodes. The task that the agent has to learn can either be to maximize its performance over (i) that fixed period, or (ii) an indefinite period where time limits are only used during training to diversify experience. In this paper, we provide a formal account for how time limits could effectively be handled in each of the two cases and explain why not doing so can cause state-aliasing and invalidation of experience replay, leading to suboptimal policies and training instability. In case (i), we argue that the terminations due to time limits are in fact part of the environment, and thus a notion of the remaining time should be included as part of the agent’s input to avoid violation of the Markov property. In case (ii), the time limits are not part of the environment and are only used to facilitate learning. We argue that this insight should be incorporated by bootstrapping from the value of the state at the end of each partial episode. For both cases, we illustrate empirically the significance of our considerations in improving the performance and stability of existing reinforcement learning algorithms, showing state-of-the-art results on several control tasks.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning often divides interaction into episodes that end after a fixed time. This paper distinguishes two meanings of that cutoff: the agent may be solving a task whose objective truly ends then, or it may be learning an ongoing task using temporary episodes to diversify experience. The distinction changes how training should handle episode endings.

For a genuinely time-limited task, the authors argue that remaining time belongs in the agent’s input. Otherwise, situations that require different decisions can appear identical, violating the Markov property. For an ongoing task interrupted only for training, they argue that learning should bootstrap from the final state’s value, retaining the value of continuation beyond the artificial cutoff.

The paper explains how mishandling these cases can cause state aliasing, invalidate experience replay, and contribute to unstable training or suboptimal policies. Experiments demonstrate improvements in performance and stability for existing algorithms, including leading results on several control tasks. The practical lesson is to make learning updates reflect what an episode ending actually means for the task.
summary.tldr: Reinforcement learning should encode remaining time for true deadlines and bootstrap across cutoffs used only during training.

title: Time Limits in Reinforcement Learning

abstract: We identify a phenomenon, which we refer to as multi-model forgetting, that occurs when sequentially training multiple deep networks with partially-shared parameters; the performance of previously-trained models degrades as one optimizes a subsequent one, due to the overwriting of shared parameters. To overcome this, we introduce a statistically-justified weight plasticity loss that regularizes the learning of a model’s shared parameters according to their importance for the previous models, and demonstrate its effectiveness when training two models sequentially and for neural architecture search. Adding weight plasticity in neural architecture search preserves the best models to the end of the search and yields improved results in both natural language processing and computer vision tasks.

Adding weight plasticity in neural architecture search preserves the best models to the end of the search and yields improved results in both natural language processing and computer vision tasks.

paragraphs: The paper identifies a problem that occurs when several deep networks share some parameters and are trained sequentially. Optimizing a later network changes shared weights, which can degrade networks trained earlier. The authors call this multi-model forgetting, emphasizing that the interference occurs across models linked by common parameters.

Their solution adds a statistically justified weight plasticity loss. This loss regularizes updates to shared parameters according to how important those parameters are for previous models. It therefore makes the training objective sensitive to earlier models’ reliance on particular weights, addressing the overwriting mechanism that causes the loss of performance.

The authors demonstrate the approach with two sequentially trained models and with neural architecture search. In architecture search, adding weight plasticity preserves the best models through the end of the search and improves results on natural language processing and computer vision tasks. These findings show that protecting shared parameters can matter for the quality of models retained during a search.
summary.tldr: A weight plasticity loss reduces forgetting between models with shared parameters and improves reported neural architecture search results.

title: Overcoming Multi-model Forgetting

abstract: The Conditional Gradient Method is generalized to a class of non-smooth non-convex optimization problems with many applications in machine learning. The proposed algorithm iterates by minimizing so-called model functions over the constraint set. Complemented with an Armijo line search procedure, we prove that subsequences converge to a stationary point. The abstract framework of model functions provides great flexibility in the design of concrete algorithms. As special cases, for example, we develop an algorithm for additive composite problems and an algorithm for non-linear composite problems which leads to a Gauss-Newton-type algorithm. Both instances are novel in non-smooth non-convex optimization and come with numerous applications in machine learning. We perform an experiment on a non-linear robust regression problem and discuss the flexibility of the proposed framework in several matrix factorization formulations.

paragraphs: This paper extends the conditional gradient method to a class of optimization problems that are both nonsmooth and nonconvex. These problems can arise in machine learning, but their irregular objectives require a broader algorithmic framework. The proposed approach builds each iteration around minimizing a model function over the allowed constraint set.

An Armijo-style line search complements this model-based step. Within the framework, the authors prove that subsequences converge to a stationary point. This is a specific convergence guarantee: it concerns subsequences and stationarity, so it should not be interpreted as a guarantee that every iterate converges to a global optimum.

The freedom to choose model functions yields algorithms for additive composite objectives and nonlinear composite objectives, with the latter producing a Gauss-Newton-type method. The authors present an experiment on nonlinear robust regression and discuss several matrix-factorization formulations. These examples illustrate why the framework matters: a shared convergence analysis can support different concrete algorithms suited to different objective structures.
summary.tldr: A model-function extension of conditional gradients handles nonsmooth, nonconvex problems and proves subsequential convergence to a stationary point.

title: Model Function Based Conditional Gradient Method with Armijo-like Line Search

abstract: Multi-task learning shares information between related tasks, sometimes reducing the number of parameters required. State-of-the-art results across multiple natural language understanding tasks in the GLUE benchmark have previously used transfer from a single large task: unsupervised pre-training with BERT, where a separate BERT model was fine-tuned for each task. We explore multi-task approaches that share a \hbox{single} BERT model with a small number of additional task-specific parameters. Using new adaptation modules, PALs or ‘projected attention layers’, we match the performance of separately fine-tuned models on the GLUE benchmark with $\approx$7 times fewer parameters, and obtain state-of-the-art results on the Recognizing Textual Entailment dataset.

paragraphs: Using BERT for several language-understanding tasks can require keeping a separate fine-tuned model for each task. Although these models begin from the same pretrained model, their parameters are stored separately. This paper investigates whether a single shared BERT model can serve multiple tasks while retaining enough task-specific flexibility to perform well.

The authors introduce projected attention layers, or PALs, as adaptation modules. These add a small number of parameters specific to each task while allowing the main BERT model to be shared. The approach makes multi-task learning a way to reuse model capacity across related tasks, with dedicated additions providing adaptation for individual tasks.

On the GLUE benchmark, the resulting system matches the performance of separately fine-tuned models while using approximately seven times fewer parameters. It also achieves a reported state-of-the-art result on Recognizing Textual Entailment. The parameter comparison concerns serving the collection of tasks, illustrating how shared modeling can reduce the total capacity needed without sacrificing the reported benchmark performance.
summary.tldr: PALs let one shared BERT model match separately fine-tuned models on GLUE with approximately seven times fewer parameters.

title: BERT and PALs: Projected Attention Layers for Efficient Adaptation in Multi-Task Learning

abstract: Tuning hyperparameters for unsupervised learning problems is difficult in general due to the lack of ground truth for validation. However, the success of most clustering methods depends heavily on the correct choice of the involved hyperparameters. Take for example the Lagrange multipliers of penalty terms in semidefinite programming (SDP) relaxations of community detection in networks, or the bandwidth parameter needed in the Gaussian kernel used to construct similarity matrices for spectral clustering. Despite the popularity of these clustering algorithms, there are not many provable methods for tuning these hyperparameters. In this paper, we provide an overarching framework with provable guarantees for tuning hyperparameters in the above class of problems under two different models. Our framework can be augmented with a cross validation procedure to do model selection as well. In a variety of simulation and real data experiments, we show that our framework outperforms other widely used tuning procedures in a broad range of parameter settings.

paragraphs: Clustering depends strongly on hyperparameters, yet unsupervised learning usually lacks ground-truth labels for validating their choices. The paper considers examples such as penalty multipliers in semidefinite relaxations for network community detection and Gaussian-kernel bandwidths in spectral clustering. These parameters shape the clustering procedure, making their selection central to obtaining useful results.

The authors propose a shared framework for tuning hyperparameters across this class of problems. They establish provable guarantees under two different models, giving theoretical support to a task often handled through tuning procedures with fewer guarantees. The framework can also be combined with cross-validation to perform model selection as well as hyperparameter tuning.

Experiments on simulated and real data show the framework outperforming other widely used tuning methods over a broad range of parameter settings. The contribution links several clustering tuning problems through a common approach and supports it with both analysis and empirical comparisons. Its theoretical claims are made under the two models studied, while the experimental findings describe the tested settings.
summary.tldr: A common framework tunes clustering hyperparameters with guarantees under two models and strong results across simulated and real datasets.

title: On hyperparameter tuning in general clustering problemsm

abstract: We consider the problem of learning the weighted edges of a balanced mixture of two undirected graphs from epidemic cascades. While mixture models are popular modeling tools, algorithmic development with rigorous guarantees has lagged. Graph mixtures are apparently no exception: until now, very little is known about whether this problem is solvable. To the best of our knowledge, we establish the first necessary and sufficient conditions for this problem to be solvable in polynomial time on edge-separated graphs. When the conditions are met, i.e., when the graphs are connected with at least three edges, we give an efficient algorithm for learning the weights of both graphs with optimal sample complexity (up to log factors). We give complementary results and provide sample-optimal (up to log factors) algorithms for mixtures of directed graphs of out-degree at least three, and for mixture of undirected graphs of unbalanced and/or unknown priors.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether epidemic cascades can reveal the weighted connections of two underlying graphs when observations come from a mixture of them. Recovering both graphs requires distinguishing the structures contributing to the observed spreading behavior. The main setting is a balanced mixture of two undirected graphs.

For edge-separated graphs, the authors establish necessary and sufficient conditions for polynomial-time recovery. Within that setting, the stated conditions require connected graphs with at least three edges. When these conditions hold, their algorithm efficiently learns both sets of edge weights, using a number of samples that is optimal up to logarithmic factors.

The paper also develops complementary algorithms for directed-graph mixtures with out-degree at least three and for undirected mixtures whose proportions are unbalanced or unknown. These algorithms likewise have sample-optimal guarantees up to logarithmic factors. The contribution identifies when recovery is computationally possible in the specified graph setting and supplies methods with near-optimal data requirements for several related mixture models.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes efficient recoverability of edge-separated graph mixtures from epidemic cascades and provides near-sample-optimal algorithms.

title: Learning Mixtures of Graphs from Epidemic Cascades

abstract: Stochastic gradient methods with momentum are widely used in applications and at the core of optimization subroutines in many popular machine learning libraries. However, their sample complexities have not been obtained for problems beyond those that are convex or smooth. This paper establishes the convergence rate of a stochastic subgradient method with a momentum term of Polyak type for a broad class of non-smooth, non-convex, and constrained optimization problems. Our key innovation is the construction of a special Lyapunov function for which the proven complexity can be achieved without any tuning of the momentum parameter. For smooth problems, we extend the known complexity bound to the constrained case and demonstrate how the unconstrained case can be analyzed under weaker assumptions than the state-of-the-art. Numerical results confirm our theoretical developments.

paragraphs: Momentum is widely used in stochastic optimization, but its theoretical support has been more limited for problems that are neither convex nor smooth. This paper establishes a convergence rate for a stochastic subgradient method with Polyak-type momentum. The analysis covers a broad class of nonsmooth, nonconvex problems that may also include constraints.

The central technical contribution is a specially constructed Lyapunov function, a mathematical quantity used to track the algorithm’s progress. With this construction, the authors obtain their complexity guarantee without needing to tune the momentum parameter. This connects a commonly used optimization ingredient to a formal account of the work required for convergence.

For smooth problems, the paper extends an existing complexity bound to the constrained setting. It also analyzes unconstrained problems under weaker assumptions than previous state-of-the-art analysis. Numerical results support the theoretical developments. Together, these contributions broaden the situations in which stochastic momentum methods have stated convergence guarantees, including settings that involve both nonsmoothness and nonconvexity.
summary.tldr: A new Lyapunov analysis establishes convergence complexity for stochastic momentum methods on a broad class of nonsmooth, nonconvex constrained problems.

title: Convergence of a Stochastic Gradient Method with Momentum for Non-Smooth Non-Convex Optimization

abstract: In this paper, we aim to develop a scalable algorithm to preserve differential privacy (DP) in adversarial learning for deep neural networks (DNNs), with certified robustness to adversarial examples. By leveraging the sequential composition theory in DP, we randomize both input and latent spaces to strengthen our certified robustness bounds. To address the trade-off among model utility, privacy loss, and robustness, we design an original adversarial objective function, based on the post-processing property in DP, to tighten the sensitivity of our model. A new stochastic batch training is proposed to apply our mechanism on large DNNs and datasets, by bypassing the vanilla iterative batch-by-batch training in DP DNNs. An end-to-end theoretical analysis and evaluations show that our mechanism notably improves the robustness and scalability of DP DNNs.

paragraphs: This paper addresses three linked goals for deep neural networks: preserving differential privacy, maintaining useful predictions, and providing certified robustness against adversarial examples. These goals interact, so the proposed method treats their trade-offs as part of the training design rather than considering privacy and robustness separately.

The mechanism randomizes both inputs and latent representations. It uses sequential composition in differential privacy to combine these operations and strengthen robustness bounds. The authors also design an adversarial objective using the post-processing property of differential privacy, aiming to tighten model sensitivity while addressing predictive utility, privacy loss, and robustness together.

For scalability, the paper introduces stochastic batch training that bypasses the conventional iterative batch-by-batch approach used in differentially private neural-network training. End-to-end theoretical analysis and evaluations report notable improvements in robustness and scalability. The contribution combines a mechanism for certified protection with a training procedure intended for large networks and datasets, making the relationship between privacy accounting, robustness guarantees, and practical training cost central to the approach.
summary.tldr: The method combines input and latent randomization with a new training procedure to improve scalability and certified robustness in differentially private networks.

title: Scalable Differential Privacy with Certified Robustness in Adversarial Learning

abstract: We consider PAC learning a good item from $k$-subsetwise feedback sampled from a Plackett-Luce probability model, with instance-dependent sample complexity performance. In the setting where subsets of a fixed size can be tested and top-ranked feedback is made available to the learner, we give an optimal instance-dependent algorithm with a sample complexity bound for PAC best arm identification algorithm of $O\bigg(\frac{\Theta_{[k]}}{k}\sum_{i = 2}^n\max\Big(1,\frac{1}{\Delta_i^2}\Big) \ln\frac{k}{\delta}\Big(\ln \frac{1}{\Delta_i}\Big)\bigg)$, $\Delta_i$ being the Plackett-Luce parameter gap between the best and the $i^{th}$ best item, and $\Theta_{[k]}$ is the sum of the Plackett-Luce parameters for top-$k$ items. The algorithm is based on a wrapper around a PAC winner-finding algorithm with weaker performance guarantees to adapt to the hardness of the input instance. The sample complexity is also shown to be multiplicatively better depending on the length of rank-ordered feedback available in each subset-wise play. We show optimality of our algorithms with matching sample complexity lower bounds. We next address the winner-finding problem in Plackett-Luce models in the fixed-budget setting with instance dependent upper and lower bounds on the misidentification probability, of $\Omega\left(\exp(-2 \tilde \Delta Q) \right)$ for a given budget $Q$, where $\tilde \Delta$ is an explicit instance-dependent problem complexity parameter. Numerical performance results are also reported for the algorithms.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to identify a good or winning item from noisy comparisons governed by the Plackett-Luce model. Each comparison tests a fixed-size subset and returns top-ranked feedback. The objective is to make the required number of observations depend on the difficulty of the particular collection of items.

The authors wrap a winner-finding algorithm with weaker guarantees in a procedure that adapts to instance difficulty. Their sample-complexity bound depends on the gaps between the best item and its competitors, the subset size, and the strength of the top items. They also show a multiplicative improvement when each comparison supplies a longer ranked list. Matching lower bounds establish the stated optimality of their algorithms.

The paper additionally considers a fixed-budget setting, where the learner must choose a winner after a prescribed number of comparisons. Here, the authors derive instance-dependent upper and lower bounds on the probability of selecting the wrong item. Numerical results accompany the theory. Together, the analyses characterize both the observations needed for reliable identification and the error possible when observations are limited.
summary.tldr: Adaptive winner-finding algorithms achieve instance-optimal sample complexity for Plackett-Luce comparisons, with further gains from longer ranked feedback.

title: From PAC to Instance-Optimal Sample Complexity in the Plackett-Luce Model

abstract: Bayesian inference using Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) on large datasets has developed rapidly in recent years. However, the underlying methods are generally limited to relatively simple settings where the data have specific forms of independence. We propose a novel technique for speeding up MCMC for time series data by efficient data subsampling in the frequency domain. For several challenging time series models, we demonstrate a speedup of up to two orders of magnitude while incurring negligible bias compared to MCMC on the full dataset. We also propose alternative control variates for variance reduction based on data grouping and coreset constructions.

Subsampling can reduce that burden, but existing methods commonly depend on particular forms of independence in the data. Time series present a challenge for those requirements because their observations have temporal structure. This paper develops a subsampling approach for stationary time series.

The method carries out efficient data subsampling in the frequency domain. Moving the computation into this representation provides the basis for accelerating MCMC on the time-series models considered. The authors also propose alternative control variates, which reduce variance, using data grouping and coreset constructions. These are additional tools for controlling the variability introduced into the computation.

Across several challenging time-series models, the reported speedup reaches two orders of magnitude, or about one hundred times, with negligible bias relative to full-dataset MCMC. This is an observed maximum across the reported evaluations. The result shows that frequency-domain subsampling can offer substantial computational savings while closely preserving the inference obtained from using all the data.
summary.tldr: Frequency-domain subsampling accelerates MCMC for stationary time series, with reported speedups up to one hundred times and negligible bias.

title: Spectral Subsampling MCMC for Stationary Time Series

abstract: Neural networks (NNs) have been extremely successful across many tasks in machine learning. Quantization of NN weights has become an important topic due to its impact on their energy efficiency, inference time and deployment on hardware. Although post-training quantization is well-studied, training optimal quantized NNs involves combinatorial non-convex optimization problems which appear intractable. In this work, we introduce a convex optimization strategy to train quantized NNs with polynomial activations. Our method leverages hidden convexity in two-layer neural networks from the recent literature, semidefinite lifting, and Grothendieck’s identity. Surprisingly, we show that certain quantized NN problems can be solved to global optimality provably in polynomial time in all relevant parameters via tight semidefinite relaxations. We present numerical examples to illustrate the effectiveness of our method.

paragraphs: Quantized neural networks restrict their weights, making them relevant to energy efficiency, inference speed, and hardware deployment. Finding optimal weights under those restrictions introduces combinatorial, nonconvex optimization problems. This paper investigates whether some of these training problems can instead be handled through a convex optimization formulation.

The proposed strategy applies to networks with polynomial activations. It combines hidden convexity in two-layer networks with semidefinite lifting and Grothendieck’s identity. These mathematical tools allow the authors to formulate semidefinite relaxations and analyze when those relaxations recover the original optimization problem exactly.

For certain quantized-network problems, the relaxations are tight, yielding provable global optimality in time polynomial in all relevant parameters. The qualification matters: the result establishes tractability for the identified problems within the studied network setting. Numerical examples illustrate the method’s effectiveness. The main contribution is a constructive route from a seemingly intractable discrete training problem to a convex program with an exact optimality guarantee in those cases.
summary.tldr: Tight semidefinite relaxations solve certain quantized neural-network training problems to global optimality in polynomial time.

title: Training Quantized Neural Networks to Global Optimality via Semidefinite Programming

abstract: Federated Learning (FL) is a distributed learning paradigm that scales on-device learning collaboratively and privately. Standard FL algorithms such as FEDAVG are primarily geared towards smooth unconstrained settings. In this paper, we study the Federated Composite Optimization (FCO) problem, in which the loss function contains a non-smooth regularizer. Such problems arise naturally in FL applications that involve sparsity, low-rank, monotonicity, or more general constraints. We first show that straightforward extensions of primal algorithms such as FedAvg are not well-suited for FCO since they suffer from the "curse of primal averaging," resulting in poor convergence. As a solution, we propose a new primal-dual algorithm, Federated Dual Averaging (FedDualAvg), which by employing a novel server dual averaging procedure circumvents the curse of primal averaging. Our theoretical analysis and empirical experiments demonstrate that FedDualAvg outperforms the other baselines.

paragraphs: Federated learning coordinates learning across devices, but standard algorithms such as FedAvg are mainly designed for smooth objectives without constraints. This paper studies objectives that also contain a nonsmooth regularizer. Such objectives arise when applications require properties including sparsity, low rank, monotonicity, or more general constraints on the learned solution.

This identifies an obstacle in the way local learning results are combined, making a simple extension of the standard federated procedure unsuitable for the composite optimization problems studied.

Their solution is Federated Dual Averaging, a primal-dual algorithm with a new server-side dual averaging procedure. That procedure is designed to avoid the identified averaging problem. Both theoretical analysis and empirical experiments show improvements over the compared baselines. The contribution therefore expands the optimization machinery available for federated applications whose objectives include nonsmooth structure.
summary.tldr: FedDualAvg uses server-side dual averaging to improve federated optimization with nonsmooth regularizers and constraints.

title: Federated Composite Optimization

abstract: Vector Quantized-Variational AutoEncoders (VQ-VAE) are generative models based on discrete latent representations of the data, where inputs are mapped to a finite set of learned embeddings. To generate new samples, an autoregressive prior distribution over the discrete states must be trained separately. This prior is generally very complex and leads to slow generation. In this work, we propose a new model to train the prior and the encoder/decoder networks simultaneously. We build a diffusion bridge between a continuous coded vector and a non-informative prior distribution. The latent discrete states are then given as random functions of these continuous vectors. We show that our model is competitive with the autoregressive prior on the mini-Imagenet and CIFAR dataset and is efficient in both optimization and sampling. Our framework also extends the standard VQ-VAE and enables end-to-end training.

paragraphs: Vector-quantized variational autoencoders represent inputs using a finite collection of learned embeddings. Generating new examples also requires a distribution over these discrete representations. In the setup described by the authors, that distribution is learned separately with a complex autoregressive model, creating a bottleneck for generation.

This paper replaces the separate training arrangement with a model that learns the prior together with the encoder and decoder. Its central construction is a diffusion bridge connecting a continuous coded vector to a non-informative prior distribution. Discrete latent states are then obtained as random functions of the continuous vectors, linking the discrete representation to the continuous diffusion construction.

The framework extends standard VQ-VAE and permits end-to-end training of the combined system. On mini-ImageNet and CIFAR, the authors report performance competitive with an autoregressive prior, alongside efficient optimization and sampling. The stated result is a practical alternative for learning and generating with discrete latent representations while bringing their component networks into one training process.
summary.tldr: A diffusion bridge enables joint training of a VQ-VAE’s prior, encoder, and decoder with competitive generation and efficient sampling.

title: Diffusion bridges vector quantized variational autoencoders

abstract: As opaque predictive models increasingly impact many areas of modern life, interest in quantifying the importance of a given input variable for making a specific prediction has grown. Recently, there has been a proliferation of model-agnostic methods to measure variable importance (VI) that analyze the difference in predictive power between a full model trained on all variables and a reduced model that excludes the variable(s) of interest. A bottleneck common to these methods is the estimation of the reduced model for each variable (or subset of variables), which is an expensive process that often does not come with theoretical guarantees. In this work, we propose a fast and flexible method for approximating the reduced model with important inferential guarantees. We replace the need for fully retraining a wide neural network by a linearization initialized at the full model parameters. By adding a ridge-like penalty to make the problem convex, we prove that when the ridge penalty parameter is sufficiently large, our method estimates the variable importance measure with an error rate of O(1/n) where n is the number of training samples. We also show that our estimator is asymptotically normal, enabling us to provide confidence bounds for the VI estimates. We demonstrate through simulations that our method is fast and accurate under several data-generating regimes, and we demonstrate its real-world applicability on a seasonal climate forecasting example.

The difficulty is computational: each variable or subset can require another model to be trained. This paper develops a faster approximation to the reduced model for wide neural networks, while also providing statistical guarantees.

The method linearizes the network around the parameters of the already trained full model. A ridge-like penalty makes the approximation problem convex. The contribution therefore combines a cheaper route to reduced-model estimation with tools for expressing uncertainty about the resulting importance measurements.
summary.tldr: A penalized linear approximation avoids full neural-network retraining for variable importance and provides conditional error guarantees and confidence bounds.

title: Lazy Estimation of Variable Importance for Large Neural Networks

abstract: Image cartoonization is recently dominated by generative adversarial networks (GANs) from the perspective of unsupervised image-to-image translation, in which an inherent challenge is to precisely capture and sufficiently transfer characteristic cartoon styles (e.g., clear edges, smooth color shading, vivid colors, etc.). Existing advanced models try to enhance cartoonization effect by learning to promote edges adversarially, introducing style transfer loss, or learning to align style from multiple representation space. This paper demonstrates that more distinct and vivid cartoonization effect could be easily achieved with only basic adversarial loss. Observing that cartoon style is more evident in cartoon-texture-salient local image regions, we build a region-level adversarial learning branch in parallel with the normal image-level one, which constrains adversarial learning on cartoon-texture-salient local patches for better perceiving and transferring cartoon texture features. To this end, a novel cartoon-texture-saliency-sampler (CTSS) module is proposed to adaptively sample cartoon-texture-salient patches from training data. We present that such texture saliency adaptive attention is of significant importance in facilitating and enhancing cartoon stylization, which is a key missing ingredient of related methods. The superiority of our model in promoting cartoonization effect, especially for high-resolution input images, are fully demonstrated with extensive experiments.

paragraphs: Image cartoonization must transfer recognizable style features such as clear edges, smooth shading, and vivid colors. This paper studies cartoonization as unsupervised image-to-image translation with generative adversarial networks. Its central observation is that cartoon texture is especially apparent in certain local image regions, making those regions useful targets for learning the style.

The proposed model adds a region-level adversarial branch alongside the usual image-level branch. A cartoon-texture-saliency sampler adaptively selects patches where the relevant texture is prominent. Training on these patches gives the local branch a focused view of cartoon characteristics, while the image-level branch retains its whole-image role. The approach uses basic adversarial loss to achieve the reported stylization improvements.

Extensive experiments show stronger cartoonization effects, particularly for high-resolution inputs. The authors interpret these results as evidence that directing learning toward texture-salient regions is an important ingredient in cartoon style transfer. The contribution is a concrete training mechanism for making distinctive local style features more visible to adversarial learning.
summary.tldr: Adaptive sampling of cartoon-texture patches strengthens adversarial cartoonization, with reported benefits especially for high-resolution images.

title: Learning to Incorporate Texture Saliency Adaptive Attention to Image Cartoonization

abstract: Differential privacy is widely accepted as the de facto method for preventing data leakage in ML, and conventional wisdom suggests that it offers strong protection against privacy attacks. However, existing semantic guarantees for DP focus on membership inference, which may overestimate the adversary’s capabilities and is not applicable when membership status itself is non-sensitive. In this paper, we derive the first semantic guarantees for DP mechanisms against training data reconstruction attacks under a formal threat model. We show that two distinct privacy accounting methods—Renyi differential privacy and Fisher information leakage—both offer strong semantic protection against data reconstruction attacks.

In this paper, we derive the first semantic guarantees for DP mechanisms against training data reconstruction attacks under a formal threat model. We show that two distinct privacy accounting methods—Renyi differential privacy and Fisher information leakage—both offer strong semantic protection against data reconstruction attacks.

paragraphs: Privacy in machine learning involves different questions about what an attacker can discover. Membership inference asks whether a particular record appeared in training, while reconstruction concerns recovering training data. This paper focuses on reconstruction, motivated by the fact that membership status may itself be harmless to reveal even when the underlying information needs protection.

The authors derive semantic guarantees for differential privacy mechanisms against reconstruction attacks under a formal threat model. Such guarantees connect privacy accounting to the meaning of protection for an attacker pursuing this specific objective. The paper also argues that existing membership-focused guarantees can overestimate an adversary's capabilities, making a reconstruction-focused analysis valuable.

The analysis considers two distinct accounting approaches: Rényi differential privacy and Fisher information leakage. Both are shown to provide strong semantic protection against data reconstruction within the formal setting. The contribution gives a direct theoretical interpretation of protection against recovering training data, with its claims tied to the stated threat model.
summary.tldr: The paper derives formal reconstruction-attack guarantees using Rényi differential privacy and Fisher information leakage.

title: Bounding Training Data Reconstruction in Private (Deep) Learning

abstract: Approximating distributions from their samples is a canonical statistical-learning problem. One of its most powerful and successful modalities approximates every distribution to an $\ell_1$ distance essentially at most a constant times larger than its closest $t$-piece degree-$d$ polynomial, where $t\ge1$ and $d\ge0$. Letting $c_{t,d}$ denote the smallest such factor, clearly $c_{1,0}=1$, and it can be shown that $c_{t,d}\ge 2$ for all other $t$ and $d$. Yet current computationally efficient algorithms show only $c_{t,1}\le 2.25$ and the bound rises quickly to $c_{t,d}\le 3$ for $d\ge 9$. We derive a near-linear-time and essentially sample-optimal estimator that establishes $c_{t,d}=2$ for all $(t,d)\ne(1,0)$. Additionally, for many practical distributions, the lowest approximation distance is achieved by polynomials with vastly varying number of pieces. We provide a method that estimates this number near-optimally, hence helps approach the best possible approximation. Experiments combining the two techniques confirm improved performance over existing methodologies.

paragraphs: This paper studies estimating a distribution from samples using piecewise polynomials. The benchmark is the best approximation with a chosen number of pieces and polynomial degree, measured by l1 distance. The objective is to produce an estimate whose error is essentially within a small constant factor of that benchmark.

Except for the single-piece, degree-zero case, the smallest possible factor is at least two. Existing efficient methods had larger guarantees, especially at higher degrees. TURF supplies a near-linear-time estimator that is essentially sample-optimal and establishes the factor of two across all the remaining piece-count and degree combinations. It therefore closes the stated gap between achievable efficient guarantees and the lower bound.

The paper also addresses choosing the number of polynomial pieces, since suitable choices can differ greatly between practical distributions. Its selection method estimates that number near-optimally, helping the estimator approach the best available approximation. Experiments combining estimation and piece-count selection improve on existing methodologies. The contribution joins an optimal approximation factor with computational efficiency and adaptation of model complexity.
summary.tldr: TURF achieves the optimal factor-two piecewise-polynomial distribution approximation guarantee with near-linear runtime and near-optimal piece-count selection.

title: TURF: Two-Factor, Universal, Robust, Fast Distribution Learning Algorithm

abstract: Design of de novo biological sequences with desired properties, like protein and DNA sequences, often involves an active loop with several rounds of molecule ideation and expensive wet-lab evaluations. These experiments can consist of multiple stages, with increasing levels of precision and cost of evaluation, where candidates are filtered. This makes the diversity of proposed candidates a key consideration in the ideation phase. In this work, we propose an active learning algorithm leveraging epistemic uncertainty estimation and the recently proposed GFlowNets as a generator of diverse candidate solutions, with the objective to obtain a diverse batch of useful (as defined by some utility function, for example, the predicted anti-microbial activity of a peptide) and informative candidates after each round. We also propose a scheme to incorporate existing labeled datasets of candidates, in addition to a reward function, to speed up learning in GFlowNets. We present empirical results on several biological sequence design tasks, and we find that our method generates more diverse and novel batches with high scoring candidates compared to existing approaches.

paragraphs: Biological sequence design often alternates between proposing candidates and evaluating them through costly laboratory experiments. Evaluation may involve several filtering stages, each offering greater precision at greater cost. This makes the composition of a candidate batch important: the search benefits from useful proposals that also explore different possibilities and provide information for later rounds.

The paper introduces an active learning algorithm that combines GFlowNets with estimates of epistemic uncertainty, or uncertainty arising from limited knowledge. GFlowNets generate diverse candidate sequences, while the overall procedure aims to produce batches that balance usefulness and informativeness. Usefulness is defined by a chosen utility function, such as predicted antimicrobial activity for peptides.

The authors also provide a way to incorporate existing labeled candidate datasets into GFlowNet learning alongside a reward function. This is intended to speed up learning by making use of previously evaluated sequences. Across several biological sequence design tasks, their method produces batches that are more diverse and novel while containing high-scoring candidates compared with existing approaches. These findings support diversity-aware proposal generation within an iterative design process.
summary.tldr: An active learning method combines GFlowNets and uncertainty estimates to propose diverse, novel biological sequences with high utility scores.

title: Biological Sequence Design with GFlowNets

abstract: We consider the classical problem of multi-class prediction with expert advice, but with an active learning twist. In this new setting the learner will only query the labels of a small number of examples, but still aims to minimize regret to the best expert as usual; the learner is also allowed a very short "burn-in" phase where it can fast-forward and query certain highly-informative examples. We design an algorithm that utilizes Hedge (aka Exponential Weights) as a subroutine, and we show that under a very particular combinatorial constraint on the matrix of expert predictions we can obtain a very strong regret guarantee while querying very few labels. This constraint, which we refer to as $\zeta$-compactness, or just compactness, can be viewed as a non-stochastic variant of the disagreement coefficient, another popular parameter used to reason about the sample complexity of active learning in the IID setting. We also give a polynomial-time algorithm to calculate the $\zeta$-compactness of a matrix up to an approximation factor of 3.
