paragraphs: This paper studies prediction with advice from multiple experts when the learner can request only a small number of correct labels. The objective remains to keep regret low: the learner wants its accumulated performance to stay close to that of the best expert. The setting also permits a brief initial phase that can skip ahead to particularly informative examples.

The proposed algorithm uses Hedge, also called Exponential Weights, as a component. Its strong regret and label-efficiency guarantees depend on a particular structural property of the matrix containing the experts’ predictions. The authors call this property zeta-compactness. It describes a combinatorial condition under which selective label requests can support effective competition with the experts.

Compactness plays a role analogous to the disagreement coefficient used in active learning with independent, identically distributed data, but here the property is non-stochastic. The authors also provide a polynomial-time method that approximates compactness within a factor of three. Thus, the work supplies both a conditional learning guarantee and a way to assess its central structural quantity.
summary.tldr: ActiveHedge achieves strong regret guarantees with few label requests under a specific combinatorial condition on expert predictions.

title: ActiveHedge: Hedge meets Active Learning

abstract: Recently, several theories including the replica method made predictions for the generalization error of Kernel Ridge Regression. In some regimes, they predict that the method has a ‘spectral bias’: decomposing the true function $f^*$ on the eigenbasis of the kernel, it fits well the coefficients associated with the O(P) largest eigenvalues, where $P$ is the size of the training set. This prediction works very well on benchmark data sets such as images, yet the assumptions these approaches make on the data are never satisfied in practice. To clarify when the spectral bias prediction holds, we first focus on a one-dimensional model where rigorous results are obtained and then use scaling arguments to generalize and test our findings in higher dimensions. Our predictions include the classification case $f(x)=$sign$(x_1)$ with a data distribution that vanishes at the decision boundary $p(x)\sim x_1^{\chi}$. For $\chi>0$ and a Laplace kernel, we find that (i) there exists a cross-over ridge $\lambda^*_{d,\chi}(P)\sim P^{-\frac{1}{d+\chi}}$ such that for $\lambda\gg \lambda^*_{d,\chi}(P)$, the replica method applies, but not for $\lambda\ll\lambda^*_{d,\chi}(P)$, (ii) in the ridge-less case, spectral bias predicts the correct training curve exponent only in the limit $d\rightarrow\infty$.

paragraphs: Some theories predict kernel ridge regression through spectral bias: with P training examples, learning preferentially captures target-function components associated with roughly the P largest kernel eigenvalues. These predictions can work well on benchmark data even though their assumptions are not satisfied in practice. This paper investigates where that predictive account succeeds or fails for Laplace kernels.

The authors obtain rigorous results in a one-dimensional model, then use scaling arguments and tests to extend their findings to higher dimensions. One case classifies points according to the sign of their first coordinate, with data density vanishing near the decision boundary according to a positive exponent chi. The analysis connects prediction validity to regularization strength, dimension, and this boundary behavior.

They identify a crossover regularization level scaling as P raised to minus one over d plus chi. Far above it, the replica-method prediction applies; far below it, it does not. Without ridge regularization, spectral bias gives the correct training-curve exponent only as dimension tends to infinity. These findings make the prediction’s validity explicitly dependent on the learning regime.
summary.tldr: For the studied Laplace-kernel setting, spectral-bias predictions depend on regularization and dimension, with failures below a derived crossover scale.

title: Failure and success of the spectral bias prediction for Laplace Kernel Ridge Regression: the case of low-dimensional data

abstract: We study the problem of differentially private (DP) stochastic convex optimization (SCO) under the notion of user-level differential privacy. In this problem, there are $n$ users, each contributing $m>1$ samples to the input dataset of the private SCO algorithm, and the notion of indistinguishability embedded in DP is w.r.t. replacing the entire local dataset of any given user. Under smoothness conditions of the loss, we establish the optimal rates for user-level DP-SCO in both the central and local models of DP. In particular, we show, roughly, that the optimal rate is $\frac{1}{\sqrt{nm}}+\frac{\sqrt{d}}{\varepsilon n \sqrt{m}}$ in the central setting and is $\frac{\sqrt{d}}{\varepsilon \sqrt{nm}}$ in the local setting, where $d$ is the dimensionality of the problem and $\varepsilon$ is the privacy parameter. Our algorithms combine new user-level DP mean estimation techniques with carefully designed first-order stochastic optimization methods. For the central DP setting, our optimal rate improves over the rate attained for the same setting in Levy et al. (2021) by $\sqrt{d}$ factor. One of the main ingredients that enabled such an improvement is a novel application of the generalization properties of DP in the context of multi-pass stochastic gradient methods.

paragraphs: User-level differential privacy protects a person’s entire contribution, rather than just one record. This paper studies stochastic convex optimization with n users, each supplying more than one sample. Privacy requires indistinguishability when one user’s whole local dataset is replaced. Under smoothness conditions on the loss, the authors establish optimal rates in both central and local privacy models.

The approximate central rate is 1/sqrt(nm) + sqrt(d)/(epsilon n sqrt(m)); the local rate is sqrt(d)/(epsilon sqrt(nm)). Here m is the number of samples per user, d is the problem dimension, and epsilon controls privacy. These expressions describe how the stated optimal rates depend jointly on user count, individual data quantity, dimensionality, and privacy strength.

The algorithms combine new private mean-estimation techniques at the user level with carefully designed first-order stochastic optimization. In the central setting, the result improves the prior rate by a factor of sqrt(d). A key ingredient is a new use of differential privacy’s generalization properties in stochastic-gradient methods that make multiple passes through the data.
summary.tldr: Under loss-smoothness conditions, new user-level private optimization methods achieve optimal rates in both central and local privacy settings.

title: User-level Private Stochastic Convex Optimization with Optimal Rates

abstract: When facing data with imbalanced classes or groups, practitioners follow an intriguing strategy to achieve best results. They throw away examples until the classes or groups are balanced in size, and then perform empirical risk minimization on the reduced training set. This opposes common wisdom in learning theory, where the expected error is supposed to decrease as the dataset grows in size. In this work, we leverage extreme value theory to address this apparent contradiction. Our results show that the tails of the data distribution play an important role in determining the worst-group-accuracy of linear classifiers. When learning on data with heavy tails, throwing away data restores the geometric symmetry of the resulting classifier, and therefore improves its worst-group generalization.

paragraphs: When training data contain unequal numbers of examples from different classes or groups, practitioners sometimes discard examples until the groups are balanced. They then minimize training error on the smaller dataset. This paper investigates why that can improve performance for the worst-served group, despite the usual expectation that more data should improve learning.

The analysis uses extreme value theory to study linear classifiers. It identifies the tails of the data distribution as an important influence on worst-group accuracy. The tails describe the behavior of unusually extreme observations, so the explanation depends on distributional structure as well as the number of examples. This gives a way to analyze why imbalance can matter geometrically for the learned classifier.

For heavy-tailed data in the studied setting, discarding examples restores geometric symmetry in the resulting classifier and improves worst-group generalization. The result explains how reducing sample size can improve this particular objective. Its force comes from the connection among heavy tails, classifier geometry, and group balance; it does not establish that discarding data improves every classifier or distribution.
summary.tldr: For linear classifiers in the studied heavy-tailed setting, balancing groups by discarding data restores geometric symmetry and improves worst-group generalization.

title: Why does Throwing Away Data Improve Worst-Group Error?

abstract: We give an improved theoretical analysis of score-based generative modeling. Under a score estimate with small $L^2$ error (averaged across timesteps), we provide efficient convergence guarantees for any data distribution with second-order moment, by either employing early stopping or assuming smoothness condition on the score function of the data distribution. Our result does not rely on any log-concavity or functional inequality assumption and has a logarithmic dependence on the smoothness. In particular, we show that under only a finite second moment condition, approximating the following in reverse KL divergence in $\epsilon$-accuracy can be done in $\tilde O\left(\frac{d \log (1/\delta)}{\epsilon}\right)$ steps: 1) the variance-$\delta$ Gaussian perturbation of any data distribution; 2) data distributions with $1/\delta$-smooth score functions. Our analysis also provides a quantitative comparison between different discrete approximations and may guide the choice of discretization points in practice.

paragraphs: This paper strengthens theoretical guarantees for score-based generative models. Its starting requirement is a score estimate with small squared error averaged across time steps. Given that estimate, it establishes efficient convergence for data distributions with finite second moments, using either early stopping or an additional smoothness condition on the data distribution's score.

The analysis avoids assumptions of log-concavity or functional inequalities and depends only logarithmically on smoothness. It considers two approximation targets: a data distribution after adding Gaussian noise of variance delta, and a data distribution whose score has smoothness bounded by one over delta. The distinction makes clear how smoothing the target and assuming score smoothness enter the guarantees.

For reverse-KL accuracy epsilon, the stated step bound scales approximately as dimension times log of one over delta, divided by epsilon, with additional logarithmic factors suppressed. The analysis also quantitatively compares discrete approximations. These comparisons may help choose discretization points in practice, although that practical guidance is presented as a possibility.
summary.tldr: The paper proves efficient score-based generation guarantees under finite second moments and accurate score estimation, with early stopping or score smoothness.

title: Improved Analysis of Score-based Generative Modeling: User-Friendly Bounds under Minimal Smoothness Assumptions

abstract: We present CLUSTSEG, a general, transformer-based framework that tackles different image segmentation tasks ($i.e.,$ superpixel, semantic, instance, and panoptic) through a unified, neural clustering scheme. Regarding queries as cluster centers, CLUSTSEG is innovative in two aspects: 1) cluster centers are initialized in heterogeneous ways so as to pointedly address task-specific demands ($e.g.,$ instance- or category-level distinctiveness), yet without modifying the architecture; and 2) pixel-cluster assignment, formalized in a cross-attention fashion, is alternated with cluster center update, yet without learning additional parameters. These innovations closely link CLUSTSEG to EM clustering and make it a transparent and powerful framework that yields superior results across the above segmentation tasks.

These innovations closely link CLUSTSEG to EM clustering and make it a transparent and powerful framework that yields superior results across the above segmentation tasks.

paragraphs: Image segmentation involves grouping pixels, but different tasks ask for different kinds of groups. CLUSTSEG presents a transformer-based framework that handles superpixel, semantic, instance, and panoptic segmentation through a common neural clustering procedure. Its organizing idea is to treat transformer queries as cluster centers around which pixel groups are formed.

The framework accommodates task-specific needs by initializing these centers in different ways. For example, distinguishing object instances and distinguishing categories call for different forms of distinctiveness. Those differences are handled through initialization without changing the architecture. This makes the clustering formulation a shared mechanism across the supported segmentation tasks.

CLUSTSEG then alternates between assigning pixels to clusters through cross-attention and updating the cluster centers, without learning additional parameters for this alternation. The authors connect this process to expectation-maximization clustering, making the roles of assignment and updating more explicit. They report superior results across the listed tasks, supporting the usefulness of a common clustering approach with task-sensitive initialization.
summary.tldr: CLUSTSEG unifies several segmentation tasks by treating transformer queries as cluster centers and alternating pixel assignments with center updates.

title: CLUSTSEG: Clustering for Universal Segmentation

abstract: Proteins power a vast array of functional processes in living cells. The capability to create new proteins with designed structures and functions would thus enable the engineering of cellular behavior and development of protein-based therapeutics and materials. Structure-based protein design aims to find structures that are designable (can be realized by a protein sequence), novel (have dissimilar geometry from natural proteins), and diverse (span a wide range of geometries). While advances in protein structure prediction have made it possible to predict structures of novel protein sequences, the combinatorially large space of sequences and structures limits the practicality of search-based methods. Generative models provide a compelling alternative, by implicitly learning the low-dimensional structure of complex data distributions. Here, we leverage recent advances in denoising diffusion probabilistic models and equivariant neural networks to develop Genie, a generative model of protein structures that performs discrete-time diffusion using a cloud of oriented reference frames in 3D space. Through in silico evaluations, we demonstrate that Genie generates protein backbones that are more designable, novel, and diverse than existing models. This indicates that Genie is capturing key aspects of the distribution of protein structure space and facilitates protein design with high success rates. Code for generating new proteins and training new versions of Genie is available at https://github.com/aqlaboratory/genie.

paragraphs: Designing protein structures involves three related goals: structures should be realizable by protein sequences, differ from natural protein geometries, and cover a broad range of shapes. Searching directly through the enormous space of sequences and structures is difficult. This paper develops Genie, a generative model intended to produce promising structures directly.

Genie combines denoising diffusion with equivariant neural networks. It represents a protein structure as a collection of oriented reference frames in three-dimensional space and applies a discrete-time diffusion process to that representation. The representation includes orientation as well as spatial placement, giving the model a geometric basis for generating protein backbones.

Computational evaluations show that Genie produces backbones that are more designable, novel, and diverse than those generated by existing models. The authors interpret these results as evidence that Genie captures important features of the distribution of protein structures and supports protein design with high success rates. The stated evidence comes from in silico evaluation, so the reported achievement concerns computationally assessed structure generation and designability.
summary.tldr: Genie uses geometric diffusion to generate protein backbones with improved designability, novelty, and diversity in computational evaluations.

title: Generating Novel, Designable, and Diverse Protein Structures by Equivariantly Diffusing Oriented Residue Clouds

abstract: During the recent years the interest of optimization and machine learning communities in high-probability convergence of stochastic optimization methods has been growing. One of the main reasons for this is that high-probability complexity bounds are more accurate and less studied than in-expectation ones. However, SOTA high-probability non-asymptotic convergence results are derived under strong assumptions such as boundedness of the gradient noise variance or of the objective’s gradient itself. In this paper, we propose several algorithms with high-probability convergence results under less restrictive assumptions. In particular, we derive new high-probability convergence results under the assumption that the gradient/operator noise has bounded central $\alpha$-th moment for $\alpha \in (1,2]$ in the following setups: (i) smooth non-convex / Polyak-Lojasiewicz / convex / strongly convex / quasi-strongly convex minimization problems, (ii) Lipschitz / star-cocoercive and monotone / quasi-strongly monotone variational inequalities. These results justify the usage of the considered methods for solving problems that do not fit standard functional classes studied in stochastic optimization.

paragraphs: Stochastic optimization uses noisy information to make progress toward a solution. A guarantee about average behavior does not directly specify what happens with high probability in a particular run. This paper develops finite-time, high-probability convergence guarantees while relaxing noise assumptions used by existing results, including assumptions of bounded variance.

The authors instead assume a bounded central moment of order alpha, where alpha is greater than one and at most two. When alpha is below two, this condition can accommodate noise without bounded variance. The analysis still imposes a quantitative restriction on the noise, but permits a broader class than analyses requiring a finite second moment.

Several algorithms receive guarantees across smooth minimization settings, including non-convex problems and multiple convexity-related conditions. The paper also covers variational inequalities under specified regularity and monotonicity conditions. Its contribution is theoretical justification for the considered methods in these broader settings, extending high-confidence convergence analysis to problems whose noise or structural properties fall outside commonly studied assumptions.
summary.tldr: New high-probability convergence guarantees allow stochastic optimization noise with bounded lower-order moments even when variance may be unbounded.

title: High-Probability Bounds for Stochastic Optimization and Variational Inequalities: the Case of Unbounded Variance

abstract: We advance the study of incentivized bandit exploration, in which arm choices are viewed as recommendations and are required to be Bayesian incentive compatible. Recent work of Sellke-Slivkins (Operations Research 2022) has shown that for the special case of independent arms, after collecting enough initial samples, the popular Thompson sampling algorithm becomes incentive compatible. This was generalized to the combinatorial semibandit in Hu-Ngo-Slivkins-Wu (NeurIPS 2022). We give an analog of this result for linear bandits, where the independence of the prior is replaced by a natural convexity condition. This opens up the possibility of efficient and regret-optimal incentivized exploration in high-dimensional action spaces. In the semibandit model, we also improve the sample complexity for the pre-Thompson sampling phase of initial data collection.

paragraphs: In incentivized bandit exploration, an algorithm recommends actions to people whose interests must be respected. Recommendations are required to be Bayesian incentive compatible, so exploration must fit with the users' incentives under the model. The challenge is to gather useful information while maintaining that compatibility.

Previous results established that Thompson sampling becomes incentive compatible after sufficient initial data collection for independent arms, with a subsequent extension to combinatorial semibandits. This paper proves an analogous result for linear bandits. In its analysis, a natural convexity condition replaces the earlier independence assumption on the prior, extending the circumstances in which this exploration strategy can be justified.

The extension opens the possibility of efficient, regret-optimal incentivized exploration in high-dimensional action spaces. The abstract presents that prospect as an implication of the result, rather than an unconditional guarantee for all such spaces. The paper also improves the sample complexity of initial data collection in the semibandit setting, reducing the preparation needed before switching to Thompson sampling.
summary.tldr: The paper extends incentive-compatible Thompson sampling to linear bandits under a convexity condition and improves semibandit initialization sample complexity.

title: Incentivizing Exploration with Linear Contexts and Combinatorial Actions

abstract: This paper investigates the problem of exact community recovery in the symmetric $d$-uniform $(d \geq 2)$ hypergraph stochastic block model ($d$-HSBM). In this model, a $d$-uniform hypergraph with $n$ nodes is generated by first partitioning the $n$ nodes into $K\geq 2$ equal-sized disjoint communities and then generating hyperedges with a probability that depends on the community memberships of $d$ nodes. Despite the non-convex and discrete nature of the maximum likelihood estimation problem, we develop a simple yet efficient iterative method, called the projected tensor power method , to tackle it. As long as the initialization satisfies a partial recovery condition in the logarithmic degree regime of the problem, we show that our proposed method can exactly recover the hidden community structure down to the information-theoretic limit with high probability. Moreover, our proposed method exhibits a competitive time complexity of $\mathcal{O}(n\log^2n/\log\log n)$ when the aforementioned initialization condition is met. We also conduct numerical experiments to validate our theoretical findings.

paragraphs: A hypergraph allows one connection to involve several nodes. This paper studies recovering hidden communities in a symmetric model where every hyperedge joins the same number of nodes and communities have equal sizes. Hyperedge probabilities depend on the community memberships of the participating nodes, providing the statistical signal used for recovery.

The authors develop an iterative projected tensor power method to address the discrete, nonconvex maximum-likelihood problem. Their guarantee requires an initialization that already achieves partial recovery and applies in the logarithmic-degree regime. Under those conditions, the method recovers the entire hidden community structure with high probability down to the information-theoretic limit.

With the same initialization condition, the stated time complexity is O(n log² n / log log n), making the algorithm computationally competitive for the analyzed problem. Numerical experiments validate the theoretical findings. The contribution combines statistical accuracy near the recoverability boundary with efficient computation, while retaining explicit assumptions about the random hypergraph model and the quality of the starting point.
summary.tldr: A projected tensor iteration achieves exact hypergraph community recovery at the information-theoretic limit under stated model and initialization conditions.

title: Projected Tensor Power Method for Hypergraph Community Recovery

abstract: Constant (naive) imputation is still widely used in practice as this is a first easy-to-use technique to deal with missing data. Yet, this simple method could be expected to induce a large bias for prediction purposes, as the imputed input may strongly differ from the true underlying data. However, recent works suggest that this bias is low in the context of high-dimensional linear predictors when data is supposed to be missing completely at random (MCAR). This paper completes the picture for linear predictors by confirming the intuition that the bias is negligible and that surprisingly naive imputation also remains relevant in very low dimension. To this aim, we consider a unique underlying random features model, which offers a rigorous framework for studying predictive performances, whilst the dimension of the observed features varies. Building on these theoretical results, we establish finite-sample bounds on stochastic gradient (SGD) predictors applied to zero-imputed data, a strategy particularly well suited for large-scale learning. If the MCAR assumption appears to be strong, we show that similar favorable behaviors occur for more complex missing data scenarios.

paragraphs: Replacing missing values with a constant is easy, but it can make the completed inputs look unlike the underlying data. That raises a prediction question: how much bias does this simple substitution introduce? This paper examines why naive imputation can nevertheless work well for linear predictors.

The analysis uses one underlying random-features model while varying the number of observed features. This provides a common framework for comparing predictive behavior across dimensions. The results confirm negligible bias in the studied setting and show that naive imputation can remain relevant even in very low dimensions, extending the picture beyond earlier high-dimensional findings.

Building on that analysis, the authors derive finite-sample bounds for stochastic-gradient predictors trained on data whose missing entries are filled with zeros. This connects the theoretical findings to a method suited to large-scale learning. Missing completely at random is an important assumption in the analysis, but the paper also reports similarly favorable behavior in more complex missing-data scenarios. The findings explain success within these studied models without implying that constant imputation is reliable for every pattern of missingness.
summary.tldr: A random-features analysis explains how constant imputation can have negligible prediction bias and remain useful across feature dimensions.

title: Random features models: a way to study the success of naive imputation

abstract: Neural networks extract features from data using stochastic gradient descent (SGD). In particular, higher-order input cumulants (HOCs) are crucial for their performance. However, extracting information from the $p$th cumulant of $d$-dimensional inputs is computationally hard: the number of samples required to recover a single direction from an order-$p$ tensor (tensor PCA) using SGD grows as $d^{p−1}$, which is prohibitive for high-dimensional inputs. This result raises the question of how neural networks extract relevant directions from the HOCs of their inputs efficiently. Here, we show that correlations between latent variables along the directions encoded in different input cumulants speed up learning from higher-order correlations. We show this effect analytically by deriving nearly sharp thresholds for the number of samples required by a single neuron to recover these directions using online SGD from a random start in high dimensions. Our analytical results are confirmed in simulations of two-layer neural networks and unveil a new mechanism for hierarchical learning in neural networks

paragraphs: Higher-order input statistics can contain useful features, but extracting them with stochastic gradient descent can be expensive. In the tensor-PCA problem described by the authors, recovering one direction from an order-p statistic of d-dimensional data requires a number of samples growing as d^(p−1). This creates a puzzle about how networks can efficiently learn information carried by complex correlations.

The paper identifies correlations between latent variables as a mechanism that can accelerate learning. When latent variables connect directions represented in different input cumulants, learning higher-order information becomes faster. The contribution is to show how relationships among the hidden sources of the data can change the difficulty suggested by studying a higher-order statistic in isolation.

The authors derive nearly sharp sample thresholds for a single neuron trained with online SGD from a random initialization in high dimensions. Simulations with two-layer networks confirm the analytical effect. These findings establish a mechanism for hierarchical learning in the studied setting: correlations across latent variables can help networks reach statistically more complex features with fewer samples.
summary.tldr: Correlations between latent variables can accelerate SGD’s recovery of features encoded in higher-order input statistics.

title: Sliding Down the Stairs: How Correlated Latent Variables Accelerate Learning with Neural Networks

abstract: In this paper, we discuss feature engineering for single-pass uncertainty estimation. For accurate uncertainty estimates, neural networks must extract differences in the feature space that quantify uncertainty. This could be achieved by current single-pass approaches that maintain feature distances between data points as they traverse the network. While initial results are promising, maintaining feature distances within the network representations frequently inhibits information compression and opposes the learning objective. We study this effect theoretically and empirically to arrive at a simple conclusion: preserving feature distances in the output is beneficial when the preserved features contribute to learning the label distribution and act in opposition otherwise. We then propose Transitional Uncertainty with Layered Intermediate Predictions (TULIP) as a simple approach to address the shortcomings of current single-pass estimators. Specifically, we implement feature preservation by extracting features from intermediate representations before information is collapsed by subsequent layers. We refer to the underlying preservation mechanism as transitional feature preservation. We show that TULIP matches or outperforms current single-pass methods on standard benchmarks and in practical settings where these methods are less reliable (imbalances, complex architectures, medical modalities).

paragraphs: Estimating uncertainty in a single network pass requires features that distinguish when predictions are reliable. Some approaches preserve distances between examples as information moves through the network. This paper studies a tension in that strategy: preserving those distances can interfere with the information compression needed to learn the prediction task.

The theoretical and empirical analysis finds that preserving output features helps when those features contribute to learning the label distribution, but works against learning otherwise. The authors propose TULIP, which draws on intermediate representations before later layers collapse information. They call this mechanism transitional feature preservation, using layered intermediate predictions to retain information relevant to uncertainty.

This design makes intermediate stages useful for uncertainty estimation without requiring every useful distinction to survive in the final representation. Experiments show that TULIP matches or exceeds current single-pass methods on standard benchmarks. The reported evaluation also covers class imbalances, complex architectures, and medical modalities, settings where existing methods are less reliable. The findings support intermediate feature extraction as a practical response to the identified compression conflict.
summary.tldr: TULIP uses intermediate network predictions to preserve uncertainty information before later layers compress it.

title: Transitional Uncertainty with Layered Intermediate Predictions

abstract: High-dimensional optimization problems have long been considered the Achilles’ heel of Bayesian optimization algorithms. Spurred by the curse of dimensionality, a large collection of algorithms aim to make BO more performant in this setting, commonly by imposing various simplifying assumptions on the objective, thereby decreasing its presumed complexity. In this paper, we identify the degeneracies that make vanilla BO poorly suited to high-dimensional tasks, and further show how existing algorithms address these degeneracies through the lens of model complexity. Motivated by the model complexity measure, we derive an enhancement to the prior assumptions that are typical of the vanilla BO algorithm, which reduces the complexity to manageable levels without imposing structural restrictions on the objective. Our modification - a simple scaling of the Gaussian process lengthscale prior in the dimensionality - reveals that standard BO works drastically better than previously thought in high dimensions. Our insights are supplemented by substantial out-performance of existing state-of-the-art on multiple commonly considered real-world high-dimensional tasks.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization is often considered poorly suited to problems with many input dimensions. Many proposed remedies simplify the objective by assuming it has a particular structure. This paper investigates why standard Bayesian optimization deteriorates in high dimensions and interprets both that failure and existing remedies through model complexity.

The proposed change is simple: scale the prior over the Gaussian process lengthscale with the number of dimensions. Lengthscales control how the model relates function values at different inputs. Adjusting their prior changes the model's assumed complexity, bringing it to a manageable level without imposing structural restrictions on the objective being optimized.

The authors report substantial improvements over existing state-of-the-art methods on multiple commonly studied real-world high-dimensional tasks. These results suggest that standard Bayesian optimization can perform much better in such settings when its prior is adjusted appropriately. The central lesson concerns the modeling assumptions: dimension-dependent prior design can address important failure behavior without requiring a more elaborate optimization framework or restrictive objective structure.
summary.tldr: Scaling the Gaussian process lengthscale prior with dimension substantially improves standard Bayesian optimization on evaluated high-dimensional tasks.

title: Vanilla Bayesian Optimization Performs Great in High Dimensions

abstract: Prior interpretability research studying narrow distributions has preliminarily identified self-repair, a phenomena where if components in large language models are ablated, later components will change their behavior to compensate. Our work builds off this past literature, demonstrating that self-repair exists on a variety of models families and sizes when ablating individual attention heads on the full training distribution. We further show that on the full training distribution self-repair is imperfect, as the original direct effect of the head is not fully restored, and noisy, since the degree of self-repair varies significantly across different prompts (sometimes overcorrecting beyond the original effect). We highlight two different mechanisms that contribute to self-repair, including changes in the final LayerNorm scaling factor and sparse sets of neurons implementing Anti-Erasure. We additionally discuss the implications of these results for interpretability practitioners and close with a more speculative discussion on the mystery of why self-repair occurs in these models at all, highlighting evidence for the Iterative Inference hypothesis in language models, a framework that predicts self-repair.

paragraphs: Removing a component from a language model does not necessarily reveal its contribution in isolation: later components may change their behavior to compensate. This phenomenon is called self-repair. Earlier evidence came from narrow input distributions. The authors extend the investigation by ablating individual attention heads across multiple model families and sizes on the full training distribution.

They find that compensation occurs, but it is neither complete nor consistent. The removed head’s original direct effect is not fully restored, and the amount of repair varies substantially between prompts. Some prompts even produce overcorrection. This makes self-repair relevant to interpreting ablation experiments, because the observed outcome includes both the removed contribution and downstream responses to its removal.

The paper identifies two contributing mechanisms: changes in final LayerNorm scaling and sparse groups of neurons implementing Anti-Erasure. It also discusses evidence for the Iterative Inference hypothesis, which predicts self-repair. That broader explanation is presented speculatively, distinct from the demonstrated compensation patterns and mechanisms.
summary.tldr: Language models partly compensate for removed attention heads, but the repair is prompt-dependent, imperfect, and sometimes excessive.

title: Explorations of Self-Repair in Language Models

abstract: We consider the problem of sequential change detection under minimal assumptions on the distribution generating the stream of observations. Formally, our goal is to design a scheme for detecting any changes in a parameter or functional $\theta$ of the data stream distribution that has small detection delay, but guarantees control on the frequency of false alarms in the absence of changes. We describe a simple reduction from sequential change detection to sequential estimation using confidence sequences (CSs): begin a new level-$(1-\alpha)$ CS at each time step, and proclaim a change as soon as the intersection of all active CSs becomes empty. We prove that the average run length of our scheme is at least $1/\alpha$, resulting in a change detection scheme with minimal structural assumptions (thus allowing for possibly dependent observations, and nonparametric distribution classes), but strong guarantees. We also describe an interesting parallel with Lorden’s reduction from change detection to sequential testing and connections to the recent ”e-detector” framework.

paragraphs: Sequential change detection monitors a data stream for changes while trying to avoid frequent false alarms. This paper targets changes in a chosen parameter or functional of the stream's distribution. Its approach builds detection from sequential estimation, allowing confidence statements maintained over time to drive the alarm rule.

At every time step, the procedure starts a new confidence sequence at level one minus alpha. It declares a change when all active confidence sequences have an empty intersection. Intuitively, an alarm occurs when the estimates from the different starting points no longer share any compatible value for the quantity being monitored.

The authors prove that, without a change, the average run length is at least one divided by alpha. This supplies a formal false-alarm guarantee under minimal structural assumptions, including settings that allow dependent observations and nonparametric distribution classes. The result makes confidence sequences a reusable foundation for change detection. The paper also relates this construction to earlier reductions based on sequential testing and to the e-detector framework.
summary.tldr: Starting a confidence sequence at every time step yields a change detector with a proven lower bound on average time to false alarm.

title: Reducing sequential change detection to sequential estimation

abstract: Feature attribution explains machine decisions by quantifying each feature’s contribution. While numerous approaches rely on exact gradient measurements, recent work has adopted gradient estimation to derive explanatory information under query-level access, a restrictive yet more practical accessibility assumption known as the black-box setting. Following this direction, this paper introduces GEFA (Gradient-estimation-based Explanation For All), a general feature attribution framework leveraging proxy gradient estimation. Unlike the previous attempt that focused on explaining image classifiers, the proposed explainer derives feature attributions in a proxy space, making it generally applicable to arbitrary black-box models, regardless of input type. In addition to its close relationship with Integrated Gradients, our approach, a path method built upon estimated gradients, surprisingly produces unbiased estimates of Shapley Values. Compared to traditional sampling-based Shapley Value estimators, GEFA avoids potential information waste sourced from computing marginal contributions, thereby improving explanation quality, as demonstrated in quantitative evaluations across various settings.

paragraphs: Feature attribution explains a prediction by assigning contributions to its input features. Many methods need direct access to model gradients, which is unavailable when a model can only be queried for outputs. GEFA addresses this black-box setting by estimating gradients, extending a direction of work previously focused on explaining image classifiers.

The framework computes attributions in a proxy space rather than tying the explanation procedure to a particular input type. This design makes it applicable to arbitrary black-box models according to the paper. Its explanations follow a path built from estimated gradients, connecting the method closely to Integrated Gradients while operating under more restricted model access.

The authors also show that this path-based approach produces unbiased estimates of Shapley Values. Compared with traditional sampling procedures based on marginal contributions, GEFA avoids a potential source of information waste. Quantitative evaluations across several settings show improved explanation quality. The contribution combines broad applicability under query access with a theoretical connection to a well-established attribution target.
summary.tldr: GEFA estimates gradients in a proxy space to explain black-box models and produce unbiased Shapley Value estimates.

title: GEFA: A General Feature Attribution Framework Using Proxy Gradient Estimation

abstract: Training a precise binary classifier with limited supervision in weakly supervised learning scenarios holds considerable research significance in practical settings. Leveraging pairwise unlabeled data with confidence differences has been demonstrated to outperform learning from pointwise unlabeled data. We theoretically analyze the various supervisory signals reflected by confidence differences in confidence difference (ConfDiff) classification and identify challenges arising from noisy signals when confidence differences are small. To address this, we partition the dataset into two subsets with distinct supervisory signals and propose a consistency regularization-based risk estimator to encourage similar outputs for similar instances, mitigating the impact of noisy supervision. We further derive and analyze its estimation error bounds theoretically. Extensive experiments on benchmark and UCI datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our method. Additionally, to effectively capture the influence of real-world noise on the confidence difference, we artificially perturb the confidence difference distribution and demonstrate the robustness of our method under noisy conditions through comprehensive experiments.

paragraphs: Binary classifiers can sometimes learn from differences in confidence between pairs of unlabeled examples instead of receiving a label for each example. This paper examines what supervisory information those differences contain. It identifies a particular difficulty: small confidence differences can carry noisy signals that make learning less reliable.

The authors divide the data into two subsets with different supervisory signals and construct a risk estimator with consistency regularization. This regularization encourages similar examples to receive similar outputs, reducing the influence of noisy supervision. The approach uses the structure of the available confidence information to guide how the classifier learns.

The paper also derives and analyzes estimation-error bounds, giving a theoretical account of the proposed estimator. Experiments on benchmark and UCI datasets demonstrate the method's effectiveness. To investigate noise more directly, the authors artificially perturb the confidence-difference distribution and test the method under those conditions. These experiments provide evidence of robustness to the tested noise, complementing the analysis of why small confidence differences can be problematic.
summary.tldr: Separating confidence-difference supervision into distinct subsets and encouraging consistent predictions improves learning under the tested noisy conditions.

title: Confidence Difference Reflects Various Supervised Signals in Confidence-Difference Classification

abstract: The importance of higher-order relations is widely recognized in numerous real-world systems. However, annotating them is a tedious and sometimes even impossible task. Consequently, current approaches for data modelling either ignore the higher-order interactions altogether or simplify them into pairwise connections. To facilitate higher-order processing, even when a hypergraph structure is not available, we introduce SPHINX, a model that learns to infer a latent hypergraph structure in an unsupervised way, solely from the final task-dependent signal. To ensure broad applicability, we design the model to be end-to-end differentiable, capable of generating a discrete hypergraph structure compatible with any modern hypergraph networks, and easily optimizable without requiring additional regularization losses. Through extensive ablation studies and experiments conducted on four challenging datasets, we demonstrate that our model is capable of inferring suitable latent hypergraphs in both transductive and inductive tasks. Moreover, the inferred latent hypergraphs are interpretable and contribute to enhancing the final performance, outperforming existing methods for hypergraph prediction.

paragraphs: Some systems contain relationships among groups of entities that are not naturally captured by pairwise links. Hypergraphs represent such higher-order interactions, but obtaining annotated hypergraph structures can be difficult or impossible. SPHINX learns a latent hypergraph from the final task signal, avoiding the need for direct supervision of those relationships.

The model is differentiable end to end while producing a discrete hypergraph that can be used by modern hypergraph networks. It also avoids additional regularization losses for optimization. These design choices make structure inference part of the task-learning process: the inferred relationships are developed through their usefulness to the final prediction task.

Ablation studies and experiments on four challenging datasets show suitable inferred structures in both transductive and inductive tasks. The authors report that the latent hypergraphs are interpretable and improve final performance, outperforming existing hypergraph-prediction methods. The findings support learning higher-order structure from task feedback when an explicit structural annotation is unavailable.
summary.tldr: SPHINX learns interpretable discrete hypergraphs from task feedback, improving prediction without requiring annotated higher-order relationships.

title: SPHINX: Structural Prediction using Hypergraph Inference Network

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit strong potential in mathematical reasoning, yet their effectiveness is often limited by a shortage of high-quality queries. This limitation necessitates scaling up computational responses through self-generated data, yet current methods struggle due to spurious correlated data caused by ineffective exploration across all reasoning stages. To address such challenge, we introduce MARGE: Improving Math Reasoning with Guided Exploration, a novel method that enhances mathematical reasoning through hit-guided exploration. MARGE systematically explores intermediate reasoning states derived from self-generated solutions, enabling adequate exploration and improved credit assignment throughout the reasoning process. Notably, MARGE improves both single-shot accuracy and exploration diversity, mitigating a common trade-off in alignment methods. These results demonstrate MARGE’s effectiveness in enhancing mathematical reasoning capabilities and unlocking the potential of scaling self-generated training data.

paragraphs: Language models can generate mathematical solutions for their own training, but producing more data does not automatically produce better reasoning. The paper identifies ineffective exploration across reasoning stages as a source of spurious correlations in self-generated data. MARGE addresses this problem by changing how the model explores the reasoning process.

Its hit-guided exploration systematically examines intermediate states taken from self-generated solutions. These partial reasoning states become opportunities to explore, helping the method cover more of the solution process and improve credit assignment. Credit assignment concerns which parts of a reasoning trajectory should receive responsibility for its outcome, making intermediate exploration relevant to what the model learns from its generated work.

The authors report improvements in both single-shot accuracy and exploration diversity. This combination matters because alignment methods can face a tradeoff between producing a strong individual answer and retaining varied exploration. MARGE's stated results suggest that guided exploration can mitigate that tradeoff, supporting the use of self-generated training data as a scalable resource for improving mathematical reasoning.
summary.tldr: MARGE explores intermediate states of self-generated math solutions to improve credit assignment, single-shot accuracy, and exploration diversity.

title: MARGE: Improving Math Reasoning with Guided Exploration

abstract: When trained on large-scale object classification datasets, certain artificial neural network models begin to approximate core object recognition behaviors and neural response patterns in the primate brain. While recent machine learning advances suggest that scaling compute, model size, and dataset size improves task performance, the impact of scaling on brain alignment remains unclear. In this study, we explore scaling laws for modeling the primate visual ventral stream by systematically evaluating over 600 models trained under controlled conditions on benchmarks spanning V1, V2, V4, IT and behavior. We find that while behavioral alignment continues to scale with larger models, neural alignment saturates. This observation remains true across model architectures and training datasets, even though models with stronger inductive biases and datasets with higher-quality images are more compute-efficient. Increased scaling is especially beneficial for higher-level visual areas, where small models trained on few samples exhibit only poor alignment. Our results suggest that while scaling current architectures and datasets might suffice for alignment with human core object recognition behavior, it will not yield improved models of the brain’s visual ventral stream, highlighting the need for novel strategies in building brain models.

paragraphs: Neural networks trained for object classification can resemble primate visual behavior and neural responses. This paper asks whether increasing model size, data, and computation improves both kinds of resemblance. The authors systematically evaluate more than 600 models trained under controlled conditions, using benchmarks for V1, V2, V4, IT, and behavior.

They find a separation between behavioral and neural alignment. Behavioral alignment continues to improve with larger models, while neural alignment saturates. This pattern holds across the architectures and datasets studied. Stronger architectural inductive biases and higher-quality training images improve compute efficiency, but do not remove the observed saturation. Scaling is particularly helpful for higher-level visual areas, where small models trained on few samples align poorly.

The results distinguish matching recognition behavior from matching the brain activity supporting it. The authors suggest that scaling current architectures and datasets might suffice for human core object-recognition behavior, while further improving models of the visual ventral stream requires new strategies. The conclusion concerns the limits of the studied scaling approach to neural alignment.
summary.tldr: Across more than 600 models, scaling improves alignment with visual behavior while alignment with neural responses saturates.

title: Scaling Laws for Task-Optimized Models of the Primate Visual Ventral Stream

abstract: The application of deep learning for partial differential equation (PDE)-constrained control is gaining increasing attention. However, existing methods rarely consider safety requirements crucial in real-world applications. To address this limitation, we propose Safe Diffusion Models for PDE Control (SafeDiffCon), which introduce the uncertainty quantile as model uncertainty quantification to achieve optimal control under safety constraints through both post-training and inference phases. Firstly, our approach post-trains a pre-trained diffusion model to generate control sequences that better satisfy safety constraints while achieving improved control objectives via a reweighted diffusion loss, which incorporates the uncertainty quantile estimated using conformal prediction. Secondly, during inference, the diffusion model dynamically adjusts both its generation process and parameters through iterative guidance and fine-tuning, conditioned on control targets while simultaneously integrating the estimated uncertainty quantile. We evaluate SafeDiffCon on three control tasks: 1D Burgers’ equation, 2D incompressible fluid, and controlled nuclear fusion problem. Results demonstrate that SafeDiffCon is the only method that satisfies all safety constraints, whereas other classical and deep learning baselines fail. Furthermore, while adhering to safety constraints, SafeDiffCon achieves the best control performance. The code can be found at https://github.com/AI4Science-WestlakeU/safediffcon.

paragraphs: Controlling systems governed by partial differential equations requires pursuing a target while respecting safety constraints. The paper argues that existing deep-learning approaches rarely address this safety requirement. SafeDiffCon adapts a pretrained diffusion model using an uncertainty quantile estimated through conformal prediction, incorporating uncertainty into both additional training and control generation.

During post-training, a reweighted diffusion loss encourages control sequences that better satisfy safety constraints while improving the control objective. During inference, the model continues adapting: iterative guidance changes its generation process, and fine-tuning updates its parameters. Both steps use the control target together with the uncertainty estimate, connecting safety considerations to the actual search for control sequences.

The evaluation covers the one-dimensional Burgers equation, two-dimensional incompressible fluid control, and a controlled nuclear fusion problem. In these experiments, SafeDiffCon is the only evaluated method to satisfy every safety constraint and also achieves the best control performance while doing so. These are results on the reported tasks, supporting uncertainty-aware adaptation as a way to jointly improve safety compliance and control quality.
summary.tldr: SafeDiffCon integrates conformal uncertainty estimates into diffusion-model adaptation and achieves the best reported safe control performance on three PDE tasks.

title: From Uncertain to Safe: Conformal Adaptation of Diffusion Models for Safe PDE Control

abstract: We introduce Lavender, a simple supervised fine-tuning (SFT) method that boosts the performance of advanced vision-language models (VLMs) by leveraging state-of-the-art image generation models such as Stable Diffusion. Specifically, Lavender aligns the text-vision attention in the VLM transformer with the equivalent used by Stable Diffusion during SFT, instead of adapting separate encoders. This alignment enriches the model’s visual understanding and significantly boosts performance across in- and out-of-distribution tasks. Lavender requires just 0.13 million training examples—2.5% of typical large-scale SFT datasets—and fine-tunes on standard hardware (8 GPUs) in a single day. It consistently improves state-of-the-art open-source multimodal LLMs (e.g., Llama-3.2-11B, MiniCPM-Llama3-v2.5), achieving up to 30% gains and a 68% boost on challenging out-of-distribution medical QA tasks. By efficiently transferring the visual expertise of image generators with minimal supervision, Lavender offers a scalable solution for more accurate vision-language systems. Code, training data, and models are available on the project page.

paragraphs: Lavender transfers visual expertise from image generation models into vision-language models during supervised fine-tuning. Its central idea is to align the vision-language transformer’s attention between text and images with the corresponding attention used by Stable Diffusion. This targets how the model connects the two modalities, rather than adapting separate encoders.

The method uses 130,000 training examples, described as 2.5% of typical large-scale supervised fine-tuning datasets. The reported training setup finishes fine-tuning in one day on eight GPUs. These figures explain the efficiency claim: the approach draws on knowledge already present in an image generator while using a relatively small amount of supervised training data.

The authors report consistent improvements for advanced open-source multimodal models, including Llama-3.2-11B and MiniCPM-Llama3-v2.5, across both in-distribution and out-of-distribution tasks. Reported gains reach 30%, with a 68% improvement on challenging out-of-distribution medical question answering. These findings support attention alignment as a useful route for transferring visual knowledge into models that must interpret images and respond through language.
summary.tldr: Lavender improves vision-language models by aligning their text-image attention with Stable Diffusion during relatively small-scale supervised fine-tuning.

title: Diffusion Instruction Tuning

abstract: Continual Learning (CL) strives to learn incrementally across tasks while mitigating catastrophic forgetting. A key challenge in CL is balancing stability (retaining prior knowledge) and plasticity (learning new tasks). While representative gradient projection methods ensure stability, they often limit plasticity. Model merging techniques offer promising solutions, but prior methods typically rely on empirical assumptions and carefully selected hyperparameters. In this paper, we explore the potential of model merging to enhance the stability-plasticity trade-off, providing theoretical insights that underscore its benefits. Specifically, we reformulate the merging mechanism using Bayesian continual learning principles and derive a closed-form solution for the optimal merging coefficient that adapts to the diverse characteristics of tasks. To validate our approach, we introduce a two-stage framework named BECAME, which synergizes the expertise of gradient projection and adaptive merging. Extensive experiments show that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art CL methods and existing merging strategies https://github.com/limei0818/BECAME.

paragraphs: Continual learning asks a model to learn successive tasks while retaining what it learned earlier. Its central tension is between stability, which protects existing knowledge, and plasticity, which permits learning new tasks. Gradient projection methods support stability but can constrain plasticity. Combining models offers another route, although earlier merging approaches depend on empirical assumptions and carefully chosen settings.

This paper develops a Bayesian interpretation of model merging for continual learning. From that formulation, the authors derive a closed-form expression for an optimal merging coefficient that adapts to task characteristics. The coefficient controls the combination, so adapting it provides a principled way to adjust how knowledge is merged as the learning problem changes.

BECAME implements these ideas in a two-stage framework combining gradient projection with adaptive merging. Theoretical analysis explains benefits for the stability-plasticity trade-off, and extensive experiments report better performance than the compared continual learning methods and merging strategies. The contribution connects a theoretically motivated merging rule with a practical continual learning framework.
summary.tldr: BECAME combines gradient projection with Bayesian adaptive model merging to balance retaining old knowledge and learning new tasks.

title: BECAME: Bayesian Continual Learning with Adaptive Model Merging

abstract: Attention mechanisms have emerged as transformative tools in core AI domains such as natural language processing and computer vision. Yet, their largely untapped potential for modeling intricate physical systems presents a compelling frontier. Learning such systems often entails discovering operators that map between functional spaces using limited instances of function pairs—a task commonly framed as a severely ill-posed inverse PDE problem. In this work, we introduce Neural Interpretable PDEs (NIPS), a novel neural operator architecture that builds upon and enhances Nonlocal Attention Operators (NAO) in both predictive accuracy and computational efficiency. NIPS employs a linear attention mechanism to enable scalable learning and integrates a learnable kernel network that acts as a channel-independent convolution in Fourier space. As a consequence, NIPS eliminates the need to explicitly compute and store large pairwise interactions, effectively amortizing the cost of handling spatial interactions into the Fourier transform. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that NIPS consistently surpasses NAO and other baselines across diverse benchmarks, heralding a substantial leap in scalable, interpretable, and efficient physics learning. Our code and data accompanying this paper are available at https://github.com/fishmoon1234/Nonlocal-Attention-Operator.

abstract: In this work, we develop a hypothesis testing framework to determine whether pairwise comparison data is generated by an underlying generalized Thurstone model $\mathcal{T}_F$ for a given choice function $F$. While prior work has predominantly focused on parameter estimation and uncertainty quantification for such models, we address the fundamental problem of minimax hypothesis testing for $\mathcal{T}_F$ models. We formulate this testing problem by introducing a notion of separation distance between general pairwise comparison models and the class of $\mathcal{T}_F$ models. We then derive upper and lower bounds on the critical threshold for testing that depend on the topology of the observation graph. For the special case of complete observation graphs, this threshold scales as $\Theta((nk)^{-1/2})$, where $n$ is the number of agents and $k$ is the number of comparisons per pair. Furthermore, we propose a hypothesis test based on our separation distance, construct confidence intervals, establish time-uniform bounds on the probabilities of type I and II errors using reverse martingale techniques, and derive minimax lower bounds using information-theoretic methods. Finally, we validate our results through experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets.

paragraphs: Pairwise comparison models describe outcomes of comparisons between agents. This paper asks whether observed comparisons are compatible with a generalized Thurstone model for a specified choice function. That question comes before estimating a model’s parameters: it tests whether the proposed model class is an appropriate description of the data.

The authors define a separation distance between general comparison models and the chosen Thurstone class. They derive upper and lower bounds on how far an alternative must be from that class for testing to be possible. These bounds depend on the observation graph, which records which pairs are compared. When every pair is observed, the critical threshold scales as the inverse square root of nk, with n agents and k comparisons per pair.

The framework includes a test based on this distance, confidence intervals, and time-uniform control of both types of testing error using reverse martingales. Information-theoretic arguments establish minimax lower bounds. Synthetic and real-world experiments validate the results, linking the theoretical testing limits to practical comparison data.
summary.tldr: The paper develops tests and statistical limits for determining whether pairwise comparisons fit a specified generalized Thurstone model.

title: Hypothesis Testing for Generalized Thurstone Models

abstract: As the space of causal sequence modeling architectures continues to grow, the need to develop a general framework for their analysis becomes increasingly important. With this aim, we draw insights from classical signal processing and control theory, to develop a quantitative measure of memory utilization: the internal mechanisms through which a model stores past information to produce future outputs. This metric, which we call effective state-size (ESS), is tailored to the fundamental class of systems with input-invariant and input-varying linear operators, encompassing a variety of computational units such as variants of attention, convolutions, and recurrences. Unlike prior work on memory utilization, which either relies on raw operator visualizations (e.g. attention maps), or simply the total memory capacity (i.e. cache size) of a model, our metrics provide highly interpretable and actionable measurements. In particular, we show how ESS can be leveraged to improve initialization strategies, inform novel regularizers and advance the performance-efficiency frontier through model distillation. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the effect of context delimiters (such as end-of-speech tokens) on ESS highlights cross-architectural differences in how large language models utilize their available memory to recall information. Overall, we find that ESS provides valuable insights into the dynamics that dictate memory utilization, enabling the design of more efficient and effective sequence models.

The contribution is both a measurement framework and evidence that its measurements can guide choices about how sequence models are trained and made more efficient.
summary.tldr: Effective state-size measures how sequence models use memory and helps guide training, regularization, and distillation.

title: Quantifying Memory Utilization with Effective State-Size

abstract: The rapid development of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), such as GPT-4, marks a significant step toward artificial general intelligence. Existing methods typically align vision encoders with LLMs via supervised fine-tuning (SFT), but this often deteriorates their ability to handle multiple languages as training progresses. We empirically observe that imbalanced SFT datasets, largely English-centric, degrade performance on non-English languages due to the failure in multilingual token alignment. To address this, we propose Parrot, a novel approach that leverages textual guidance for visual token alignment at the language level. Parrot conditions visual tokens on diverse language inputs and uses Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) to align multilingual tokens. By computing cross-attention between initial visual features and textual embeddings, we select the most relevant experts, converting visual tokens into language-specific representations. Additionally, we introduce the Massive Multilingual Multimodal Benchmark (MMMB), a new benchmark comprising 6 languages, 15 categories, and 12,000 questions, to assess multilingual capabilities. Parrot achieves state-of-the-art performance on both the multilingual benchmarks and a wide range of multimodal tasks. Code and dataset are available at: https://github.com/AIDC-AI/Parrot.

paragraphs: Connecting a vision encoder to a language model through supervised fine-tuning can weaken multilingual performance. The authors empirically link this deterioration to training datasets dominated by English and to failures in multilingual token alignment. Parrot addresses how image information is represented for the language being used in an interaction.

Parrot achieves state-of-the-art results on the multilingual benchmarks and across a broad set of multimodal tasks. These findings support treating language-aware visual alignment as a central component of multilingual multimodal training, particularly when the available supervision is unevenly distributed across languages.
summary.tldr: Parrot uses language-guided expert selection to align visual tokens and improve multilingual multimodal performance.

title: Parrot: Multilingual Visual Instruction Tuning

abstract: We introduce Spatial Reasoning Models (SRMs), a framework to perform reasoning over sets of continuous variables via denoising generative models. SRMs infer continuous representations on a set of unobserved variables, given observations on observed variables. Current generative models on spatial domains, such as diffusion and flow matching models, often collapse to hallucination in case of complex distributions. To measure this, we introduce a set of benchmark tasks that test the quality of complex reasoning in generative models and can quantify hallucination. The SRM framework allows to report key findings about importance of sequentialization in generation, the associated order, as well as the sampling strategies during training. It demonstrates, for the first time, that order of generation can successfully be predicted by the denoising network itself. Using these findings, we can increase the accuracy of specific reasoning tasks from $<$1% to $>$50%. Our project website provides additional videos, code, and the benchmark datasets.

paragraphs: Spatial Reasoning Models, or SRMs, use denoising generative models to reason about sets of continuous variables. Given observations for some variables, they infer representations for the remaining ones. The paper focuses on the difficulty of doing this reliably for complex distributions, where spatial generative models can produce hallucinated outputs.

The authors introduce benchmark tasks designed to measure complex reasoning and quantify hallucination. Within the SRM framework, they investigate sequential generation, the order in which variables are generated, and sampling strategies during training. This treats the generation procedure as an important part of reasoning performance, alongside the model’s ability to represent the underlying variables.

A central finding is that the denoising network itself can successfully predict the order of generation, which the authors describe as a first demonstration. Using the resulting insights raises accuracy on specific reasoning tasks from below 1% to above 50%. The gains are stated for those tasks, showing that generation order and training choices can materially affect reasoning in this framework.
summary.tldr: SRMs show that generation order and training choices can sharply improve continuous-variable reasoning, with denoising networks learning to predict generation order.

title: Spatial Reasoning with Denoising Models

abstract: Training data quality is one of the most important drivers of final model quality. In this work, we introduce a method for evaluating data integrity based on the assumption that low-quality input prompts result in high variance and low quality responses. This is achieved by measuring the rejected response quality and the reward gap between the chosen and rejected preference pair. Our method, Rejecting Instruction Preferences (RIP) can be used to filter prompts from existing training sets, or to make high quality synthetic datasets, yielding large performance gains across various benchmarks compared to unfiltered data. Using Llama 3.1-8B-Instruct, RIP improves AlpacaEval2 LC Win Rate by 9.4%, Arena-Hard by 8.7%, and WildBench by 9.9%. Using Llama 3.3-70B-Instruct, RIP improves Arena-Hard from 67.5 to 82.9, from 18th place to 6th overall in the leaderboard.

paragraphs: Rejecting Instruction Preferences evaluates training prompts through the responses they elicit. Its starting assumption is that low-quality prompts tend to produce responses that are both low in quality and highly variable. This shifts attention from judging a prompt in isolation to using evidence from the model's behavior on that prompt.

RIP measures the quality of the rejected response in a preference pair and the reward difference between the chosen and rejected responses. These signals are used to filter prompts from an existing dataset or construct higher-quality synthetic datasets. The approach links prompt selection to both response quality and the contrast represented by a preference pair.

The paper reports large gains over unfiltered data across several benchmarks. For Llama 3.1-8B-Instruct, reported improvements are 9.4% on AlpacaEval2 LC Win Rate, 8.7% on Arena-Hard, and 9.9% on WildBench. For Llama 3.3-70B-Instruct, Arena-Hard rises from 67.5 to 82.9. These results support the usefulness of response-based prompt filtering under the method's stated data-quality assumption.
summary.tldr: RIP filters training prompts using rejected-response quality and preference reward gaps, yielding reported gains over unfiltered datasets.

title: R.I.P.: Better Models by Survival of the Fittest Prompts

abstract: Label completion serves as a preprocessing approach to handling the sparse crowdsourced label matrix problem, significantly boosting the effectiveness of the downstream label aggregation. In recent advances, worker modeling has been proved to be a powerful strategy to further improve the performance of label completion. However, in real-world scenarios, workers typically annotate only a few instances, leading to insufficient worker modeling and thus limiting the improvement of label completion. To address this issue, we propose a novel transfer learning-based label completion (TLLC) method. Specifically, we first identify all high-confidence instances from the whole crowdsourced data as a source domain and use it to pretrain a Siamese network. The abundant annotated instances in the source domain provide essential knowledge for worker modeling. Then, we transfer the pretrained network to the target domain with the instances annotated by each worker separately, ensuring worker modeling captures unique characteristics of each worker. Finally, we leverage the new embeddings learned by the transferred network to complete each worker’s missing labels. Extensive experiments on several widely used real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of TLLC. Our codes and datasets are available at https://github.com/jiangliangxiao/TLLC.

paragraphs: Crowdsourced labeling often produces a sparse matrix because each worker labels only a small portion of the available examples. Filling missing entries can improve later label aggregation, but modeling each worker is difficult when their annotations are scarce. TLLC addresses this problem by transferring information learned from the broader collection into individual worker models.

The method first gathers high-confidence examples from the full crowdsourced dataset and uses them as a source domain to pretrain a Siamese network. It then transfers that network separately to each worker’s annotated examples. This second stage adapts the shared knowledge to the particular worker, aiming to capture individual annotation characteristics despite limited worker-specific data.

The transferred networks produce new embeddings, which TLLC uses to complete missing labels for each worker. Experiments on several commonly used real-world datasets demonstrate effectiveness. The contribution is the separation of shared learning and worker-specific adaptation: information from the overall dataset supports personalized label completion before the downstream aggregation step.
summary.tldr: TLLC transfers knowledge from high-confidence crowdsourced examples into worker-specific models to fill missing annotations.

title: TLLC: Transfer Learning-based Label Completion for Crowdsourcing

abstract: Dataset Distillation (DD) compresses large datasets into smaller, synthetic subsets, enabling models trained on them to achieve performance comparable to those trained on the full data. However, these models remain vulnerable to adversarial attacks, limiting their use in safety-critical applications. While adversarial robustness has been extensively studied in related fields, research on improving DD robustness is still limited. To address this, we propose ROME, a novel method that enhances the adversarial RObustness of DD by leveraging the InforMation BottlenEck (IB) principle. ROME includes two components: a performance-aligned term to preserve accuracy and a robustness-aligned term to improve robustness by aligning feature distributions between synthetic and perturbed images. Furthermore, we introduce the Improved Robustness Ratio (I-RR), a refined metric to better evaluate DD robustness. Extensive experiments on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 demonstrate that ROME outperforms existing DD methods in adversarial robustness, achieving maximum I-RR improvements of nearly 40% under white-box attacks and nearly 35% under black-box attacks. Our code is available at https://github.com/zhouzhengqd/ROME.
